knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness converts normalized approximate normals into an exact limiting-normal balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated assumptions, there exist a subsequence \((k_j)\) and vectors \(x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), such that
\[
x_{i,k_j}^*\to x_i^*,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1.
\]
Thus the normalized approximate normal relations admit a nontrivial exact limiting-normal relation at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, normalized and asymptotically balanced nearby Fréchet normals have a subsequence converging to nonzero limiting normals at the reference point whose sum is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\).
For each \(k\), points \(x_{ik}\to\bar x\) and Fréchet normals \(x_{ik}^*\in\widehat N_{\Omega_i}(x_{ik})\) satisfy \(\sum_i\lVert x_{ik}^*\rVert=1\) and \(\lVert\sum_i x_{ik}^*\rVert\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After passage to a subsequence, \(x_{ik}^*\to x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\), \(\sum_i\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1\), and \(\sum_i x_i^*=0\).

children.title: Asplund-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Limiting and fuzzy generalized differentiation in Asplund spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund Banach space, and \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in\bigcap_i\Omega_i\).
The family is locally extremal at \(\bar x\): arbitrarily small translations make its members locally disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and \(x_i^*\in\widehat N_{\Omega_i}(x_i)\) with \(\sum_i\|x_i^*\|=1\) and \(\|\sum_i x_i^*\|<\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: open ball of radius epsilon about the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fuzzy Fréchet-normal extremal principle in an Asplund ambient space.

source_refs.locator: 2.2 Extremal Principle in Asplund Spaces p. 180
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), one can choose points \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and Fréchet normals \(x_i^*\in\widehat N_{\Omega_i}(x_i)\) such that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m\|x_i^*\|=1
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left\|\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*\right\|<\varepsilon.
\]
The points and normals may depend on \(\varepsilon\); the conclusion is therefore fuzzy rather than an exact Fréchet-normal relation at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local extremality in an Asplund space produces normalized Fréchet normals at nearby points whose sum is arbitrarily small.

children.title: General Banach-Space Regime
children.top_down_role: Approximate and axiomatic constructions beyond Asplund spaces.

assumptions_latex: Generalized differentiation is based on Fréchet or limiting constructions whose fuzzy calculus would require Asplund structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without additional geometry, one cannot assert the Asplund fuzzy sum rule or the corresponding Fréchet-normal extremal principle for all lower semicontinuous functions and closed sets in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of Fréchet and limiting calculus beyond Asplund spaces.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Versions of Extremal Principle in Banach Spaces p. 230
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a general Banach space, the Asplund-space conclusion
\[
x_i^*\in\widehat N_{\Omega_i}(x_i),\qquad
\sum_i\|x_i^*\|=1,
\qquad
\left\|\sum_i x_i^*\right\|<\varepsilon
\]
for every locally extremal finite family cannot be adopted without further assumptions. Applicable substitutes must use additional smoothness, an approximate or enlarged normal construction, or an axiomatic subdifferential possessing the required variational and sum-rule properties. Thus the ambient-space hypothesis is part of the calculus, not merely a technical convenience.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside Asplund spaces, the standard fuzzy Fréchet-normal calculus may fail; approximate, enlarged, smooth, or axiomatic substitutes require explicit additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: General Banach-Space Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Abstract extremal principle for a prenormal structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate prenormal separation and SNC-dependent limiting separation for an extremal system of two closed sets in a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\Omega_1,\Omega_2,\bar x\}\) be an extremal system of closed sets in a Banach space \(X\), and let \(\widehat{\mathcal N}\) define a prenormal structure on \(X\). Then: (i) for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap(\bar x+\varepsilon\mathbb B)\), \(i=1,2\), and \(x^*\in X^*\) with \(\|x^*\|=1\) such that \[x^*\in\bigl(\widehat{\mathcal N}(x_1;\Omega_1)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*\bigr)\cap\bigl(-\widehat{\mathcal N}(x_2;\Omega_2)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*\bigr).\] (ii) If one of \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) is \(\widehat{\mathcal N}\)-sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\), then there exists \(x^*\in\mathbb B^*\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[x^*\in\overline{\mathcal N}(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap\bigl(-\overline{\mathcal N}(\bar x;\Omega_2)\bigr),\] where \(\overline{\mathcal N}\) is the generated topological normal structure. If, in addition, \(\mathbb B^*\subset X^*\) is weak-star sequentially compact, then there exists \(x^*\in\mathbb B^*\setminus\{0\}\) such that \[x^*\in\mathcal N(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap\bigl(-\mathcal N(\bar x;\Omega_2)\bigr),\] where \(\mathcal N\) is the generated sequential normal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every two-set extremal system admits arbitrarily accurate nearby opposing prenormal certificates. If either set is sequentially normally compact, a nonzero opposing topological-normal certificate exists at the reference point; if the dual ball is also weak-star sequentially compact, a nonzero opposing sequential-normal certificate exists.
assumptions_latex: \widehat{\mathcal N}\text{ defines a prenormal structure on }X
\text{For the topological-normal conclusion, one of }\Omega_1,\Omega_2\text{ is }\widehat{\mathcal N}\text{-SNC at }\bar x
\text{For the sequential-normal conclusion, additionally }\mathbb B^*\subset X^*\text{ is weak* sequentially compact}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists x_1,x_2,x^*\text{ satisfying the approximate opposing-prenormal inclusion};\quad \widehat{\mathcal N}\text{-SNC of one set}\Longrightarrow\exists x^*\in\mathbb B^*\setminus\{0\}\text{ in the opposing topological normals};\quad \widehat{\mathcal N}\text{-SNC and weak* sequential compactness of }\mathbb B^*\Longrightarrow\exists x^*\in\mathbb B^*\setminus\{0\}\text{ in the opposing sequential normals}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon, approximate, and exact extremal principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines three balanced normal-certificate versions of the extremal principle, their space-wide validity, and the Banach-space implication from the approximate to the epsilon version.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extremal system \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n,\bar x\}: (i) the \varepsilon-extremal principle means that for every \varepsilon>0 there exist x_i\in\Omega_i\cap(\bar x+\varepsilon B) and x_i^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(x_i;\Omega_i) such that \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^*=0 and \sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i^*\|=1; (ii) the approximate extremal principle replaces these inclusions by x_i^*\in\widehat N(x_i;\Omega_i)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^* while retaining the same balance and normalization; (iii) the exact extremal principle requires x_i^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega_i) with the same balance and normalization. A version holds in X if it holds for every extremal system whose sets are locally closed around \bar x. If X is a Banach space, the approximate extremal principle implies the \varepsilon-extremal principle because \widehat N(x;\Omega)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*\subset\widehat N_\varepsilon(x;\Omega).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon and approximate principles use balanced, normalized nearby approximate-normal certificates, while the exact principle uses balanced, normalized basic normals at the reference point. Space-wide validity quantifies over locally closed extremal systems. In a Banach space, the approximate version implies the epsilon version.
assumptions_latex: \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n,\bar x\}\text{ is an extremal system in }X
\varepsilon>0\text{ in the epsilon and approximate versions}
\Omega_i\text{ are locally closed around }\bar x\text{ when validity in }X\text{ is asserted}
X\text{ is Banach for the implication from the approximate to the epsilon principle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^*=0,\quad\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i^*\|=1,\quad x_i^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(x_i;\Omega_i),\ \widehat N(x_i;\Omega_i)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*,\text{ or }N(\bar x;\Omega_i)\text{ according to the version}

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Extremal Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact limiting-normal extremal principle for a finite family in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist limiting normals \(x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\), for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), satisfying
\[
\sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sum_{i=1}^m\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1.
\]
Equivalently, local extremality admits a nontrivial exact normal certificate at the common reference point. The normalization excludes the zero family and may be replaced by any equivalent positive homogeneous normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally extremal finite family of Euclidean sets that are locally closed at the common point has nonzero limiting normals there that balance exactly to zero.
assumptions_latex: The family is locally extremal at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\), not all zero, such that \(\sum_i x_i^*=0\); they may be normalized by \(\sum_i\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1\).

children.title: Sequential Extremal Approximation
children.top_down_role: Links between approximate extremality and limiting normal constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Extremal Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential encoding of nearby-point and approximate-balance extremal conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose any sequence \((\varepsilon_k)\) with \(\varepsilon_k>0\) and \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and for each \(k\) apply the stated approximate extremal conclusion with tolerance \(\varepsilon_k\). The resulting points and normals can be denoted by \(x_{ik}\) and \(x_{ik}^*\) so that
\[
x_{ik}\to\bar x,
\qquad x_{ik}^*\in N^{\mathrm a}_{\Omega_i}(x_{ik}),
\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\lVert x_{ik}^*\rVert=1,
\qquad \left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^m x_{ik}^*\right\rVert\to0.
\]
This representation does not assert convergence of the individual dual vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying an approximate extremal conclusion along vanishing tolerances gives nearby points converging to the reference point and normalized admissible normals whose total imbalance converges to zero.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\), and \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\).

For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the applicable approximate extremal conclusion provides \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and \(x_i^*\in N^{\mathrm a}_{\Omega_i}(x_i)\) satisfying \(\sum_i\lVert x_i^*\rVert=1\) and \(\lVert\sum_i x_i^*\rVert<\varepsilon\).
The symbol \(N^{\mathrm a}\) denotes the fixed normal construction in that applicable conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every sequence \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), corresponding approximants can be selected with \(x_{ik}\to\bar x\) and \(\lVert\sum_i x_{ik}^*\rVert\to0\), while \(\sum_i\lVert x_{ik}^*\rVert=1\).

notation.meaning: the fixed normal construction used by the applicable approximate extremal conclusion
positive approximation tolerances converging to zero

children.title: Extremality of Set Systems
children.top_down_role: Local separation geometry for collections of sets.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\), and \(\bar x\in\bigcap_i\Omega_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system is locally extremal at \(\bar x\) exactly when arbitrarily small translations can destroy its intersection inside one fixed neighborhood of \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: translation of a set by minus a vector
a neighborhood of the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local translational extremality for a finite set system.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Extremal Principle in Variational Analysis p. 171
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite system \(\{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\}\) is locally extremal at \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and vectors \(a_{ik}\in X\) such that
\[
a_{ik}\to0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),
\qquad
\bigcap_{i=1}^m(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\cap U=\varnothing
\quad\text{for every }k.
\]
Thus one fixed localization is rendered infeasible by translations whose magnitudes vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set system is locally extremal when vanishing translations make all translated sets have empty intersection in a fixed neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremality of Set Systems

children.title: Subextremality of Set Systems
children.top_down_role: Quantitative weaker separation behavior of set collections.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\subset X\), and \(\bar x\in\Omega:=\bigcap_i\Omega_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linear subextremality holds when the distance to \(\Omega\) is locally bounded by a constant times the largest individual-set distance.

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear error-bound sense of subextremality for finite set systems.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The system \(\{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\}\) is linearly subextremal at \(\bar x\) if there exist constants \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
d\!\left(x,\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\right)
\le \kappa\max_{1\le i\le m}d(x,\Omega_i)
\quad\text{for every }x\in B_\delta(\bar x).
\]
This is a local metric error bound for the feasibility system; replacing the maximum by a finite sum changes only the admissible constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear subextremality is the local error bound controlling distance to the common intersection by the largest individual constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.title: Subextremality of Set Systems

source_witnesses.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

children.title: Extremality–Subextremality Gap
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating exact extremality from weaker metric behavior.

assumptions_latex: Set-system extremality is understood through local separation by vanishing translations.
Subextremality is understood as the local linear distance error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither property implies the other without additional hypotheses.

notation.meaning: the real line or Euclidean plane, as specified

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete independence examples for translational extremality and linear subextremality.

source_refs.locator: 5.4.1 Linear Subextremality of Set Systems p. 110
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X=\mathbb{R}\) and \(\Omega_1=\Omega_2=X\), the subextremality inequality holds trivially, but translations cannot make the intersection locally empty, so extremality fails. Conversely, in \(X=\mathbb{R}^2\), let
\[
\Omega_1=\{(s,t):t\ge s^2\},
\qquad
\Omega_2=\{(s,t):t\le0\}.
\]
Small vertical translations separate the sets locally, so they are extremal at \((0,0)\). Along \(x_s=(s,0)\), however, \(d(x_s,\Omega_1)=O(s^2)\) while \(d(x_s,\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2)=|s|\), so no linear subextremality constant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subextremality can hold without extremality for two full spaces, while tangentially meeting planar sets can be extremal without satisfying a linear error bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Extremality–Subextremality Gap

children.title: Ekeland Variational Principle
children.top_down_role: Metric perturbation foundation for approximate minimization.

assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete, and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar x\in X\) with \(d(\bar x,x_0)\le\lambda\), \(f(\bar x)\le f(x_0)\), and \(f(x)>f(\bar x)-(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,\bar x)\) for every \(x\ne\bar x\).

notation.meaning: effective domain of the extended-real-valued function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard complete-metric-space form with linear distance perturbation.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Ekeland Variational Principle p. 204
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists \(\bar x\in X\) such that
\[
f(\bar x)\le f(x_0),
\qquad d(\bar x,x_0)\le\lambda,
\]
and, for every \(x\in X\setminus\{\bar x\}\),
\[
f(x)>f(\bar x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, \(\bar x\) is the unique strict minimizer of \(x\mapsto f(x)+(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every approximate minimizer of a lower semicontinuous bounded-below function on a complete metric space yields a nearby strict minimizer after a small distance penalty.
knowledge_statements.title: Ekeland Variational Principle

children.title: Smooth Variational Principles
children.top_down_role: Smooth perturbation principles in favorable Banach spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space admitting a continuously Fréchet differentiable Lipschitz bump function.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist a bounded Lipschitz function \(g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) of class \(C^1\) and a point \(\bar x\in X\) such that
\[
\|g\|_\infty<\varepsilon,
\qquad

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Variational Principles and Smooth Structure of Banach Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concave-support and bump-function variants, including their converse smooth-geometry requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a Banach space, let $\mathcal A$ consist of all proper lower-semicontinuous bounded-below functions $\varphi:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}$, and fix $\varepsilon,\lambda>0$. (i) If $X$ admits a Fréchet smooth renorm, then for every $\varphi\in\mathcal A$ and $x_0$ with $\varphi(x_0)<\inf_X\varphi+\varepsilon$, there exist $ ar x$ and a concave Fréchet differentiable $s:X	o\mathbb R$ such that $\| ar x-x_0\|<\lambda$, $\varphi( ar x)<\inf_X\varphi+\varepsilon$, $\|
abla s( ar x)\|<\varepsilon/\lambda$, $\varphi( ar x)=s( ar x)$, and $\varphi(x)\geq s(x)+\|x- ar x\|^2$ for all $x$. (ii) If $X$ admits an $\mathcal S$-smooth bump function for $\mathcal S\in\{\mathcal F,\mathcal{LF},\mathcal{LC}^1\}$, then such a $ ar x$ exists together with an $\mathcal S$-smooth bump $b$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $\|
abla b( ar x)\|<\varepsilon/\lambda$, $\varphi( ar x)=b( ar x)+c$, and $\varphi(x)\geq b(x)+c$ for all $x$. Moreover, there are $\mathcal S$-smooth $s:X	o\mathbb R$ and $	heta:X	o[0,\infty)$ with $\|
abla s( ar x)\|<\varepsilon/\lambda$, $	heta(x)=0$ if and only if $x=0$, $	heta(x)\leq\|x\|^2$ for $x$ in the unit ball, $\varphi( ar x)=s( ar x)$, and $\varphi(x)\geq s(x)+	heta(x- ar x)$ for all $x$. (iii) Conversely, the concave $\mathcal F$-smooth variational principle can hold in $X$ only if $X$ admits a Fréchet smooth renorm, and the $\mathcal S$-smooth variational principle can hold only if $X$ admits a corresponding $\mathcal S$-smooth bump function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fréchet-smooth renorm or an appropriate smooth bump function yields smooth supporting perturbations at nearby strict approximate minimizers, with controlled derivative and prescribed growth. Conversely, the corresponding smooth variational principle requires the indicated smooth renorm or bump function.
assumptions_latex: \varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is proper, l.s.c., and bounded below}
\text{For (ii), }X\text{ admits an }\mathcal S\text{-smooth bump function, }\mathcal S\in\{\mathcal F,\mathcal{LF},\mathcal{LC}^1\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The corresponding smooth supporting perturbations exist at a nearby }\bar x\text{ with derivative norm }<\varepsilon/\lambda;\text{ conversely, each principle requires the stated smooth renorm or bump-function property.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke mean-value theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nonsmooth mean-value principle for a locally Lipschitz scalar function along a line segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n with x\ne y, and let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be locally Lipschitz on an open set U with [x,y]\subset U. Then there exist z\in(x,y) and v\in\partial_C f(z) such that f(y)-f(x)=v^T(y-x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is locally Lipschitz on an open set containing the segment between distinct points x and y, then at some interior point z a Clarke subgradient realizes the difference f(y) minus f(x) along y minus x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists z\in(x,y),\ \exists v\in\partial_C f(z):\ f(y)-f(x)=v^T(y-x)

children.title: Gradient-Generation Principle
children.top_down_role: Generation of generalized gradients from nearby classical gradients.

assumptions_latex: \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open, \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz, \(x\in U\), and \(D_f\) is the differentiability set of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(x)\).

notation.meaning: limits of gradients at differentiability points approaching x
Clarke subdifferential of f at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke subgradient generation by limiting classical gradients in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[G_f(x):=\left\{p\in\mathbb R^n:\exists x_k\in D_f,\ x_k\to x,\ \nabla f(x_k)\to p\right\}.\] Then the Clarke subdifferential is generated by reachable gradients: \[\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(x).\] In finite dimensions, local Lipschitz continuity makes the nearby gradients locally bounded, and the right-hand side is a nonempty compact convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At any base point in the open domain, the Clarke subdifferential is the closed convex hull of all limits of classical gradients at differentiability points approaching that base point.
knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Generation Principle

children.title: Nearby Smooth-Point Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Reconstruction regimes based on differentiability points approaching a reference point.

assumptions_latex: \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open, \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz, \(x\in U\), and \(D_f\) is the differentiability set of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(p\in G_f(x)\) is realized as \(p=\lim_k\nabla f(x_k)\) for some \(x_k\in D_f\) with \(x_k\to x\).

notation.meaning: set of gradients reachable from nearby differentiability points
set where f is classically differentiable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential reconstruction from nearby differentiability points.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x\in U\), define the reachable-gradient set by \[G_f(x):=\bigcap_{r>0}\operatorname{cl}\{\nabla f(y):y\in D_f\cap B_r(x)\}.\] Equivalently, \(p\in G_f(x)\) exactly when there is a sequence \(x_k\in D_f\) such that \(x_k\to x\) and \(\nabla f(x_k)\to p\). Thus limiting first-order information at a nonsmooth point is reconstructed from classical gradients at arbitrarily nearby differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a specified base point in the open domain, a reachable gradient is exactly a limit of gradients evaluated at differentiability points converging to that base point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional, upper Dini, and Clarke directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definitions and comparisons of one-sided directional models, directional differentiability, and Clarke regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be real-valued and defined on a neighborhood of $x$ in a normed space $X$, and let $d\in X$. When the limit exists, the directional derivative is $f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}$. The upper Dini directional derivative is $f^{(D)}(x;d):=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}$. If $f$ is Lipschitz near $x$, its Clarke generalized directional derivative is $f^\circ(x;d):=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(y+td)-f(y)}{t}$. Under this Lipschitz hypothesis, the upper Dini and Clarke derivatives are finite and satisfy $f^{(D)}(x;d)\leq f^\circ(x;d)$. If $f'(x;d)$ exists, then $f'(x;d)=f^{(D)}(x;d)$. The function is directionally differentiable at $x$ if $f'(x;d)$ exists for every $d\in X$. It is Clarke regular at $x$ if it is directionally differentiable there and $f'(x;d)=f^\circ(x;d)$ for every $d\in X$; it is regular if it is regular at every point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ordinary directional derivative uses a one-sided limit. The upper Dini derivative uses a limsup, while the Clarke derivative additionally permits perturbations of the base point. For locally Lipschitz functions the upper Dini derivative does not exceed the Clarke derivative. Clarke regularity means that all directional derivatives exist and agree with their Clarke counterparts.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is real-valued and defined on a neighborhood of }x
f\text{ is Lipschitz near }x\text{ for the Clarke derivative, finiteness, comparison, and regularity statements}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{(D)}(x;d)\leq f^\circ(x;d),\qquad f'(x;d)\text{ exists}\Longrightarrow f'(x;d)=f^{(D)}(x;d),\qquad f\text{ is Clarke regular at }x\iff\forall d\in X,\ f'(x;d)\text{ exists and }f'(x;d)=f^\circ(x;d)

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lower and upper Dini directional derivatives are fixed-direction one-sided difference-quotient limits.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower and upper Dini directional derivatives of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(v\) are \[d_D^-f(x;v):=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}{t},\qquad d_D^+f(x;v):=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}{t}.\] They take values in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\). If the two values coincide, their common value is the one-sided directional derivative \(f'(x;v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dini models use lower and upper one-sided limits of the difference quotient while keeping the direction fixed.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Radial differentiability in direction \(v\) means that the fixed-ray quotient has a limit in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\).

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is radially directionally differentiable at \(x\) in direction \(v\) when the limit \[f^r(x;v):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+tv)-f(x)}{t}\] exists in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\). This model examines only points on the ray \(x+\mathbb R_+v\); it imposes no stability with respect to perturbations of \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radial derivative is the one-sided difference-quotient limit taken strictly along the ray generated by the chosen direction.

children.title: Dini–Radial Comparison
children.top_down_role: Agreement and separation regimes for Dini versus radial information.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space, \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The radial derivative exists exactly when \(d_D^-f(x;v)=d_D^+f(x;v)\), and then all three values coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under the fixed-ray convention for radial differentiation.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed-ray quotient \(q(t):=[f(x+tv)-f(x)]/t\), one always has \[d_D^-f(x;v)\leq d_D^+f(x;v).\] The radial derivative \(f^r(x;v)\) exists in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\) if and only if \[d_D^-f(x;v)=d_D^+f(x;v).\] In that case, \[f^r(x;v)=d_D^-f(x;v)=d_D^+f(x;v).\] Equality concerns a fixed direction and does not by itself imply Hadamard directional stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The radial derivative exists precisely when the lower and upper fixed-direction Dini derivatives agree; their common value is the radial derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Dini–Radial Comparison

children.title: Hadamard Directional Models
children.top_down_role: Directionally stable models allowing perturbed directions.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are normed spaces, \(U\subset X\) is open, \(F:U\to Y\), \(x\in U\), and \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hadamard directional differentiability requires a common quotient limit for every \(t\downarrow0\) and \(v'\to v\).

notation.meaning: Hadamard directional derivative of F at x in direction v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong one-sided directional derivative with perturbed directions.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Hadamard directionally differentiable at \(x\) in direction \(v\) if there exists \(F'_H(x;v)\in Y\) such that \[F'_H(x;v)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\v'\to v}}\frac{F(x+tv')-F(x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, every pair of sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(v_k\to v\), with \(x+t_kv_k\in U\), yields the same limit. If the derivative exists in direction \(v\), then for every \(\alpha>0\) it exists in direction \(\alpha v\) and satisfies \[F'_H(x;\alpha v)=\alpha F'_H(x;v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hadamard derivative is a directional difference-quotient limit stable under simultaneous small perturbations of the positive step and the direction; its values scale positively with the direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Directional Models

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are normed spaces, \(F:X\to Y\), \(x\in X\), and \(h\in X\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand semidifferentiable at \(x\) in direction \(h\) if a vector \(F'_B(x;h)\in Y\) exists such that \[F'_B(x;h)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}\frac{F(x+th')-F(x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, \[F(x+th')=F(x)+tF'_B(x;h)+r(t,h'),\qquad \frac{\|r(t,h')\|}{t}\to0\] as \(t\downarrow0\) and \(h'\to h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand semidifferentiability in a specified direction requires all nearby-direction difference quotients to converge to one first-order vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the Clarke generalized directional model is \[f^{\circ}(\bar x;d):=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.\] It is finite, positively homogeneous, and subadditive in \(d\). Defining \(\partial_C f(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq f^{\circ}(\bar x;d)\text{ for all }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\), one has \[f^{\circ}(\bar x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial_C f(\bar x)}\langle v,d\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke model convexifies nearby upper directional quotients and equals the support function of the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Generalized Directional Models

children.title: Regular Subderivative Models
children.top_down_role: Epigraphically stable first-order subderivative constructions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d f(\bar x)(w)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,w'\to w}[f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)]/t\).

notation.meaning: lower Hadamard, or epigraphically regularized, subderivative

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower epigraphically stable first-order subderivative; terminology varies across references.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The regular lower subderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is the extended-real quantity \[d f(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\ w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, its epigraph is the outer limit of the epigraphs of the first-order difference quotients \(w\mapsto [f(\bar x+t w)-f(\bar x)]/t\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Thus perturbations of both step size and direction are included in the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular lower subderivative is the lower limit of first-order quotients under simultaneous perturbation of step and direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Subderivative Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz continuity upgrades directional differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An implication from fixed-direction differentiability to Hadamard directional differentiability, with preservation of the local Lipschitz modulus in the direction variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $g:X\to Y$ is directionally differentiable at $x$ and is Lipschitz continuous with modulus $c$ on a neighborhood of $x$. Then $g$ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at $x$, and $$\|g'(x,h_1)-g'(x,h_2)\|\le c\|h_1-h_2\|\qquad\forall h_1,h_2\in X.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a mapping is directionally differentiable at x and locally Lipschitz near x with modulus c, it is Hadamard directionally differentiable there, and its directional derivative is Lipschitz in the direction variable with the same modulus.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\in X\) if, for every \(d\in X\), there exists an element \(F'(\bar x;d)\in Y\) such that \[F'(\bar x;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{F(\bar x+t d)-F(\bar x)}{t}.\] The direction \(d\) remains fixed in this limit. The resulting map \(d\mapsto F'(\bar x;d)\) is positively homogeneous whenever it is defined in all directions, but linearity is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional differentiability requires a one-sided derivative along every fixed direction, without requiring the derivative map to be linear.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite One-Sided Directional Derivative in a Fixed Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition requiring a fixed nonzero direction and a finite right-hand difference-quotient limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}\). The function \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) in direction \(p\) if the finite limit \[f'(x;p)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha p)-f(x)}{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}\] exists. This value is the directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional differentiability at a domain point along a fixed nonzero direction means that the forward difference quotient has a finite real limit as the positive step tends to zero. That limit is the directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is differentiable at }x\text{ in direction }p\iff \exists f'(x;p)\in\mathbb{R}:\ f'(x;p)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha p)-f(x)}{\alpha}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the directional derivative along a fixed nonzero direction and records the negative-derivative descent implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(v\ne0\), whenever the limit exists, the directional derivative is \[f'(x;v):=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha v)-f(x)}{\alpha}.\] If \(f'(x;v)<0\), then \(v\) is a descent direction at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the one-sided rate of change along a fixed nonzero direction. If it is negative, the direction gives descent for sufficiently small positive steps.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative and one-sided derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-direction derivatives of a proper extended-real-valued function, conditioned on existence of the indicated extended-real limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(y\in\mathcal H\). Provided the limit exists in \([ -\infty,+\infty]\), \[f'(x;y)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha}.\] If \(\mathcal H=\mathbb R\), then, whenever the respective limits exist, \[f'_+(x)=f'(x;1)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha)-f(x)}{\alpha}\] and \[f'_-(x)=-f'(x;-1)=\lim_{\alpha\uparrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha)-f(x)}{\alpha}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional derivative is the right-hand difference-quotient limit along a fixed direction, when that limit exists in the extended reals. In one dimension, directions 1 and −1 give the right and left derivatives with the stated sign convention.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each derivative is defined only when its indicated extended-real limit exists}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;y)=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+\alpha y)-f(x)}{\alpha},\qquad \mathcal H=\mathbb R\Rightarrow\left\{\begin{aligned}f'_+(x)&=f'(x;1),\\f'_-(x)&=-f'(x;-1).\end{aligned}\right.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Hadamard directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\in X\) if, for every \(d\in X\), there exists \(F'_H(\bar x;d)\in Y\) such that \[F'_H(\bar x;d)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\ d'\to d}}\frac{F(\bar x+t d')-F(\bar x)}{t}.\] Equivalently, the displayed quotient converges to the same value along every pair of sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(d_k\to d\). This stability under directional perturbations distinguishes it from ordinary directional differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hadamard differentiability requires directional quotients to converge even when the direction varies toward the target direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Differentiability

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient characterizations of strict Hadamard differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between strict Hadamard differentiability and singleton limiting-subgradient behavior under local Lipschitz continuity in an Asplund space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be finite at \(\bar x\), and let \(\xi\in X^*\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(\varphi\) is Lipschitz continuous around \(\bar x\), and for every sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\) and every choice \(x_k^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k)\), one has \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}\xi\); (b) \(\varphi\) is Lipschitz continuous around \(\bar x\) and \(\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\{\xi\}\); and (c) \(\varphi\) is strictly Hadamard differentiable at \(\bar x\) with \(\nabla\varphi(\bar x)=\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function finite at a reference point in an Asplund space, strict Hadamard differentiability with derivative ξ is equivalent to local Lipschitz continuity together with either weak-star convergence of every nearby Fréchet-subgradient selection to ξ or a singleton limiting subdifferential at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [(\(\varphi\) is locally Lipschitz and every \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(x_k^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k)\) satisfies \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}\xi\))]\(\Longleftrightarrow\)[\(\varphi\) is locally Lipschitz and \(\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\{\xi\}\)]\(\Longleftrightarrow\)[\(\varphi\) is strictly Hadamard differentiable at \(\bar x\) with \(\nabla\varphi(\bar x)=\xi\)].

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(\bar x\) if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(B:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \[F(\bar x+h)=F(\bar x)+B(h)+r(h),\qquad \lim_{h\to0,\,h\neq0}\frac{\lVert r(h)\rVert}{\lVert h\rVert}=0.\] The map \(B\) is the Bouligand derivative. It need not be linear; when directional derivatives exist, the approximation forces \(B(d)=F'(\bar x;d)\) for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability provides a uniform first-order approximation by a continuous positively homogeneous, possibly nonlinear, derivative map.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert F(x)-F(\bar x)\rVert\leq\kappa\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\) locally at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-valued pointwise calmness; set-valued calmness requires a different graph-based formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is calm at \(\bar x\in X\) if there exist constants \(\kappa\geq0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \[\lVert F(x)-F(\bar x)\rVert\leq\kappa\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\qquad\text{whenever }\lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\delta.\] Unlike local Lipschitz continuity, this estimate compares nearby values only with the fixed reference value \(F(\bar x)\), not with each other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness bounds change from one fixed base value linearly in the distance from the base point.

children.title: Directional Lipschitz Behavior
children.top_down_role: Lipschitz growth restricted to selected directional regions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is Lipschitz on a sufficiently small conical neighborhood of direction \(d\) from \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: truncated conical neighborhood based at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise Lipschitz behavior on a truncated cone around one nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon,[39mdelta>0\), set \[C(\bar x,d;\varepsilon,\delta):=\{\bar x+t w:0\leq t<\delta,\ \lVert w-d\rVert<\varepsilon\}.\] The function \(f\) has directional Lipschitz behavior at \(\bar x\) along \(d\) if there exist \(L,[39mepsilon,\delta>0\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\lVert x-y\rVert\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C(\bar x,d;\varepsilon,\delta).\] This is a pairwise estimate restricted to a directional neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional Lipschitz behavior is ordinary pairwise Lipschitz continuity restricted to a small cone around a chosen direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Lipschitz Behavior

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied for this particular cone-based meaning of directional Lipschitz behavior, so its neighborhood geometry and pairwise estimate cannot be validated against the intended terminology. The statement also contains stray `[39m` control-text fragments. A sourced formulation is required before a reliable replacement can be made.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Lipschitzness for an extended-real-valued function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional growth regularity at a point where the function is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(v\in X\), define
\[
f^+(x;v):=\limsup_{\substack{(y,\alpha)\downarrow_f x,\ w\to v\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(y+tw)-\alpha}{t}.
\]
Assuming \(f(x)\) is finite, \(f\) is directionally Lipschitz at \(x\) with respect to \(v\) when \(f^+(x;v)\neq+\infty\). It is directionally Lipschitz at \(x\) when this holds for at least one \(v\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite point x, f is directionally Lipschitz with respect to v when its epigraphically perturbed upper directional growth is not plus infinity. Directional Lipschitzness at x requires at least one such direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is directionally Lipschitz at }x\iff\exists v\in X:\ f^+(x;v)\neq+\infty

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is calm at \(0\) but is not directionally Lipschitz there along \(d=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of pointwise calmness from pairwise directional Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \(|f(x)-f(0)|\leq |x|^2\), so on \(|x|<1\) one has \(|f(x)-f(0)|\leq|x|\); hence \(f\) is calm at \(0\). For \(x\neq0\), \[f'(x)=2x\sin(x^{-2})-2x^{-1}\cos(x^{-2}),\] which is unbounded on every interval \((0,\delta)\). Consequently, \(f\) cannot be Lipschitz on any truncated cone around the positive direction \(d=1\). Thus calmness does not imply directional Lipschitz behavior.

children.title: Limiting Slopes
children.top_down_role: Sequential closures of local slope information.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{|\partial f|}(x)=\liminf_{y\to x,\,f(y)\to f(x)}|\partial f|(y)\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuous relaxation of the local slope along graph-convergent points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Given the local slope \(|\partial f|\), its limiting slope at \(x\) is \(\overline{|\partial f|}(x):=\liminf_{y\to x,\,f(y)\to f(x)}|\partial f|(y)\). Equivalently, the limit inferior is taken over all sequences \(y_n\to x\) satisfying \(f(y_n)\to f(x)\); the constant sequence is permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting slope is the lower relaxation of the local slope along points converging both spatially and in function value.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Slopes

children.title: Asymptotic Slopes
children.top_down_role: Slope behavior along escaping or degenerating sequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{|\partial f|}^{>}(x)=\liminf_{y\to x,\,f(x)<f(y)\to f(x)}|\partial f|(y)\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict outer relaxation of the local slope near a reference level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The asymptotic, or strict outer, slope at \(x\) is \(\overline{|\partial f|}^{>}(x):=\liminf_{y\to x,\,f(x)<f(y)\to f(x)}|\partial f|(y)\), with value \(+\infty\) if no such approaching points exist. Thus only points lying strictly above the reference level participate in the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymptotic slope relaxes local slopes along nearby points whose values decrease to the reference value strictly from above.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Slopes

children.title: Limiting–Asymptotic Slope Separation
children.top_down_role: Nonregular regimes where sequential and asymptotic slope information diverge.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{|\partial f|}(x)\le\overline{|\partial f|}^{>}(x)\), with strict inequality possible
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison and strict separation for limiting versus strict outer slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the preceding definitions, \(\overline{|\partial f|}(x)\le \overline{|\partial f|}^{>}(x)\) because the asymptotic relaxation uses a smaller class of approaching points. Equality need not hold. For \(f(t)=|t|\) on \(\mathbb R\) at \(x=0\), one has \(|\partial f|(0)=0\) and \(|\partial f|(t)=1\) for \(t\ne0\). Consequently, \(\overline{|\partial f|}(0)=0\), whereas \(\overline{|\partial f|}^{>}(0)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting slope never exceeds the strict outer slope, and the absolute-value function separates them at its minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting–Asymptotic Slope Separation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the descending local slope satisfies \(|\partial f|(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x)):=\inf\{\|v\|:v\in\partial f(x)\}\), where the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). Hence vanishing slope is equivalent to \(0\in\partial f(x)\) and therefore to global minimality of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space, the local slope equals the distance from zero to its convex subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, and let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be convex. For every \(x\in U\) and \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), the one-sided directional derivative exists and obeys \(f'(x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}(f(x+td)-f(x))/t=\max_{g\in\partial f(x)}\langle g,d\rangle\). Thus the directional derivative is precisely the support function of the nonempty compact convex subdifferential \(\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point of a finite convex function, every directional derivative is the support value of its convex subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative as the Support Function of the Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex directional calculus at an interior point of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex and let $x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)$. Define $f'(x_0;p):=\lim_{\alpha\downarrow0}\frac{f(x_0+\alpha p)-f(x_0)}{\alpha}$. Then $p\mapsto f'(x_0;p)$ is finite and convex on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $\partial_2f'(x_0;0)=\partial f(x_0)$, and $f'(x_0;p)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x_0)}\langle g,p\rangle$ for every $p\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior point of the domain of a proper convex function, the directional derivative is a finite convex function of the direction. Its subdifferential at the zero direction equals the original subdifferential, and each directional derivative is the support value of that subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x_0;\cdot)\text{ is finite and convex},\quad \partial_2f'(x_0;0)=\partial f(x_0),\quad f'(x_0;p)=\max_{g\in\partial f(x_0)}\langle g,p\rangle\quad\forall p\in\mathbb{R}^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Representation of the Convex Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes the general closure formula from the relative-interior regime where no closure is needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and convex. If \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\), then \((\operatorname{cl}f')(x;\cdot)\) is the support function of \(\partial f(x)\). If \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), then \(f'(x;\cdot)\) is closed and is itself the support function of \(\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the convex subdifferential is nonempty, the closure of the directional-derivative function is its support function. At relative-interior domain points, the directional derivative is already closed and directly equals that support function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow(\operatorname{cl}f')(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d);\qquad x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Rightarrow f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial f(x)}(d)\quad(\forall d).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Convex Lipschitz Optimality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the stated minimizer, generalized-subgradient, and directional-derivative equivalences. The closing announcement of a subsequent strong-minimum theorem and the unsupported aside about convex functions being Lipschitz are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Let }f:X\to\mathbb{R}\text{ be convex and Lipschitz. Then }x^*\text{ is a local minimizer of }f\Longleftrightarrow 0\in\partial f(x^*)\Longleftrightarrow f^o(x^*;d)\geq 0\ \forall d\in X.\text{ Moreover, }f^o(x;d)=f'(x;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex Lipschitz function, x* is a local minimizer exactly when zero belongs to its generalized subdifferential, equivalently when its generalized directional derivative is nonnegative in every direction. In this regime the generalized directional derivative equals the ordinary one-sided directional derivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) given by \(f(t)=-|t|\), the ordinary one-sided directional derivative at \(0\) exists in every direction and equals \(f'(0;d)=-|d|\). However, \(\partial_C f(0)=[-1,1]\), so its support function is \(\max_{g\in[-1,1]}gd=|d|=f^\circ(0;d)\). Hence, for every \(d\ne0\), \(f'(0;d)<f^\circ(0;d)\); Clarke convexification loses the descending directional sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the negative absolute-value function, ordinary directional derivatives are negative while Clarke support values are positive in every nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonregular Directional–Dual Gaps

notation.meaning: one-sided directional derivative at zero in direction one

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A locally Lipschitz function whose ordinary directional quotient oscillates.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(t)=t\sin(\log(1/|t|))\) for \(t\ne0\). This function is locally Lipschitz near \(0\). In direction \(d=1\), its difference quotient is \((f(0+s)-f(0))/s=\sin(\log(1/s))\) for \(s>0\). The quotient has subsequences converging to \(1\) and \(-1\), so the ordinary directional derivative \(f'(0;1)\) does not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz continuity does not ensure an ordinary directional derivative: an oscillatory Lipschitz function has no derivative at zero in direction one.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be defined by \(f(t)=\sqrt t\) for \(t\ge0\) and \(f(t)=+\infty\) for \(t<0\). At \(x=0\) in direction \(d=1\), \((f(0+sd)-f(0))/s=1/\sqrt s\) for \(s>0\). Therefore the extended directional limit exists but equals \(+\infty\), showing that finiteness fails without a local linear growth bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square-root function has an extended directional derivative of positive infinity at zero, because its growth is not locally linear.

children.title: Finite-Limit Failure Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\) with constant \(L\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)\text{ exists}\implies |f'(x;d)|\le L\|d\|\), but existence need not follow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and finiteness require distinct regularity controls.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(x\in U\), and let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz near \(x\) with constant \(L\). For every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), each sufficiently small \(t>0\) satisfies \(|(f(x+td)-f(x))/t|\le L\|d\|\). Thus any existing ordinary directional derivative is finite, but local Lipschitz continuity alone does not ensure that the limit exists. Directional differentiability supplies existence; a local Lipschitz bound supplies finiteness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz continuity bounds directional quotients and guarantees finiteness only when their limit exists; directional differentiability is a separate requirement.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Limit Failure Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) given by \(f(t)=|t|\) and fixed direction \(d=1\), the one-sided directional derivative satisfies \(f'(0;1)=1\). If \(x_k=-1/k\), then \(x_k\to0\), while \(f'(x_k;1)=-1\) for every \(k\). Consequently, \(x\mapsto f'(x;1)\) is not continuous at \(0\), despite \(f\) being convex and globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for absolute value, the directional derivative in a fixed direction jumps when negative base points approach the kink.

knowledge_statements.title: Direction Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional directional derivatives; instability is discontinuity in the direction argument at a fixed base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Direction instability occurs at \((x,d)\) when \(f'(x;d)\) exists and there is a sequence \(d_k\to d\) such that every \(f'(x;d_k)\) exists but \(f'(x;d_k)\not\to f'(x;d)\). Equivalently, the mapping \(v\mapsto f'(x;v)\), restricted to the directions where the derivative exists and is finite, is not continuous at \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direction instability means that directional derivatives along directions converging to a fixed direction fail to converge to the derivative in that limiting direction.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space, \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and the finite one-sided directional derivative \(f'(x;d)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of directional derivatives does not by itself imply continuity with respect to the direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Joint perturbation instability occurs at \((x,d)\) if there are sequences \(x_k\to x\) and \(d_k\to d\) for which \(f'(x_k;d_k)\) and \(f'(x;d)\) are finite, yet \(f'(x_k;d_k)\not\to f'(x;d)\). Equivalently, the mapping \((y,v)\mapsto f'(y;v)\), restricted to its finite-valued domain, is not continuous at \((x,d)\). The failure may persist even when the maps \(y\mapsto f'(y;d)\) and \(v\mapsto f'(x;v)\) are separately continuous, because separate continuity does not imply joint continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint instability occurs when simultaneous perturbations of the base point and direction produce derivative values that do not converge correctly.

children.title: Information Loss under Convexification
children.top_down_role: Erasure of nonconvex directional structure.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty, nonconvex set of directional data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(D\) by its closed convex hull can erase nonconvex directional distinctions.

notation.meaning: support function of a set E

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexification preserves linear support values but can destroy attainable-direction information.

source_refs.locator: D. Cones and Convex Sets p. 118

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexification is information-losing whenever \(D\ne\overline{\operatorname{co}}D\): points of \(\overline{\operatorname{co}}D\setminus D\) become indistinguishable from genuine directions after replacement. For example, if \(D=\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\), then \((1/2,1/2)\in\operatorname{co}D\) although \((1/2,1/2)\notin D\). Nevertheless, every linear probe is preserved in the sense that \(\sigma_D(z)=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{co}}D}(z)\) for all \(z\in\mathbb R^n\). Hence support-function or polar data cannot reconstruct the original nonconvex directional set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexification adds averaged directions and preserves all linear support values, so support or polar data cannot recover the original nonconvex directional structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Information Loss under Convexification

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The contingent tangent cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is \[T_C(x):=\left\{v\in X:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ \exists\,x_k\in C,\ x_k\to x,\ \frac{x_k-x}{t_k}\to v\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(v\in T_C(x)\) if and only if \(\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{dist}(v,(C-x)/t)=0\). The set \(T_C(x)\) is closed and positively homogeneous, but it need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is contingent tangent when some sequence of feasible points approaches the base point with that vector as its rescaled limiting velocity.
knowledge_statements.title: Contingent Tangent Cones

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance-derivative representations of contingent and convex tangent cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the contingent cone through the lower Dini derivative and records the convex-set representation and Clarke comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For x\in S\subset\mathbf E, K_S(x)=\{h\in\mathbf E:d_S^{-}(x;h)=0\}. This is a closed cone, may be nonconvex, and contains the Clarke tangent cone T_S^{\mathrm C}(x). If S is convex, then \{h\in\mathbf E:d_S'(x;h)=0\} is the closed convex tangent cone and coincides with T_S^{\mathrm C}(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero directions of the lower Dini derivative of the distance function form the contingent cone, which is closed, may be nonconvex, and contains the Clarke tangent cone. For a convex set, the zero directions of the ordinary directional derivative form the closed convex tangent cone and agree with the Clarke cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K_S(x)=\{h:d_S^{-}(x;h)=0\},\quad T_S^{\mathrm C}(x)\subseteq K_S(x);\qquad S\text{ convex}\Rightarrow \{h:d_S'(x;h)=0\}=T_S^{\mathrm C}(x)\text{ is a closed convex cone}.

children.title: Adjacent Tangent Cones
children.top_down_role: Tangent approximations based on prescribed approach sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a subset of a finite-dimensional normed space \(X\), and \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adjacent cone requires approximation along every sufficiently small scale, not merely along a selected sequence.

notation.meaning: adjacent tangent cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacent cone is taken as the lower Painlevé–Kuratowski limit of scaled feasible sets.

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The adjacent tangent cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is \[T_C^{\mathrm a}(x):=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-x}{t}=\left\{v\in X:\lim_{t\downarrow0}\operatorname{dist}\!\left(v,\frac{C-x}{t}\right)=0\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(v\in T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\) precisely when, for every sequence \(t_k\downarrow0\), there are \(x_k\in C\) such that \((x_k-x)/t_k\to v\). Consequently \(T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\subset T_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjacent tangent direction must be approximable by feasible displacements along every sequence of positive scales tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjacent Tangent Cones

children.title: Inner Tangent Cones
children.top_down_role: Tangent directions stable across nearby approach scales.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a subset of a finite-dimensional normed space \(X\), and \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inner tangent cone records directions whose nearby rays remain inside the set for all sufficiently small steps.

notation.meaning: radial inner tangent cone to C at x under the stated convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the radial eventual-feasibility convention; literature uses “inner tangent” for several inequivalent cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the radial eventual-feasibility convention, the inner tangent cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is \[T_C^{\mathrm i}(x):=\left\{v\in X:\exists\,\varepsilon>0\ \text{such that}\ x+t v\in C\ \text{for every}\ t\in[0,\varepsilon]\right\}.\] It is positively homogeneous and satisfies \(T_C^{\mathrm i}(x)\subset T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\subset T_C(x)\). The first inclusion can be strict because adjacent tangency permits scale-dependent corrections to the direction, whereas radial inner tangency requires the unperturbed ray itself to remain feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the radial convention, an inner tangent direction keeps the exact short ray from the base point feasible, a stronger requirement than adjacent tangency.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner Tangent Cones

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The radial eventual-feasibility formula and its inclusions are mathematically coherent, but “inner tangent cone” has multiple inequivalent conventions and no source is supplied to establish that this is the intended local convention.

children.title: Adjacent–Inner Tangent Gap
children.top_down_role: Set geometries where adjacent and inner approximations fail to coincide.

assumptions_latex: Adjacent and inner tangent cones are interpreted by the conventions stated in their corresponding records.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scale-dependent feasible corrections can make the adjacent cone strictly larger than the radial inner cone.

notation.meaning: adjacent and radial inner tangent cones

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete strict gap under the radial eventual-feasibility definition of inner tangency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{epi}g\subset\mathbb R^2\), where \(g(s)=s^2\), and let \(x=(0,0)\). For \(v=(1,0)\) and every \(t>0\), the point \((t,t^2)\in C\) satisfies \((t,t^2)/t=(1,t)\to(1,0)\); hence \(v\in T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\). But \(x+t v=(t,0)\notin C\) for every \(t>0\), so \(v\notin T_C^{\mathrm i}(x)\). Therefore \(T_C^{\mathrm i}(x)\subsetneq T_C^{\mathrm a}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the parabola epigraph at its vertex, the horizontal direction is adjacent tangent but its exact ray is never feasible, creating a strict gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjacent–Inner Tangent Gap

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parabola-epigraph example correctly yields a strict gap under the stated radial inner-cone convention, and counterexample is the appropriate kind. A source is nevertheless required because the claim depends on the presently unsupported convention.

children.top_down_role: Robust convex tangent geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a closed subset of a finite-dimensional normed space \(X\), and \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Clarke tangent cone consists of directions feasible robustly under simultaneous perturbations of the base point and scale.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Clarke tangent cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is the set of all \(v\in X\) such that, whenever \(x_k\in C\), \(x_k\to x\), and \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(v_k\to v\) with \(x_k+t_kv_k\in C\) for every \(k\). Equivalently, \[T_C^{\mathrm C}(x)=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{\substack{y\to x,\ y\in C\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{C-y}{t}.\] This cone is closed and convex, and \(T_C^{\mathrm C}(x)\subset T_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Clarke tangent direction remains approximately feasible for every nearby feasible base point and every vanishing sequence of step sizes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke tangent cone and its necessary optimality condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the cone through the Clarke derivative of the distance function, records its geometry, and conditionally states the associated first-order necessary condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For x\in S\subset\mathbf E, define T_S(x)=\{h\in\mathbf E:d_S^{\circ}(x;h)=0\}. Because d_S^{\circ}(x;\cdot) is finite, nonnegative, and sublinear, T_S(x) is a closed convex cone. If, additionally, f is locally Lipschitz near x and x is a local minimizer of f on S, then for every sufficiently large L\ge0 and every h\in\mathbf E, 0\le (f+Ld_S)^{\circ}(x;h)\le f^{\circ}(x;h)+L d_S^{\circ}(x;h); consequently, h\in T_S(x) implies f^{\circ}(x;h)\ge0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke tangent cone is the set of directions where the Clarke derivative of the distance function vanishes, and it is a closed convex cone. For a locally Lipschitz objective at a constrained local minimum, its Clarke directional derivative is nonnegative in every Clarke tangent direction.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the optimality conclusion, }f:\mathbf E\to\mathbf R\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }x
\text{For the optimality conclusion, }x\text{ is a local minimizer of }f\text{ on }S
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S(x)=\{h:d_S^{\circ}(x;h)=0\}\text{ is a closed convex cone};\qquad h\in T_S(x)\Rightarrow f^{\circ}(x;h)\ge0\text{ under the stated optimality assumptions}.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearization Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abadie-type exactness for smooth finite-dimensional equality-and-inequality constraint systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Linearization is exact at \(\bar x\) when \[T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x).\] For a differentiable equality-and-inequality constraint system, one always has \(T_C(\bar x)\subset L_C(\bar x)\). Consequently, exactness is equivalent to the reverse inclusion \(L_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\); this equality is Abadie’s constraint qualification at \(\bar x\). Any stronger constraint qualification known to imply Abadie’s condition therefore guarantees linearization exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearization is exact when every direction satisfying the first-order constraint system is a contingent tangent direction, so the tangent and linearized cones coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ h_j(x)=0,\ j=1,\ldots,p\}\), the constraint functions are differentiable at \(\bar x\in C\), and \(L_C(\bar x)\) is the corresponding linearized cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Linearization is exact at \(\bar x\) if and only if \(T_C(\bar x)=L_C(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand Tangent, Regular Normal, and Limiting Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional tangent and normal-cone definitions, with the convex-set specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and \(\bar z\in\Omega\), \(T_\Omega(\bar z)=\{u\in\mathbb R^d\mid \exists t_k\downarrow0,\ u_k\to u,\ \bar z+t_ku_k\in\Omega\ \forall k\}\). The regular normal cone is \(\widehat N_\Omega(\bar z)=T_\Omega(\bar z)^\circ\), and \(N_\Omega(\bar z)=\{z^*\mid \exists z_k\in\Omega,\ z_k\to\bar z,\ z_k^*\to z^*,\ z_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(z_k)\ \forall k\}\). If \(\Omega\) is convex, then \(\widehat N_\Omega(\bar z)=N_\Omega(\bar z)=\{z^*\mid \langle z^*,z-\bar z\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in\Omega\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand tangent cone consists of sequential limits of feasible infinitesimal directions. Its polar is the regular normal cone, while limiting normals are limits of regular normals at nearby feasible points. For a convex set, both normal cones equal the classical convex normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat N_\Omega(\bar z)=T_\Omega(\bar z)^\circ,\qquad N_\Omega(\bar z)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{z\to_\Omega\bar z}\widehat N_\Omega(z),\qquad \Omega\text{ convex}\Rightarrow \widehat N_\Omega(\bar z)=N_\Omega(\bar z)=\{z^*:\langle z^*,z-\bar z\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in\Omega\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic normal cone for closed convex sets in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex normal cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is \[N_C(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every}\ y\in C\right\}.\] If \(x\notin C\), set \(N_C(x):=\varnothing\). For \(x\in C\), the set \(N_C(x)\) is a closed convex cone and satisfies \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\). Every nonzero \(v\in N_C(x)\) is the normal of a supporting hyperplane to \(C\) through \(x\); the zero vector also belongs to \(N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex normal has nonpositive inner product with every feasible displacement from the base point; each nonzero convex normal defines a supporting hyperplane there.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of \(\mathbb R^n\), and \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex normal cone consists of the zero vector together with all nonzero vectors defining supporting hyperplanes to \(C\) at \(x\).

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone to C at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Normal Cone and Tangent-Cone Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the extract's nonnegative polar convention and includes the empty-value extension outside the closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be convex and x\in\operatorname{cl}\Omega. Define N_\Omega(x):=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle\xi,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for all }y\in\Omega\}. For K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, let K^*:=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle\xi,k\rangle\ge0\ \text{for all }k\in K\}. Then N_\Omega(x)=-(T_\Omega(x))^*. Extend the normal-cone multifunction by N_\Omega(y):=\varnothing whenever y\notin\operatorname{cl}\Omega.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex normal cone consists of supporting vectors at the base point. With the stated polar convention it equals the negative polar of the tangent cone, and its multifunction extension is empty outside the closure of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_\Omega(x)=\{\xi:\langle\xi,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in\Omega\}=-(T_\Omega(x))^*,\qquad N_\Omega(y)=\varnothing\ \text{for }y\notin\operatorname{cl}\Omega.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the support-based normal cone at a point of a closed convex set, including its positive-scaling property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex, and let \(x\in\Omega\). The normal cone to \(\Omega\) at \(x\) is
\[
N_\Omega(x)=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:d^T(y-x)\leq 0\text{ for all }y\in\Omega\right\}.
\]
If \(d\in N_\Omega(x)\) and \(t>0\), then \(td\in N_\Omega(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set Omega and a point x in Omega, the normal cone contains exactly the vectors whose inner product with every feasible displacement from x is nonpositive. It is closed under positive scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_\Omega(x)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:d^T(y-x)\leq0\ \forall y\in\Omega\},\qquad d\in N_\Omega(x),\ t>0\Rightarrow td\in N_\Omega(x).

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean proximal normals defined through metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(x\in C\). The proximal normal cone to \(C\) at \(x\) is
\[
N_C^P(x):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\ x\in P_C(x+r v)\text{ for some }r>0\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in N_C^P(x)\) precisely when some \(r>0\) satisfies
\[
\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq \frac{1}{2r}\|y-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.
\]
In particular, \(N_C^P(x)\) is a cone containing the zero vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is proximal normal when moving from the point in that direction leaves the point as a nearest point of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^P(x)=\{v:x\in P_C(x+r v)\text{ for some }r>0\}\).

notation.meaning: set of Euclidean nearest points in C to z

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal Normal and Proximal Normal Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based normal geometry for subsets of a Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $S\subset\mathbf E$, $x\in S$, and $y\in\mathbf E$, the vector $y$ is a proximal normal to $S$ at $x$ if there exists $t>0$ such that $x$ is a nearest point in $S$ to $x+ty$. The set of all such vectors is the proximal normal cone $N_S^p(x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector y is proximal normal to S at x if, for some positive t, x is a nearest point in S to x+ty. These vectors form the proximal normal cone at x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\in N_S^p(x)\iff \exists t>0:\ x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in S}\|x+ty-z\|.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Proximal Normal Agreement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agreement of proximal and convex-analytic normals for closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in C\). Then
\[
N_C^P(x)=N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }y\in C\}.
\]
Moreover, if \(v\in N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)\), then \(x\in P_C(x+r v)\) for every \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, proximal normals are exactly the usual supporting normals, and every positive projection step is allowed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^P(x)=N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet normals for locally closed subsets of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\). The regular, or Fréchet, normal cone is
\[
\widehat N_C(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\limsup_{\substack{y\to x,\ y\in C\\y\neq x}}\frac{\langle v,y-x\rangle}{\|y-x\|}\leq0\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat N_C(x)\) when
\[
\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq o(\|y-x\|)\quad\text{as }y\to x\text{ within }C.
\]
Thus regular normals are first-order supporting vectors at the specified point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular normal makes a nonpositive first-order angle with every feasible displacement approaching the base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(x)=\{v:\limsup_{y\to x,\,y\in C\setminus\{x\}}\langle v,y-x\rangle/\|y-x\|\leq0\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mordukhovich normals obtained as outer limits of regular normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\). The limiting, or Mordukhovich, normal cone is
\[
N_C(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }x_k\to x\text{ with }x_k\in C,\\ v_k\to v\text{ with }v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(N_C(x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{y\to x,\,y\in C}\widehat N_C(y)\). The cone \(N_C(x)\) is closed but need not be convex, and it always contains \(\widehat N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limiting normals are limits of regular normals taken at nearby feasible points; the resulting cone can be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{y\to x,\,y\in C}\widehat N_C(y)\).
