knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convexification of the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\). The Clarke normal cone is the closed convex hull of the limiting normal cone:
\[
N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}N_C(x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\widehat N_C(x)\subset N_C(x)\subset N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x),
\]
and \(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)\) is always a closed convex cone. Convexification may discard the branch-sensitive, nonconvex structure retained by limiting normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke normal cone is the closed convex hull of all limiting normals and is therefore closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}N_C(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Tangent–Normal Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polar duality for a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in C\). Define
\[
T_C(x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-x),\qquad K^\circ:=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }d\in K\}.
\]
Then the convex normal and tangent cones are exact polar duals:
\[
N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,
\qquad
T_C(x)=N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)^\circ.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a closed convex set, the tangent and normal cones are mutual negative polars.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\) and \(T_C(x)=N_C^{\mathrm{cvx}}(x)^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polarity between Bouligand tangents and regular normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\), and define the Bouligand tangent cone by
\[
T_C(x):=\{d:\exists\,t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d\text{ with }x+t_kd_k\in C\}.
\]
With the negative-polar convention \(K^\circ:=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in K\}\), the regular normal cone satisfies the exact identity
\[
\widehat N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ.
\]
The reverse polar gives \(\widehat N_C(x)^\circ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}T_C(x)\), which need not equal the generally nonconvex cone \(T_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular normals are exactly the negative polar of the Bouligand tangent cone; reversing polarity convexifies the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact polarity between Clarke tangent and normal cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(x\in C\). Its Clarke tangent cone consists of vectors \(d\) such that, for every \(x_k\to x\) in \(C\) and every \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(d_k\to d\) with \(x_k+t_kd_k\in C\). Then
\[
N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\bigl(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)\bigr)^\circ,
\qquad
T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\bigl(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)\bigr)^\circ,
\]
where \(K^\circ:=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\leq0\text{ for all }d\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke tangent and Clarke normal cones are closed convex cones that are exact negative polars of one another.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x))^\circ\) and \(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=(N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x))^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regular–Clarke Polarity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A crossing set exhibits strict regular-to-Clarke enlargement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C:=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R)\subset\mathbb R^2,
\qquad x=(0,0).
\]
Its Bouligand tangent cone is \(T_C(x)=C\), hence regular polarity gives
\[
\widehat N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ=\{0\}.
\]
Normals obtained along either branch yield
\[
N_C(x)=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R),
\qquad N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\mathbb R^2.
\]
Thus \(\widehat N_C(x)\subsetneq N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)\), while the Clarke tangent cone is \(T_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the crossing of two coordinate axes, the regular normal is zero but the Clarke normal fills the plane.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is the union of the two coordinate axes in \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(x)=\{0\}\subsetneq N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(x)=\mathbb R^2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Normals beyond Exact Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex limiting normals cannot generally be recovered by one polar operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every set \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), its negative polar \(K^\circ\) is a closed convex cone. A limiting normal cone need not be convex and therefore need not equal the polar of any tangent-like set. For example, for
\[
C:=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R),\qquad x=(0,0),
\]
one has
\[
N_C(x)=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R),
\]
which is nonconvex. Hence no set \(K\) satisfies \(N_C(x)=K^\circ\); polarity instead describes regular or Clarke normals after the appropriate convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because every polar cone is convex, a nonconvex limiting normal cone cannot be represented as one polar cone.
assumptions_latex: Negative polarity is defined by \(K^\circ=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\leq0\ \forall d\in K\}\).
The ambient space is finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)\) need not equal \(K^\circ\) for any set \(K\).

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Regular Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone definition of Clarke regularity at a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\). The set \(C\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\) when its regular and limiting normal cones agree:
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, every limiting normal generated by nearby points already satisfies the first-order regular-normal inequality at \(\bar x\). Under this equality the common cone is convex and also equals the Clarke normal cone:
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)=N_C^{\mathrm{Cl}}(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is Clarke regular at a point when every limiting normal there is already a regular normal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is Clarke regular at }\bar x\iff\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convexity implies normal regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion and normal-cone representation are local to the specified neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space, let \(\bar x\in\Omega\subset X\), and let \(U\) be a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) such that \(\Omega\cap U\) is convex. Then \(\Omega\) is normally regular at \(\bar x\), and
\[
N(\bar x;\Omega)=\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }x\in\Omega\cap U\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a set is convex in a neighborhood of the reference point, it is normally regular there, and its normal cone is characterized by the supporting inequality on that local convex portion.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is a neighborhood of }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N(\bar x;\Omega)=\widehat N(\bar x;\Omega)=\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,x-\bar x\rangle\le 0\ \forall x\in\Omega\cap U\}

children.title: Prox-Regular Sets

knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regular Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform local quadratic support formulation of prox-regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\). The set \(C\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(r>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, whenever \(x,y\in C\cap B_\varepsilon(\bar x)\) and \(v\in N_C(x)\) with \(\|v\|=1\),
\[
\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2r}\|y-x\|^2.
\]
Thus every nearby unit limiting normal supports \(C\) with one uniform quadratic curvature bound. If the condition holds at every point of \(C\), then \(C\) is called a prox-regular set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is prox-regular when all nearby unit limiting normals obey a uniform local quadratic support inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists r,\varepsilon>0\ \forall x,y,v:\ \langle v,y-x\rangle\leq\|y-x\|^2/(2r)\) under the stated local conditions.

notation.meaning: open Euclidean ball of radius epsilon

knowledge_statements.title: Subsmooth Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition using the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is subsmooth at \(\bar x\in C\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge -\varepsilon\|x_1-x_2\|
\]
whenever \(x_1,x_2\in C\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\) and \(v_i\in N_C(x_i)\cap\mathbb B\) for \(i=1,2\). It is locally subsmooth on \(C\) if it is subsmooth at every point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed set is subsmooth when its unit limiting normals satisfy a local approximate monotonicity inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-\varepsilon\|x_1-x_2\|\) locally for unit limiting normals.

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to C at x
open ball of radius delta about bar x

review_flags: Exact source for the limiting-normal formulation of subsmoothness is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Subsmooth Sets container and is internally well formed, but no citation is supplied. A direct source is required because subsmoothness conventions vary with the chosen normal cone and ambient setting.

knowledge_statements.title: Superregular Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise finite-dimensional superregularity in normal-cone form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is superregular at \(\bar x\in C\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\langle v,z-x\rangle\le \varepsilon\|v\|\,\|z-x\|
\]
for all \(x,z\in C\cap B_\delta(\bar x)\) and every \(v\in N_C(x)\). Thus nearby normal vectors make, up to an arbitrarily small relative error, nonacute angles with displacements directed from their base points into the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Superregularity bounds every nearby normal’s outward component along chords joining nearby points of the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle v,z-x\rangle\le\varepsilon\|v\|\|z-x\|\) for all sufficiently nearby admissible \(x,z,v\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to C at x
open ball of radius delta about bar x

review_flags: Exact source fixing the normal-cone convention for superregularity is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-cone inequality is a plausible finite-dimensional definition of superregularity, but the convention needs a direct source. In addition, the final sentence's description as a nonacute-angle condition is inconsistent with the displayed upper bound, which expresses an approximately nonpositive inner product.

children.title: Subsmooth–Superregular Comparison
children.top_down_role: Inclusion and separation regimes between the two regularity classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Subsmooth–Superregular Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence under the shared finite-dimensional limiting-normal convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(\bar x\in C\). Under the displayed limiting-normal definitions, \(C\) is subsmooth at \(\bar x\) if and only if it is superregular at \(\bar x\). Indeed, the subsmooth inequality with one normal set to zero yields the superregular inequality after scaling; conversely, applying superregularity to each of two unit normals and adding the resulting inequalities gives
\[
\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-2\eta\|x_1-x_2\|,
\]
where \(\eta\) may be chosen as \(\varepsilon/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With limiting normals in finite dimensions, subsmoothness and superregularity are equivalent local regularity properties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is subsmooth at }\bar x\iff C\text{ is superregular at }\bar x\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone used in both definitions

review_flags: A source explicitly establishing equivalence under identical normal-cone conventions is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison belongs in this property container, but the equivalence depends on using exactly compatible normal-cone definitions and is unsupported by a citation. The sentences beginning with "Indeed" also constitute proof text and must be removed from any sourced replacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Amenable Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth inverse-image definition with convex target and basic constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is amenable at \(\bar x\in C\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), a continuously differentiable mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\), and a closed convex set \(D\subset\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[
C\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)\in D\},
\]
and the basic constraint qualification
\[
N_D(F(\bar x))\cap\ker \nabla F(\bar x)^*=\{0\}
\]
holds. The set is amenable if it is amenable at each of its points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An amenable set is locally a smooth inverse image of a closed convex set satisfying a normal-cone constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap U=F^{-1}(D)\cap U\) and \(N_D(F(\bar x))\cap\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^*=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to D at y
adjoint of the derivative of F at bar x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has the correct definitional role and states a standard finite-dimensional amenability formulation, but no inspectable source locator supports the precise smoothness, convexity, and constraint-qualification convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangential regularity and cone formulas for amenable sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Amenable and fully amenable sets

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(Q\subset\mathbf E\) is amenable at \(\bar{x}\in Q\) if there exist an open neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar{x}\), a Euclidean space \(\mathbf Y\), a closed convex set \(R\subset\mathbf Y\), and a continuously differentiable map \(h:U\to\mathbf Y\) such that \[Q\cap U=h^{-1}(R)\] and \[N_R(h(\bar{x}))\cap\ker((\nabla h(\bar{x}))^*)=\{0\}.\] It is fully amenable at \(\bar{x}\) if \(h\) can be chosen twice continuously differentiable at \(\bar{x}\). knowledge_statements.title: Subamenable Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth inverse-image definition using metric subregularity instead of the basic qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is subamenable at \(\bar x\in C\) if, on some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), there exist a continuously differentiable mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) and a closed convex set \(D\subset\mathbb R^m\) such that \(C\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)\in D\}\), and constants \(\kappa,r>0\) satisfy
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D)
\quad\text{for all }x\in B_r(\bar x).
\]
This inequality is metric subregularity of the associated constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subamenable set has a smooth convex constraint representation whose residual locally bounds distance to feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D)\) locally around \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Amenability Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local implication between amenability and subamenability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\). If \(C\) is amenable at \(\bar x\), then \(C\) is subamenable at \(\bar x\). In particular, for a local representation \(C=F^{-1}(D)\) with \(D\) closed and convex, the qualification
\[
N_D(F(\bar x))\cap\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^*=\{0\}
\]
implies a local error bound
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),D).
\]
The reverse implication need not hold because metric subregularity is weaker than the displayed qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Amenability implies subamenability; the converse can fail because a local error bound need not imply the basic constraint qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is amenable at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ amenable at }\bar x\Longrightarrow C\text{ subamenable at }\bar x\), while the converse is not automatic.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-normal polarity for a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(x\in C\). Its tangent and normal cones satisfy
\[
T_C(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}(C-x),
\qquad
N_C(x)=\{v:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\ \text{for all }y\in C\},
\]
and are polar to one another:
\[
N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ,
\qquad
T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ.
\]
Consequently, the regular, limiting, and convex-analytic normal cones coincide at every point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, tangent and normal cones are mutual polars, and the standard normal-cone constructions coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ\) and \(T_C(x)=N_C(x)^\circ\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inequality-equality representation and active-set cone formulas.

source_refs.locator: 2.6 Convex Polyhedra p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), \(E\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), and \(f\in\mathbb R^q\), and let
\[
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ Ex=f\}
\]
be a nonempty convex polyhedron. For \(x\in P\), write \(a_i^T\) for the \(i\)-th row of \(A\) and define \(I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:a_i^Tx=b_i\}\). Then
\[
T_P(x)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:a_i^Td\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x),\ Ed=0\},
\]
and
\[
N_P(x)=\{A_{I(x)}^T\lambda+E^T\mu:\lambda\in\mathbb R^{|I(x)|}_+,\ \mu\in\mathbb R^q\}.
\]
Thus both cones are polyhedral and are determined by the constraints active at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron defined by finitely many inequalities and equalities, the tangent and normal cones have explicit representations determined by the active inequalities and the equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Specialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact local first-order geometry of convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty convex polyhedron \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in P\), there exists \(r>0\) such that
\[
(P-x)\cap B_r(0)=T_P(x)\cap B_r(0).
\]
Hence the local feasible geometry is exactly conical, the tangent cone is closed and polyhedral, and
\[
\widehat N_P(x)=N_P(x)=T_P(x)^\circ.
\]
Moreover, the normal-cone mapping is constant on the relative interior of each face and is determined by the inequalities active on that face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near each point, a convex polyhedron agrees with its tangent cone; its regular and limiting normals coincide and are facewise constant.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty convex polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P-x)\cap B_r(0)=T_P(x)\cap B_r(0)\) for some \(r>0\), and \(\widehat N_P(x)=N_P(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Manifold Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical tangent and normal spaces for an embedded smooth manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a continuously differentiable embedded manifold near \(\bar x\in M\). If locally
\[
M=\{x:F(x)=0\},
\]
where \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable and \(\nabla F(\bar x)\) has full row rank, then
\[
T_M(\bar x)=\ker\nabla F(\bar x),
\qquad
N_M(\bar x)=T_M(\bar x)^\perp=\operatorname{range}\nabla F(\bar x)^*.
\]
The regular and limiting normal cones both equal this classical normal space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth embedded manifold, the tangent space is the constraint Jacobian’s kernel and the normal space is its adjoint range.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a continuously differentiable embedded manifold near \(\bar x\).
\(M\) is locally the zero set of a full-row-rank mapping \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_M(\bar x)=\ker\nabla F(\bar x)\) and \(N_M(\bar x)=\operatorname{range}\nabla F(\bar x)^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local and Global Smooth Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an embedded manifold locally as a regular level set of a twice continuously differentiable map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(M\subset\mathbf E\) is a manifold of codimension \(m\) around \(\bar x\in M\) if there exist a neighborhood \(V\) of \(\bar x\) and a \(C^2\) map \(F:V\to\mathbb R^m\) such that \(\nabla F(\bar x)\) is surjective and, for every \(z\in V\), \(z\in M\iff F(z)=0\). The set \(M\) is a manifold of codimension \(m\) if this condition holds around every \(\bar x\in M\).

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Union Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent and limiting-normal calculus for a finite union of closed sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\bigcup_{i=1}^p C_i\), where every \(C_i\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed, and let \(I(x)=\{i:x\in C_i\}\). Then
\[
T_C(x)=\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}T_{C_i}(x)
\]
and
\[
N_C(x)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}N_{C_i}(x).
\]
The normal inclusion may be strict because regular normals to the union must respect all locally active pieces before passage to limiting normals. Thus tangent directions select an active piece, whereas normal behavior records interactions among active pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union’s tangent cone is the union of active-piece tangents, while its limiting normals lie among active-piece limiting normals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(x)=\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}T_{C_i}(x)\) and \(N_C(x)\subseteq\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}N_{C_i}(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional disjunctive feasible sets with polyhedral alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) has disjunctive geometry near \(\bar x\in C\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\), a continuously differentiable mapping \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\), and a finite union of convex polyhedra
\[
D=\bigcup_{j=1}^q D_j
\]
such that
\[
C\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)\in D\}.
\]
The active disjuncts at \(\bar x\) are indexed by \(J(\bar x)=\{j:F(\bar x)\in D_j\}\); local tangent and normal formulas depend on these pieces and on a suitable qualification for the inverse-image system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjunctive geometry represents a feasible set locally as the smooth inverse image of a finite union of convex polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\cap U=\{x\in U:F(x)\in\bigcup_{j=1}^qD_j\}\) with each \(D_j\) convex polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric spectral sets generated by permutation-invariant subsets of eigenvalue space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be invariant under every coordinate permutation. Its spectral lift is the set \[\Lambda(E):=\{X\in\mathbb{S}^n:\lambda(X)\in E\},\] where \(\lambda(X)\) is the eigenvalue vector of \(X\) in any fixed order. Because \(E\) is permutation invariant, membership is independent of that order. Moreover, for every orthogonal matrix \(Q\), one has \(X\in\Lambda(E)\) if and only if \(QXQ^\top\in\Lambda(E)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the closed set \(C:=\{(-1,0),(1,0)\}\subset\mathbb{R}^2\), define \[P_C(y):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\|y-x\|.\] At \(y=0\), both points of \(C\) lie at distance \(1\), and therefore \[P_C(0)=\{(-1,0),(1,0)\}.\] Thus closedness guarantees existence of a nearest point in finite dimensions but does not guarantee uniqueness, even for a finite set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Subdifferential and Its Basic Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and elementary properties of the convex subdifferential for finite-valued convex functions on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex function \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), the convex subdifferential at \(\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is \[\partial F(\theta)=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d: F(\eta)\geq F(\theta)+z^\top(\eta-\theta)\ \text{for every }\eta\in\mathbb{R}^d\right\}.\] It is a nonempty convex set. If \(F\) is differentiable at \(\theta\), then \(\partial F(\theta)=\{\nabla F(\theta)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex subdifferential at a point consists of all slopes defining global affine lower supports there. For a finite-valued convex function on R^d it is nonempty and convex, and at a differentiability point it consists only of the gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial F(\theta)=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^d:F(\eta)\geq F(\theta)+z^\top(\eta-\theta)\ \forall\eta\in\mathbb{R}^d\},\quad \partial F(\theta)\ne\varnothing\text{ and is convex},\quad F\text{ differentiable at }\theta\Rightarrow\partial F(\theta)=\{\nabla F(\theta)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-subgradients and epsilon-subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition, outside-domain convention, tolerance monotonicity, and the zero-tolerance limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty] be proper and convex and let \epsilon>0. For x\in\operatorname{dom}f, a vector g is an \epsilon-subgradient of f at x when f(z)\geq f(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle-\epsilon for every z\in\mathbb{R}^n. The set of such vectors is \partial_\epsilon f(x), while \partial_\epsilon f(x)=\varnothing by convention for x\notin\operatorname{dom}f. If 0<\epsilon_1<\epsilon_2, then \partial_{\epsilon_1}f(x)\subseteq\partial_{\epsilon_2}f(x), and \bigcap_{\epsilon>0}\partial_\epsilon f(x)=\partial f(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient supports a proper convex function up to additive error epsilon. Epsilon-subdifferentials grow with the tolerance, are empty outside the domain by convention, and intersect to the ordinary subdifferential as the tolerance decreases to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_\epsilon f(x)=\{g\mid f(z)\geq f(x)+\langle g,z-x\rangle-\epsilon\ \forall z\in\mathbb{R}^n\},\quad \partial_{\epsilon_1}f(x)\subseteq\partial_{\epsilon_2}f(x)\ (0<\epsilon_1<\epsilon_2),\quad \bigcap_{\epsilon>0}\partial_\epsilon f(x)=\partial f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and support function of an epsilon-subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the complete assertions visible in parts (a)–(c); the extract ends immediately after the compactness assertion in part (c).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,\infty] be proper and convex, let \epsilon>0, and let x\in\operatorname{dom}f. Then \partial_\epsilon f(x) is closed and convex. If (\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=f(x), then \partial_\epsilon f(x) is nonempty and, for every d\in\mathbb{R}^n, \sigma_{\partial_\epsilon f(x)}(d)=\sup_{g\in\partial_\epsilon f(x)}\langle d,g\rangle=\inf_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)+\epsilon}{\alpha}. If f is real-valued, then \partial_\epsilon f(x) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every epsilon-subdifferential is closed and convex. At a point where the function agrees with its lower-semicontinuous closure, it is nonempty and its support function equals an infimum of epsilon-adjusted forward secant slopes. For a real-valued convex function it is nonempty and compact.
assumptions_latex: (\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=f(x)\text{ for nonemptiness and the support formula}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_\epsilon f(x)\text{ is closed and convex};\quad (\operatorname{cl}f)(x)=f(x)\Rightarrow\left[\partial_\epsilon f(x)\neq\varnothing,\ \sigma_{\partial_\epsilon f(x)}(d)=\inf_{\alpha>0}\frac{f(x+\alpha d)-f(x)+\epsilon}{\alpha}\ \forall d\right];\quad f\text{ real-valued}\Rightarrow\partial_\epsilon f(x)\text{ is nonempty and compact}

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet-like approximate subdifferential in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge 0\). The Fréchet-like approximate subdifferential of \(f\) at \(x\) with tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is
\[
\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\liminf_{\substack{y\to x\\y\ne x}}\frac{f(y)-f(x)-\langle v,y-x\rangle}{\|y-x\|}\ge-\varepsilon\right\}.
\]
If \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\), set \(\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x)=\varnothing\). At zero tolerance, \(\widehat\partial_{0}f(x)=\widehat\partial f(x)\), the regular subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate subgradients support the function locally up to a first-order error bounded by the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x)\) is defined by the displayed first-order liminf inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Tolerance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity and vanishing-tolerance behavior of Fréchet-like approximate subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the Fréchet-like family \(\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x)\), tolerances satisfy
\[
0\le\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f(x)\subseteq\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f(x),
\qquad
\bigcap_{\varepsilon>0}\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x)=\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
Consequently, if \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), \(v_k\in\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_k}f(x)\), and \(v_k\to v\), then \(v\in\widehat\partial f(x)\). Thus positive fixed tolerance gives a relaxation, while vanishing tolerance recovers regular first-order support at the fixed base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger tolerances admit more approximate subgradients; intersecting all positive-tolerance sets, or taking convergent vanishing-tolerance selections, recovers regular subgradients.
assumptions_latex: Approximate subdifferentials use the Fréchet-like liminf convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon}f(x)\) is increasing in \(\varepsilon\), and its vanishing-tolerance limit is \(\widehat\partial f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic limiting and singular subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph-normal definitions, the infinite-value convention, and the stated smooth and convex consistency properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), and let \(x\in X\). If \(|f(x)|<\infty\), define \[\partial_b f(x)=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\xi,-1)\in N((x,f(x));\operatorname{epi}f)\}\] and \[\partial^\infty f(x)=\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\xi,0)\in N((x,f(x));\operatorname{epi}f)\}.\] These are respectively the basic (limiting) and singular subdifferentials. If \(|f(x)|=\infty\), set both subdifferentials equal to \(\varnothing\). For strictly differentiable \(f\), the basic subdifferential agrees with the classical gradient, and for convex \(f\) it agrees with the convex subdifferential. The singular subdifferential is applicable to non-Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite function value, the basic limiting subdifferential consists of vectors that form an epigraph normal with vertical component minus one, while the singular subdifferential uses vertical component zero. Both are empty at infinite function values. The basic construction agrees with the classical gradient for strictly differentiable functions and with the convex subdifferential for convex functions; the singular construction applies to non-Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_b f(x)=\{\xi:(\xi,-1)\in N((x,f(x));\operatorname{epi}f)\},\quad \partial^\infty f(x)=\{\xi:(\xi,0)\in N((x,f(x));\operatorname{epi}f)\},\quad |f(x)|=\infty\Rightarrow\partial_b f(x)=\partial^\infty f(x)=\varnothing

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fréchet regular subdifferential and its epigraph-normal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The regular subdifferential is
\[
\widehat\partial f(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle+o(\|y-x\|)\text{ as }y\to x\right\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
v\in\widehat\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v,-1)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x)),
\]
where \(\widehat N\) is the regular normal cone. Set \(\widehat\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) outside the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular subgradient supplies a local affine lower approximation up to an error negligible relative to displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(x)=\{v:(v,-1)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth lower-support characterization of regular subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational characterization of the regular subdifferential at a finite-valued point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ with $f(\bar x)<\infty$. Then $v\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x)$ if and only if, on some neighborhood of $\bar x$, there exists a function $h\leq f$ such that $h(\bar x)=f(\bar x)$, $h$ is differentiable at $\bar x$, and $\nabla h(\bar x)=v$. Moreover, $h$ may be chosen smooth with $h(x)<f(x)$ for every nearby $x\neq\bar x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a regular subgradient exactly when it is the gradient at the contact point of a differentiable local minorant. The minorant may be chosen smooth and strictly below the function at every other nearby point.

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Mordukhovich limiting subdifferential generated from regular subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The limiting subdifferential is
\[
\partial f(x):=\left\{v:\exists x_k\to x,\ f(x_k)\to f(x),\ v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\partial f(x)\) exactly when \((v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\), where \(N\) denotes the limiting normal cone. Outside \(\operatorname{dom}f\), define \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limiting subgradients are limits of regular subgradients taken at nearby points whose function values converge to the base value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(x)=\{v:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential finite-dimensional definition of the horizon subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Its horizon subdifferential is
\[
\partial^\infty f(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists x_k\to x,\ f(x_k)\to f(x),\ v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k),\ \lambda_k\downarrow0,\ \lambda_kv_k\to v\right\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
v\in\partial^\infty f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x)).
\]
Every nonzero horizon subgradient requires an unbounded sequence \((v_k)\), whereas the zero horizon subgradient may also arise from bounded selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Horizon subgradients, including zero, are limits obtained by scaling nearby regular subgradients by positive factors tending to zero; equivalently, they are horizontal limiting epigraph normals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(x)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}\).

notation.meaning: positive scaling factors decreasing to zero

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular subdifferential defined through horizontal limiting epigraph normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The singular subdifferential is
\[
\partial^{\!s}f(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\right\}.
\]
Thus singular subgradients are precisely the horizontal components of limiting normals to the epigraph at \((x,f(x))\). They detect non-Lipschitzian first-order behavior; for a function locally Lipschitz near \(x\), one has \(\partial^{\!s}f(x)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singular subgradients are horizontal limiting epigraph normals and vanish, except for zero, under local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^{\!s}f(x)=\{v:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon–Singular Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of horizon and singular terminology in finite-dimensional variational analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the sequential horizon construction and the horizontal epigraph-normal construction agree:
\[
\partial^\infty f(x)=\partial^{\!s}f(x)=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,f(x))\right\}.
\]
Accordingly, under these conventions, horizon and singular subgradients are the same vectors; the two names emphasize vanishing rescalings and horizontal epigraph normals, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions and under the stated conventions, horizon and singular subdifferentials coincide, with sequential-scaling and epigraph-normal descriptions of the same set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(x)=\partial^{\!s}f(x)\).

children.title: Clarke Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient-limit representation for locally Lipschitz functions on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz near \(x\), and let \(D_f\) be its differentiability set. The Clarke subdifferential is
\[
\partial_C f(x):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\left\{\lim_{k\to\infty}\nabla f(x_k):x_k\to x,\ x_k\in D_f,\ \nabla f(x_k)\text{ converges}\right\}.
\]
In finite dimensions this equals the closed convex hull of the limiting subdifferential:
\[
\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\,\partial f(x).
\]
It is a nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential is the closed convex hull of nearby gradient limits, equivalently of limiting subgradients, for a locally Lipschitz function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C f(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\,\partial f(x)\), and this set is nonempty, compact, and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke subdifferential and generalized gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded support-inequality definition for a locally Lipschitz real-valued function on a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $f$ be Lipschitz near $x$. The generalized differential, or Clarke subdifferential, of $f$ at $x$ is $$\partial f(x):=\{\xi\in X^*: f^\circ(x;d)\geq\langle\xi,d\rangle\text{ for every }d\in X\}.$$ Each $\xi\in\partial f(x)$ is called a generalized gradient of $f$ at $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential consists of the continuous linear functionals whose value in every direction is bounded above by the Clarke generalized directional derivative. Its elements are generalized gradients.
assumptions_latex: f^\circ(x;d)\text{ is the Clarke generalized directional derivative}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{\xi\in X^*:\forall d\in X,\ \langle\xi,d\rangle\leq f^\circ(x;d)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent Cone of a Lipschitz Sublevel Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-cone characterization for a noncritical Lipschitz sublevel set, with equality and set regularity under function regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be Lipschitz near \(x\), suppose \(0\notin\partial f(x)\), and define \(C=\{y\in X:f(y)\le f(x)\}\). Then
\[
\{v\in X:f^{\circ}(x;v)\le 0\}\subset T_C(x).
\]
If \(f\) is regular at \(x\), then equality holds and \(C\) is regular at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the sublevel set through a noncritical point of a locally Lipschitz function, every direction having nonpositive Clarke directional derivative belongs to the tangent cone. If the function is regular at the point, these directions equal the tangent cone and the sublevel set is regular there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{v\in X:f^{\circ}(x;v)\le 0\}\subset T_C(x),\qquad f\text{ regular at }x\Rightarrow\left(\{v\in X:f^{\circ}(x;v)\le 0\}=T_C(x)\text{ and }C\text{ is regular at }x\right)

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Normal Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular, limiting, and horizon subdifferentials represented by epigraph normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). At \(z=(x,f(x))\), the epigraph-normal representations are
\[
\widehat\partial f(x)=\{v:(v,-1)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(z)\},
\]
\[
\partial f(x)=\{v:(v,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(z)\},
\qquad
\partial^\infty f(x)=\{v:(v,0)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(z)\}.
\]
The last coordinate distinguishes ordinary subgradients, normalized at \(-1\), from horizontal horizon directions, normalized at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular, limiting, and horizon subgradients are slices of the corresponding epigraph normal cones at vertical components minus one or zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The three subdifferentials equal the displayed slices of regular or limiting epigraph normal cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Normal Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex normal-cone representation for an active lower level set, including possible domain-boundary limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Fix \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), set \(\alpha=f(x)\), and suppose that some \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(f(y)<\alpha\). For the lower level set \(L_\alpha:=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(z)\le\alpha\}\),
\[
N_{L_\alpha}(x)=\operatorname{cl}\left(\bigcup_{\lambda>0}\lambda\,\partial f(x)\right)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\partial f(x).
\]
Thus every positive multiple of an active convex subgradient is normal to \(L_\alpha\), and every level-set normal is a limit of such multiples. The closure accounts for possible horizontal domain-boundary normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity and strict sublevel feasibility, the active level-set normal cone is the closure of the cone generated by the convex subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{L_\alpha}(x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\partial f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph–Level-Set Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex transfer from epigraph normals to active level-set normals, including horizontal domain-boundary normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), set \(\alpha=f(x)\), and assume that \(f(y)<\alpha\) for some \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then
\[
N_{\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(z)\le\alpha\}}(x)
=
\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\lambda\ge0\text{ such that }(v,-\lambda)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,\alpha)\right\}.
\]
When \(\lambda>0\), conicity gives \((v/\lambda,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,\alpha)\), hence \(v/\lambda\in\partial f(x)\). When \(\lambda=0\), the formula retains any horizontal epigraph normal associated with the boundary of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity and strict sublevel feasibility, downward and horizontal epigraph normals project exactly to normals of the active lower level set.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\{z:f(z)\le\alpha\}}(x)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\lambda\ge0,\ (v,-\lambda)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(x,\alpha)\}\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative vertical-normal multiplier; zero retains horizontal normals

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Function Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting normals represented through subgradients of distance to a closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and closed, and define \(d_C(y):=\inf_{z\in C}\|y-z\|\). For every \(x\in C\),
\[
\partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap\mathbb{B},
\qquad
N_C(x)=\bigcup_{\lambda\ge0}\lambda\,\partial d_C(x)=\operatorname{cone}\partial d_C(x),
\]
where \(\mathbb{B}\) is the closed unit ball. Thus unit-bounded limiting normals are exactly limiting subgradients of the distance function at points of the set, and arbitrary limiting normals are recovered by nonnegative scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a closed set, distance subgradients are exactly unit-bounded limiting normals; conic scaling recovers the full normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap\mathbb{B}\) and \(N_C(x)=\operatorname{cone}\partial d_C(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is quasidifferentiable at \(x\) if there exist nonempty compact convex sets \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) such that, for every direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f'(x;d)=\max_{a\in A}\langle a,d\rangle+\min_{b\in B}\langle b,d\rangle.\] The ordered pair \([A,B]\) is a quasidifferential of \(f\) at \(x\). Two pairs \([A,B]\) and \([C,D]\) are equivalent precisely when their displayed right-hand sides agree for every direction; the quasidifferential object is therefore this equivalence class rather than a unique pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasidifferential represents every directional derivative as a support function plus an antisupport function, with pairs identified when they represent the same derivative.

Canonical embedding of compact convex sets into directed sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-set encoding under the support-function-difference convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose compact convex sets \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) representing the directional derivative by \(f'(x;d)=\sigma_A(d)-\sigma_B(d)\) for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Let \(J_n\) be the canonical additive embedding of compact convex sets into the vector space of directed sets. The directed subdifferential is \[\vec\partial f(x):=J_n(A)-J_n(B).\] Because \(J_n\) preserves Minkowski addition, replacing \((A,B)\) by any equivalent pair with the same support-function difference leaves this directed difference unchanged. Thus \(\vec\partial f(x)\) encodes the generally nonconvex first-order information as one algebraically manipulable directed object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directed subdifferential embeds the two convex sets representing a directional derivative and takes their algebraic difference in directed-set space.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Subdifferentials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The specialized directed-set embedding and its invariance under equivalent quasidifferential pairs require an inspectable authoritative source. No citation is supplied, and conventions for signs and embeddings vary.

children.title: Difference-of-Convex Differential Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Difference-of-Convex Differential Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional first-order representation induced by a local DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the DC decomposition \(f=g-h\) induces the first-order representation \[f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial g(x)}(d)-\sigma_{\partial h(x)}(d).\] Thus \((\partial g(x),\partial h(x))\) is a convex-set pair representing the directional derivative. The pair can depend on the chosen DC decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DC decomposition represents the directional derivative as the difference of the support functions of the two convex subdifferentials, and the representing pair can depend on the decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(g,h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions finite near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(x;d)=\sigma_{\partial g(x)}(d)-\sigma_{\partial h(x)}(d)\) for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete unbounded regular subdifferential caused by non-Lipschitz growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(t)=\sqrt{|t|}\), the Frechet regular subdifferential at the origin is \[\widehat\partial f(0)=\mathbb{R}.\] It is therefore unbounded. The function is continuous at \(0\) but is not locally Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For √|t| at zero, every real number is a Frechet regular subgradient, so the subdifferential is unbounded; the function is continuous but not locally Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\mathbb{R}\), hence the subdifferential is unbounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Nonempty Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient local-Lipschitz regime for bounded nonempty Clarke subdifferentials, contrasted with failure of boundedness for regular subdifferentials under continuity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\), then its Clarke subdifferential \(\partial_C f(x)\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). This is a sufficient regime, not a necessary characterization. Continuity alone does not guarantee boundedness for other subdifferential constructions: for \(q(t)=\sqrt{|t|}\), \[\widehat\partial q(0)=\mathbb{R},\] although \(q\) is continuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz continuity is sufficient for a nonempty compact Clarke subdifferential. Continuity alone does not guarantee bounded regular subdifferentials, as shown by √|t| at zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\in U\), where \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is open.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C f(x)\) is nonempty, compact, and convex; continuity alone does not guarantee bounded regular subdifferentials.

children.title: Decomposition Nonuniqueness

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic nonuniqueness of convex-difference decompositions and their differential pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every proper convex function \(q\) finite near \(x\), \[f=(g+q)-(h+q).\] Whenever \((g+q,h+q)\neq(g,h)\), this is a distinct DC decomposition of \(f\). At \(x\), the associated differential pair is \[(\partial g(x)+\partial q(x),\partial h(x)+\partial q(x)),\] and it represents the same directional derivative as \((\partial g(x),\partial h(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the same convex function to both DC components can create a distinct decomposition and differential pair while preserving the represented function and directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(f=g-h\), where \(g\) and \(h\) are proper convex functions finite near \(x\).
\(q\) is a proper convex function finite near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=(g+q)-(h+q)\), and this is a distinct DC decomposition whenever \((g+q,h+q)\neq(g,h)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of support-function-difference pairs under common Minkowski addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[\sigma_{A+C}(d)-\sigma_{B+C}(d)=\sigma_A(d)-\sigma_B(d)=\phi(d).\] Hence \((A+C,B+C)\) is another convex-pair representation of \(\phi\). If \((A+C,B+C)\neq(A,B)\), the two representations are distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one compact convex set to both members preserves the support-function difference and gives a distinct representation whenever the resulting pair differs from the original pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi=\sigma_{A+C}-\sigma_{B+C}\); the representation is distinct when \((A+C,B+C)\neq(A,B)\).

children.title: Representation-Invariance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which alternative decompositions preserve differential information.

assumptions_latex: \((A,B)\) and \((C,D)\) are pairs of nonempty compact convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The directional model and the directed difference \(J_n(A)-J_n(B)\) are invariant over the equivalence class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence regime preserving directional models and directed-set encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \((A,B)\sim(C,D)\) when \[\sigma_A(d)-\sigma_B(d)=\sigma_C(d)-\sigma_D(d)\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] This equality is the complete invariance condition for the represented positively homogeneous directional model. Equivalently, using support-function uniqueness and Minkowski addition, \((A,B)\sim(C,D)\) exactly when \(A+D=B+C\). For a canonical additive embedding \(J_n\) into directed sets, equivalent pairs also satisfy \[J_n(A)-J_n(B)=J_n(C)-J_n(D).\] Hence the function represented by the support difference and its directed-set encoding depend only on the equivalence class, although the individual convex sets do not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two convex-set pairs are representation-equivalent exactly when their support-function differences agree; the directional model and directed difference then remain invariant.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Invariance Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Equality of support-function differences is standard, but the claimed exact Minkowski-sum characterization and invariance under the particular directed-set embedding require an authoritative, convention-specific source. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Graphical Derivative Family
children.top_down_role: Primal mapping derivatives generated by tangent geometry of graphs.

children.title: Contingent Graphical Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Basic tangent-based derivatives of set-valued mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Contingent Graphical Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional contingent derivative defined through the graph’s Bouligand tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The contingent graphical derivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is the positively homogeneous set-valued mapping \(DF(\bar x\mid\bar y):\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) defined by
\[
DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u):=\{v:(u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u)\) exactly when sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \((u_k,v_k)\to(u,v)\) exist such that \(\bar y+t_kv_k\in F(\bar x+t_ku_k)\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contingent graphical derivative consists of output velocities that arise jointly with a prescribed input velocity along feasible graph sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand contingent tangent cone to a set C at z
graph of the set-valued mapping F

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional contingent graphical derivative is stated precisely and fits the definition container, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Strict Graphical Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Perturbation-stable graphical differentiation.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Graphical Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict graphical derivative using graph perturbations of both the base point and direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The strict graphical derivative \(D_*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\) is defined by declaring \(v\in D_*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(u)\) when there are \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), \((x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\), \(t_k\downarrow0\), and \((u_k,v_k)\to(u,v)\) satisfying
\[
y_k+t_kv_k\in F(x_k+t_ku_k)\quad\text{for every }k.
\]
Thus its graph is the paratingent cone to \(\operatorname{gph}F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict derivative admits graph secants whose base points also vary, making it stable under nearby perturbations of the reference graph point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}D_*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=T^P_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: paratingent cone to C at z

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement fits the strict graphical derivative container, but the D_* notation and paratingent-cone convention require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Semiderivatives of Mappings
children.top_down_role: Positively homogeneous single-valued mapping models.

knowledge_statements.title: Semiderivatives of Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hadamard semiderivative of a single-valued finite-dimensional mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mapping \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is semidifferentiable at \(\bar x\) if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(f'(\bar x;\cdot):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) such that, for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f'(\bar x;u)=\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\u'\to u}}\frac{f(\bar x+tu')-f(\bar x)}{t}.
\]
Equivalently, \(f(\bar x+h)=f(\bar x)+f'(\bar x;h)+o(\lVert h\rVert)\) as \(h\to0\), with the first-order model positively homogeneous rather than necessarily linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidifferentiability gives a continuous, positively homogeneous first-order model obtained by a directional limit stable under perturbations of direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is defined on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x+h)-f(\bar x)-f'(\bar x;h)=o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: Hadamard semiderivative of f at the base point in direction u
remainder whose norm divided by the norm of h tends to zero

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hadamard semiderivative formulation and finite-dimensional remainder equivalence are plausible and locally appropriate, but the selected semiderivative convention lacks source support.

children.title: Regular-Limiting Coderivative Hierarchy

children.title: Regular Coderivatives
children.top_down_role: Coderivative objects generated from regular normals to graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Coderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fréchet-normal coderivative of a finite-dimensional set-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), the regular coderivative is the set-valued mapping \(\widehat D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y):\mathbb{R}^m\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n\) given by
\[
\widehat D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Here \(\widehat N\) is the Fréchet normal cone. The negative sign in the output-dual component is part of the coderivative convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular coderivative slices the Fréchet normal cone to the graph after reversing the sign of the output covector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\widehat D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)\iff(x^*,-y^*)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).

children.title: Limiting Coderivatives

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Coderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mordukhovich limiting-normal coderivative in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), the limiting coderivative is
\[
D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(x^*\) belongs to this set if sequences \((x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\), \(y_k^*\to y^*\), and \(x_k^*\to x^*\) exist with \((x_k,y_k)\in\operatorname{gph}F\) and \(x_k^*\in\widehat D^*F(x_k\mid y_k)(y_k^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting coderivative consists of limits of regular coderivatives taken at nearby graph points with convergent dual arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)\iff(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).

children.title: Regular–Limiting Coderivative Gap
children.top_down_role: Graphical regularity regimes governing coincidence or separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular–Limiting Coderivative Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise inclusion and the equality criterion supplied by graphical regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), every \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and every \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
\widehat D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)\subseteq D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*).
\]
The inclusion can be strict because limiting normals may arise from nearby regular normals without being regular at the reference point. If \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is normally regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), meaning \(\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\), then equality holds for every \(y^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every regular coderivative vector is limiting; equality for all dual arguments follows when the graph’s regular and limiting normal cones coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)\subseteq D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)\), with equality under normal regularity of \(\operatorname{gph}F\).

children.title: Mixed Coderivatives
children.top_down_role: Weak and strong convergence variants for infinite-dimensional analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Coderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asplund-space mixed coderivative with weak-star convergence in the domain dual and norm convergence in the range dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be Asplund spaces, let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mixed coderivative \(D_M^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y):Y^*\rightrightarrows X^*\) assigns to \(y^*\) all \(x^*\) for which sequences \((x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\), \(y_k^*\to y^*\) in norm, and \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}x^*\) exist such that
\[
x_k^*\in\widehat D^*F(x_k\mid y_k)(y_k^*)\quad\text{for every }k.
\]
Thus the two dual components use different convergence modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixed coderivative takes weak-star limits in the domain dual while requiring strong convergence of the range-dual arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_M^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)\) is the stated mixed sequential outer limit of regular coderivative values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed-Coderivative Bounds under Lipschitzian Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds mixed-coderivative norms by exact Lipschitz moduli and derives the zero-kernel property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}F\). If \(F\) is locally Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), then
\[
\|D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\|\le \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)<\infty
\]
and consequently
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)=\{0\}.
\]
If \(F\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\), then
\[
\sup_{\bar y\in F(\bar x)}\|D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\|\le \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x),
\]
and consequently
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)=\{0\}\qquad\text{for every }\bar y\in F(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixed-coderivative norm at a graph point is bounded by the exact Aubin modulus, implying a trivial value at the zero dual vector. Under local Lipschitz continuity at the base point, the bound and zero-kernel property hold uniformly over all values above that point.
assumptions_latex: \text{in part (i), }(\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\text{ and }F\text{ is locally Lipschitz-like around }(\bar x,\bar y)
\text{in part (ii), }F\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\|\le\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y),\quad D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(0)=\{0\};\qquad \sup_{\bar y\in F(\bar x)}\|D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\|\le\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x)

children.title: Clarke Coderivatives
children.top_down_role: Convexified dual differentiation of mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Coderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coderivative induced by the Clarke normal cone to the graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) have locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Its Clarke coderivative is
\[
D_C^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N^C_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
In finite dimensions the Clarke normal cone satisfies \(N_C^C(z)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}N_C(z)\). Consequently, the Clarke coderivative is obtained by slicing the closed convex hull of the limiting normal cone; it need not equal the pointwise convex hull of \(D^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke coderivative slices the closed convexification of the graph’s limiting normal cone at a fixed output covector.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is locally closed at \((\bar x,\bar y)\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in D_C^*F(\bar x\mid\bar y)(y^*)\iff(x^*,-y^*)\in N^C_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Jacobian of a Locally Lipschitz Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by the convex hull of limiting classical Jacobians; the extract also specifies the matrix norm used subsequently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be locally Lipschitz at \(x\), and let \(\Omega_h\) be the exceptional set excluded from differentiability points. Then
\[\partial h(x):=\operatorname{conv}\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\exists (x_i)\subset\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\Omega_h,\ x_i\to x,\ \nabla h(x_i)\to A\right\}.\]
The matrix norm used is
\[\|A\|_{m\times n}:=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\|A_i\|^2\right)^{1/2},\]
where \(A_i\) is the \(i\)-th row of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized Jacobian is the convex hull of limits of ordinary Jacobian matrices along differentiability points approaching x. The specified matrix norm is the square root of the sum of the squared row norms.
assumptions_latex: \Omega_h\text{ is the exceptional set excluded from differentiability points}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial h(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{A:\exists x_i\notin\Omega_h,\ x_i\to x,\ \nabla h(x_i)\to A\right\},\qquad \|A\|_{m\times n}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\|A_i\|^2\right)^{1/2}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke generalized gradient and generalized Jacobian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexified limits of classical derivatives at nearby differentiability points, for scalar and vector-valued locally Lipschitz maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\]
For a locally Lipschitz map $z:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^q$, with component gradients as the rows of its Jacobian, the generalized Jacobian is defined by the analogous convex hull of limiting Jacobian matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Jacobians
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Bouligand subdifferential of a locally Lipschitz mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), and let \(\Omega_f\) denote its set of classical differentiability points. The Bouligand Jacobian is
\[
\partial_B f(\bar x):=\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\exists x_k\in\Omega_f,\ x_k\to\bar x,\ \nabla f(x_k)\to A\right\}.
\]
Rademacher’s theorem makes \(\Omega_f\) full measure locally, and local Lipschitz continuity bounds nearby Jacobians; hence \(\partial_B f(\bar x)\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand Jacobian collects all matrix limits of ordinary Jacobians evaluated at differentiability points approaching the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_B f(\bar x)\) is the nonempty compact set of reachable Jacobian limits at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: set of points where f is classically differentiable

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Generalized Jacobians
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexified generalized Jacobian for locally Lipschitz finite-dimensional mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\). Its Clarke generalized Jacobian is
\[
\partial_C f(\bar x):=\operatorname{co}\partial_B f(\bar x),
\]
where \(\partial_B f(\bar x)\) consists of limits of classical Jacobians along differentiability points converging to \(\bar x\). In finite dimensions \(\partial_B f(\bar x)\) is compact, so \(\partial_C f(\bar x)\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized Jacobian is the convex hull of all Bouligand-reachable limiting Jacobian matrices at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}\partial_B f(\bar x)\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke generalized Jacobian and mean-value inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional generalized derivative for locally Lipschitz vector-valued maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a locally Lipschitz map F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m, let D_F be its differentiability set. Its Clarke generalized Jacobian at x is
\[
\partial F(x)=\operatorname{co}\left\{\lim_{i\to\infty}JF(x_i):x_i\to x,\ x_i\in D_F\right\}.
\]
If F is Lipschitz on an open convex set U and x,y\in U, then
\[
F(y)-F(x)\in \partial F([x,y])(y-x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized Jacobian is the convex hull of limiting ordinary Jacobians along differentiability points approaching the base point. On an open convex Lipschitz domain it satisfies the stated set-valued mean-value inclusion along each segment.
assumptions_latex: F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\text{ is locally Lipschitz for the definition}
U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is open and convex, }F\text{ is Lipschitz on }U,\text{ and }x,y\in U\text{ for the inclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial F(x)=\operatorname{co}\{\lim JF(x_i):x_i\to x,\ x_i\in D_F\},\qquad F(y)-F(x)\in\partial F([x,y])(y-x).

knowledge_statements.title: Newton Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton differentiability defined by an anticipatory matrix model evaluated at the perturbed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\). A matrix-valued mapping \(G:U\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is a Newton derivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\in U\) if
\[
\lim_{\substack{h\to0\\h\ne0}}\frac{\lVert f(\bar x+h)-f(\bar x)-G(\bar x+h)h\rVert}{\lVert h\rVert}=0.
\]
The evaluation at \(\bar x+h\), rather than necessarily at \(\bar x\), distinguishes this Newton model from classical Fréchet differentiability. The mapping \(f\) is Newton differentiable at \(\bar x\) when such a locally defined \(G\) exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton derivative supplies matrices at perturbed points whose linear action approximates the function increment with little-o error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x+h)-f(\bar x)-G(\bar x+h)h=o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: remainder negligible relative to the step norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The anticipatory evaluation formula is a recognized Newton-derivative convention and fits the leaf, but no source establishes that this is the intended convention.

children.title: Generalized Linearization Families
children.top_down_role: Families of admissible first-order linear models for nonsmooth mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Linearization Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued matrix families satisfying a uniform first-order approximation condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\). A nonempty matrix-valued family \(\mathcal A:U\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is a generalized Newton linearization family at \(\bar x\in U\) if its nearby values are bounded and
\[
\lim_{\substack{h\to0\\h\ne0}}\ \sup_{A\in\mathcal A(\bar x+h)}
\frac{\lVert f(\bar x+h)-f(\bar x)-Ah\rVert}{\lVert h\rVert}=0.
\]
Every selection \(A_h\in\mathcal A(\bar x+h)\) therefore provides a valid first-order Newton model, permitting algorithmic choice among several generalized derivative matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized linearization family contains matrices whose first-order models are uniformly accurate for every admissible nearby selection.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A(x)\) is nonempty and locally bounded near \(\bar x\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{A\in\mathcal A(\bar x+h)}\lVert f(\bar x+h)-f(\bar x)-Ah\rVert=o(\lVert h\rVert)\).

notation.meaning: family of admissible generalized linearization matrices at x
an arbitrary matrix selected from the family at the perturbed point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform supremum condition is coherent and fits a generalized linearization-family definition, but terminology and admissibility conditions vary across sources and no locator is supplied.

children.title: Newton-Model Selection

knowledge_statements.title: Newton-Model Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional selection from a generalized-Jacobian family for a Newton linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Newton-model selection is a rule assigning to each \(x\in U\) a matrix \(V_x\in\mathcal J(x)\). The associated affine Newton model is
\[
M_x(d):=F(x)+V_xd.
\]
A selected Newton step is any \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying
\[
M_x(d)=0,
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
V_xd=-F(x).
\]
Such a step exists only when the selected Newton equation is solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton-model selection chooses a matrix from the generalized-Jacobian family at each point and uses it to form an affine model. Any solution of the corresponding linear equation is a selected Newton step.
assumptions_latex: \(F:U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally Lipschitz on the open set \(U\).
\(\mathcal J(x)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a nonempty generalized-Jacobian family for every \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_x(d)=F(x)+V_xd\) is the affine Newton model determined by the selection \(V_x\in\mathcal J(x)\), and any solution of \(V_xd=-F(x)\) is a selected Newton step.

knowledge_statements.title: Semismooth Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke-generalized-Jacobian definition in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and
\[
\sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}
\|F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\|
=o(\|h\|)
\quad\text{as }h\to0.
\]
Equivalently, for every sequence \(h_k\to0\) with \(h_k\ne0\) and every choice \(V_k\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h_k)\),
\[
\|F(\bar x+h_k)-F(\bar x)-V_kh_k\|=o(\|h_k\|).
\]
Semismoothness on a set means semismoothness at every point of that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz, directionally differentiable mapping is semismooth when every nearby Clarke-generalized-Jacobian linearization has residual negligible relative to the displacement length.
assumptions_latex: \(F:U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\) exactly when the stated generalized-Jacobian residual is \(o(\|h\|)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and there exist \(c\geq0\) and a neighborhood \(W\) of \(0\) such that
\[
\|F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\|\leq c\|h\|^2
\]
for every \(h\in W\) with \(\bar x+h\in U\) and every \(V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)\). Equivalently, the supremum of this residual over \(V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)\) is \(O(\|h\|^2)\) as \(h\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong semismoothness requires every nearby generalized-Jacobian linearization error to be quadratic in the displacement, rather than merely smaller than first order.
