knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If
\[
\sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}\|R(h,V)\|=O(\|h\|^2),
\]
then necessarily
\[
\sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}\|R(h,V)\|=o(\|h\|),
\]
so strong semismoothness at \(\bar x\) implies semismoothness there. The implication is strict: the scalar function \(f(t)=|t|^{3/2}\) is locally Lipschitz, directionally differentiable, and semismooth at \(0\), but its linearization residual is of order \(|h|^{3/2}\), not \(O(|h|^2)\); hence it is not strongly semismooth at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong semismoothness always implies semismoothness. The converse fails, as shown at zero by the function assigning the three-halves power of absolute value.

children.title: Proto-Differentiability
children.top_down_role: Stability of graphical difference-quotient limits.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is proto-differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) when its graphical difference quotients converge to \(DF(\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: graph of the set-valued mapping F
graphical derivative of F at the reference graph point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional graphical definition via difference-quotient convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(t>0\), define the graphical difference quotient \(F_t:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) by
\[
F_t(u):=\frac{F(\bar x+tu)-\bar y}{t}.
\]
The mapping \(F\) is proto-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar y\) if the sets \(\operatorname{gph}F_t\) converge as \(t\downarrow0\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense. Their limit must then equal
\[
\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x,\bar y)=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y),
\]
where \(T\) is the contingent tangent cone. Thus proto-differentiability requires equality of the inner and outer graphical limits, not merely existence of tangent directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proto-differentiability means that rescaled graphs about a reference graph point converge to the graph of the graphical derivative, equivalently to the graph’s tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Proto-Differentiability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graphical-limit formulation is plausible, but proto-differentiability has convention-sensitive formulations and no source or locator is supplied to verify the precise convergence requirement and identification of the limit.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Graphical regularity holds exactly when \(\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is graphically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) when its graph is normally regular there, namely
\[
\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y).
\]
Here the left-hand side is the Frechet regular normal cone and the right-hand side is the limiting normal cone. Since \(\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\subseteq N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\) always holds for a locally closed graph, graphical regularity excludes additional limiting normals arising only from nearby graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is graphically regular at a graph point when the regular and limiting normal cones to its graph coincide there.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Proto-differentiability identifies the tangent geometry by
\[
\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x,\bar y)=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y).
\]
Graphical regularity identifies the limiting normal cone with the polar of that tangent cone. Consequently, for every \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
=\{x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n:(x^*,-y^*)\in[\operatorname{gph}DF(\bar x,\bar y)]^\circ\}.
\]
Thus the primal first-order graph limit and the dual coderivative are linked by tangent-normal polarity under the two stated regularity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When proto-differentiability and graphical regularity both hold, the graphical derivative gives the tangent cone and its polar determines the coderivative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Graphical Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative–coderivative characterizations at a locally closed graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m$, let $\bar u\in S(\bar x)$, and suppose $\operatorname{gph}S$ is locally closed at $(\bar x,\bar u)$. The following are equivalent: (a) $S$ is graphically regular at $\bar x$ for $\bar u$; (b) $\langle v,w\rangle\leq\langle y,z\rangle$ whenever $v\in D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y)$ and $z\in DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w)$; (c) $D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)=DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)^{*+}$; (d) $DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)=D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)^{*-}$; (e) $DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)=\widehat DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)$; and (f) $D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)=\widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)$. These equivalent conditions imply that $DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)$ and $D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)$ are graph-convex and hence sublinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a locally closed graph point, graphical regularity is equivalent to the stated primal-dual inequality, adjoint identities, and equality between ordinary and regular graphical derivatives and coderivatives. Each condition also implies graph-convexity and sublinearity of the graphical derivative and coderivative.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}S\text{ is locally closed at }(\bar x,\bar u)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (a)--(f) are equivalent, and each implies that }DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)\text{ and }D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\text{ are graph-convex and sublinear.}

children.title: Coderivative Scalarization
children.top_down_role: Reduction of dual mapping differentiation to scalarized subdifferentials.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is single-valued and strictly Lipschitzian at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\partial\langle y^*,f\rangle(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-coderivative scalarization for a strictly Lipschitzian single-valued mapping.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.3 Strictly Lipschitzian Behavior and Coderivative Scalarization p. 287
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\), define the scalarization \(\varphi_{y^*}(x):=\langle y^*,f(x)\rangle\). Under strict Lipschitzian behavior at \(\bar x\), the limiting coderivative admits the scalar representation
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\partial\varphi_{y^*}(\bar x)
=\partial\langle y^*,f\rangle(\bar x).
\]
Hence evaluating the dual mapping derivative at \(y^*\) reduces to computing the limiting subdifferential of a real-valued locally Lipschitz scalarization. The equality concerns limiting constructions on both sides; replacing either side by a regular or Clarke construction requires the corresponding variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly Lipschitzian mapping, applying the coderivative to a dual vector equals the limiting subdifferential of the mapping scalarized by that vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Scalarization

children.title: Inverse-Graph Duality
children.top_down_role: Transformation of graphical derivatives and coderivatives under inversion.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Graphical derivatives invert relationally, while coderivatives transform by coordinate exchange with the stated signs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inversion formulas under the standard limiting-coderivative sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because
\[
\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}=\{(y,x):(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\},
\]
coordinate exchange yields, for \(v\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
DF^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(v)=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\}.
\]
For the convention \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}\), the corresponding dual formula is
\[
D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(x^*)
=\{y^*:-x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(-y^*)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverting a set-valued mapping exchanges graph coordinates: graphical derivatives become inverse relations, and coderivatives obey the corresponding signed coordinate-exchange formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Graph Duality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate-exchange formulas appear consistent with the displayed coderivative convention, but the convention-sensitive signed dual formula has no authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Constraint-System Graph Representations
children.top_down_role: Graphical encodings of implicit constraints and generalized equations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized equation \(0\in f(x)+Q(x)\) is the zero-level inverse image of the graphically represented mapping \(M=f+Q\).

notation.meaning: solution set of the generalized equation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph encoding of an unparameterized generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the constraint mapping \(M:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) by \(M(x):=f(x)+Q(x)\). Its graph has the exact representation
\[
\operatorname{gph}M
=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m:z-f(x)\in Q(x)\}.
\]
The generalized equation and its solution set are therefore
\[
0\in f(x)+Q(x),\qquad
S:=\{x:0\in M(x)\}=M^{-1}(0)
=\{x:-f(x)\in Q(x)\}.
\]
Thus an implicit constraint system is encoded as membership of \((x,0)\) in a graph, permitting tangent, normal, derivative, and coderivative constructions to act on the same geometric object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized equation is represented by the graph of the sum mapping; feasible points are precisely the inverse image of zero under that mapping.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-System Graph Representations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph and inverse-image identities are precise and mathematically standard, and representation is the correct content kind, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator as required by the evidence contract.

children.top_down_role: Exact convex subdifferential calculus under standard finite-dimensional or locally convex settings.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\), \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact convex subdifferential sum rule under relative-interior qualification.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Calculus of Generalized Normals p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) and \(g\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). If
\[
\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing,
\]
then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\), the convex subdifferential sum rule is exact:
\[
\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).
\]
The right-hand side is the Minkowski sum of the two subdifferential sets. Without the qualification, the inclusion \(\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\subseteq\partial(f+g)(x)\) remains valid, but equality need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions whose domains have intersecting relative interiors, the subdifferential of their sum equals the sum of their subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Calculus Regime

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Calculus of Generalized Normals p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The relative-interior qualification for the finite convex family \(f_1,\ldots,f_p\) is
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^p\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\neq\varnothing.
\]
Equivalently, there exists \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\) lying in the relative interior of every effective domain. For two functions this becomes \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_1)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_2)\neq\varnothing\). Under this condition, finite-dimensional convex sum calculus is exact; in particular, at each common-domain point \(x\),
\[
\partial\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^p f_i\Bigr)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^p\partial f_i(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The qualification requires one point lying in the relative interior of every function’s effective domain; it supports exact finite-dimensional convex sum calculus.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Qualifications

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Exactness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional failure of the convex normal-cone sum rule without relative-interior qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v\ge u^2\}\) and \(D=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v\le -u^2\}\). Then \(C\cap D=\{(0,0)\}\) and \(\operatorname{ri}C\cap\operatorname{ri}D=\varnothing\). At \(z=(0,0)\), one has \(N_C(z)=\{(0,t):t\le0\}\), \(N_D(z)=\{(0,t):t\ge0\}\), and hence \(N_C(z)+N_D(z)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\), whereas \(N_{C\cap D}(z)=\mathbb R^2\). Thus the normal-cone intersection formula, equivalently the indicator-function subdifferential sum formula, can be strictly inexact when the convex interiority qualification is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two tangent convex regions meet only at the origin; their individual normals generate only a line, while the intersection normal is the entire plane.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\subset\mathbb R^2\) are the displayed closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_C(0)+N_D(0)\subsetneq N_{C\cap D}(0).\]

notation.meaning: convex normal cone to C at z

knowledge_statements.title: Locally Lipschitz Clarke Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Clarke sum calculus for locally Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\). Their Clarke subdifferentials are nonempty compact convex sets, and the finite-sum rule is \[\partial_C\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial_C f_i(\bar x).\] The inclusion is generally not an equality. If every \(f_i\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\), then directional derivatives add and the displayed inclusion becomes equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clarke calculus always gives a convexified subdifferential inclusion for finite sums of locally Lipschitz functions; regularity of all summands yields equality.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) for every \(i\).
Equality additionally assumes Clarke regularity of every summand at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial_C\!\left(\sum_i f_i\right)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_i\partial_C f_i(\bar x),\quad\text{with equality under Clarke regularity}.\]

notation.meaning: Clarke subdifferential of f at x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke chain-rule inclusion for a Lipschitz composite
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional composition rule with a vector-valued locally Lipschitz inner mapping and scalar locally Lipschitz outer function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be Lipschitz near \(x\), let \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz near \(F(x)\), and set \(\varphi=g\circ F\). Then \(\varphi\) is Lipschitz near \(x\) and
\[
\partial\varphi(x)\subset\operatorname{conv}\{Z^{\mathsf T}\xi:Z\in\partial F(x),\ \xi\in\partial g(F(x))\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite of locally Lipschitz mappings is locally Lipschitz, and its Clarke generalized gradient is contained in the convex hull of transposed generalized-Jacobian actions on generalized gradients of the outer function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi\text{ is Lipschitz near }x\quad\text{and}\quad\partial\varphi(x)\subset\operatorname{conv}\{Z^{\mathsf T}\xi:Z\in\partial F(x),\ \xi\in\partial g(F(x))\}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathcal O\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz on the open set \(\mathcal O\), and let \(\bar x\in\mathcal O\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz and locally Lipschitz functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definitions of global and neighborhood Lipschitz regularity for real-valued functions on subsets of a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be a Banach space, let $Y\subseteq X$, and let $f:Y\to\mathbb R$. The function $f$ is Lipschitz on $Y$ if there exists $K\geq0$ such that $|f(u)-f(v)|\leq K\|u-v\|$ for all $u,v\in Y$. Define $B_X(x,\epsilon):=\{y\in X:\|x-y\|\leq\epsilon\}$. For $x\in Y$, the function is Lipschitz near $x$ if there exists $\epsilon>0$ with $B_X(x,\epsilon)\subseteq Y$ such that $f$ is Lipschitz on $B_X(x,\epsilon)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is Lipschitz on its domain when one constant bounds every change in value by the corresponding change in argument. It is Lipschitz near a point when this condition holds on a sufficiently small ball contained in its domain.
assumptions_latex: x\in Y\text{ for the local definition}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz on }Y\iff\exists K\geq0\ \forall u,v\in Y:\ |f(u)-f(v)|\leq K\|u-v\|;\quad f\text{ is Lipschitz near }x\iff\exists\epsilon>0:\ B_X(x,\epsilon)\subseteq Y\text{ and }f|_{B_X(x,\epsilon)}\text{ is Lipschitz}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential Quotient Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient calculus for locally Lipschitz functions with a nonzero denominator, including the nonnegative-positive subdifferentially regular equality case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be locally Lipschitz continuous at x\in\mathbb{R}^n, with f_2(x)\neq0. Then f_1/f_2 is locally Lipschitz continuous at x and
\[
\partial\!\left(\frac{f_1}{f_2}\right)(x)\subseteq\frac{f_2(x)\partial f_1(x)-f_1(x)\partial f_2(x)}{f_2(x)^2}.
\]
If, in addition, f_1(x)\geq0, f_2(x)>0, and f_1,f_2 are subdifferentially regular at x, then f_1/f_2 is subdifferentially regular at x and equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two functions are locally Lipschitz at x and the denominator is nonzero there, their quotient is locally Lipschitz and satisfies the stated subdifferential inclusion. If the numerator value is nonnegative, the denominator value is positive, and both functions are subdifferentially regular at x, the quotient is regular and equality holds.
assumptions_latex: f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ are locally Lipschitz continuous at }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{f_1}{f_2}\text{ is locally Lipschitz continuous at }x\text{ and }\partial\!\left(\frac{f_1}{f_2}\right)(x)\subseteq\frac{f_2(x)\partial f_1(x)-f_1(x)\partial f_2(x)}{f_2(x)^2};\text{ if }f_1(x)\geq0,f_2(x)>0\text{ and both functions are subdifferentially regular at }x,\text{ then the quotient is subdifferentially regular and equality holds.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential Sum Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sum calculus for locally Lipschitz functions, including equality when one summand is continuously differentiable near the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke subgradient characterization and composite chain inclusion

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is Lipschitz near \(x\), then \[\xi\in\partial_C f(x)\iff f^{\circ}(x;d)\geq\langle\xi,d\rangle\quad\text{for every }d\in X.\] Separately, let \(f=g\circ h\), where \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_n)^T\), each \(h_i\) is Lipschitz near \(x\), and \(g\) is Lipschitz near \(h(x)\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation of the subdifferential for locally Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{If }f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is locally Lipschitz at }x,\text{ then }\partial f(x)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\xi,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}\bigl((x,f(x))\bigr)\right\}.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\xi,-1)\in N_{\operatorname{epi}f}\bigl((x,f(x))\bigr)\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential Product Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product calculus for two locally Lipschitz functions, including the nonnegative subdifferentially regular equality case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be locally Lipschitz continuous at x\in\mathbb{R}^n. Then f_1f_2 is locally Lipschitz continuous at x and
\[
\partial(f_1f_2)(x)\subseteq f_2(x)\partial f_1(x)+f_1(x)\partial f_2(x).
\]
If, in addition, f_1(x),f_2(x)\geq 0 and f_1,f_2 are subdifferentially regular at x, then f_1f_2 is subdifferentially regular at x and equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The product of two functions locally Lipschitz at x is locally Lipschitz there and satisfies the stated subdifferential inclusion. When both values are nonnegative and both functions are subdifferentially regular at x, the product is regular and the inclusion becomes equality.
assumptions_latex: f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ are locally Lipschitz continuous at }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_1f_2\text{ is locally Lipschitz continuous at }x\text{ and }\partial(f_1f_2)(x)\subseteq f_2(x)\partial f_1(x)+f_1(x)\partial f_2(x);\text{ if }f_1(x),f_2(x)\geq0\text{ and both functions are subdifferentially regular at }x,\text{ then }f_1f_2\text{ is subdifferentially regular and equality holds.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke mean-value inclusion for Lipschitz mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional mean-value theorem for a vector-valued locally Lipschitz mapping and its Clarke generalized Jacobians along a segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex, let \(F:U\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be Lipschitz on \(U\), and let \(x,y\in U\). Then
\[
F(y)-F(x)\in\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\partial F([x,y])(y-x)\bigr),
\]
where
\[
\partial F([x,y])(y-x):=\{Z(y-x):z\in[x,y],\ Z\in\partial F(z)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a vector-valued mapping that is Lipschitz on an open convex set, the increment between two points lies in the convex hull of generalized-Jacobian actions evaluated along their connecting segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(y)-F(x)\in\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\partial F([x,y])(y-x)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Clarke chain rule with a smooth outer function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact generalized-gradient formula for a locally Lipschitz vector mapping composed with a scalar outer function that is continuously differentiable near the image point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be Lipschitz near \(x\), let \(g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz near \(F(x)\), set \(\varphi=g\circ F\), and suppose that \(g\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(F(x)\). Then
\[
\partial\varphi(x)=\{Z^{\mathsf T}\nabla g(F(x)):Z\in\partial F(x)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the inner mapping is locally Lipschitz and the scalar outer function is continuously differentiable near the image point, the Clarke generalized gradient of their composite equals the generalized-Jacobian images of the outer gradient.
assumptions_latex: g\text{ is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of }F(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\varphi(x)=\{Z^{\mathsf T}\nabla g(F(x)):Z\in\partial F(x)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Subdifferential Rule for a Finite Maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-index calculus for a finite maximum of locally Lipschitz functions, with equality under componentwise subdifferential regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be locally Lipschitz continuous at x for i=1,\ldots,m, and define
\[
f(y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f_i(y),\qquad I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f_i(x)=f(x)\}.
\]
Then f is locally Lipschitz continuous at x and
\[
\partial f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).
\]
If every f_i is subdifferentially regular at x, then f is subdifferentially regular at x and equality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite maximum of functions locally Lipschitz at x is locally Lipschitz there. Its subdifferential is contained in the convex hull of the subdifferentials of the active components. If every component is subdifferentially regular at x, the maximum is regular and equality holds.
assumptions_latex: f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is locally Lipschitz continuous at }x\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is locally Lipschitz continuous at }x\text{ and }\partial f(x)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right);\text{ if every }f_i\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }x,\text{ then }f\text{ is subdifferentially regular and equality holds.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Mean Value Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth mean-value formula between two distinct points for a function Lipschitz on a neighborhood of their segment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(x\neq y\), and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz on an open set containing \([x,y]\). Then there exists \(u\in(x,y)\) such that \[f(y)-f(x)\in\langle\partial f(u),y-x\rangle=\{\langle v,y-x\rangle\mid v\in\partial f(u)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For distinct x and y, if f is Lipschitz on an open neighborhood of their segment, then at some interior point u its increment equals the inner product of y−x with a Clarke subgradient at u.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz on an open set containing }[x,y]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists u\in(x,y)\;\exists v\in\partial f(u):\ f(y)-f(x)=\langle v,y-x\rangle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent local-Lipschitz and horizon-subdifferential criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence under finiteness at the reference point and local epigraph closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that X is finite-dimensional, f is finite at x, and \operatorname{epi}f is locally closed near (x,f(x)). Then the following are equivalent: (i) \partial f(x) is nonempty and bounded; (ii) f is Lipschitz near x; (iii) \partial^{\infty}f(x)=\{0\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, when f is finite at x and its epigraph is locally closed near (x,f(x)), local Lipschitz continuity near x is equivalent to the generalized subdifferential being nonempty and bounded, and also to the horizon subdifferential being trivial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\text{ and }\partial f(x)\text{ is bounded}\bigr)\iff f\text{ is Lipschitz near }x\iff\partial^{\infty}f(x)=\{0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation of the Clarke Directional Derivative by Nearby Gradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided approximation bound along nearby differentiability points of a locally Lipschitz function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be locally Lipschitz continuous, let \varepsilon>0, and let d\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}. Then f^{\circ}(x;d)-\varepsilon\leq\limsup\{\nabla f(y)^Td\mid y\to x,\ y\notin\Omega_f\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting representations of singular subgradients in Asplund spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential outer-limit representations using Fréchet and approximate Fréchet subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, and let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and lower semicontinuous around \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\). Then
\[
\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\mathop{\operatorname{Limsup}}_{\substack{x\overset{\varphi}{\to}\bar x\\ \lambda\downarrow0}}\lambda\widehat\partial\varphi(x)=\mathop{\operatorname{Limsup}}_{\substack{x\overset{\varphi}{\to}\bar x\\ \varepsilon,\lambda\downarrow0}}\lambda\widehat\partial_\varepsilon\varphi(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper function lower semicontinuous near a domain point in an Asplund space, the singular subdifferential is the sequential outer limit of vanishing positive multiples of either Fréchet subgradients or approximate Fréchet subgradients along function-value convergence to the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\mathop{\operatorname{Limsup}}_{\substack{x\overset{\varphi}{\to}\bar x\\ \lambda\downarrow0}}\lambda\widehat\partial\varphi(x)=\mathop{\operatorname{Limsup}}_{\substack{x\overset{\varphi}{\to}\bar x\\ \varepsilon,\lambda\downarrow0}}\lambda\widehat\partial_\varepsilon\varphi(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential characterization of sequential normal epi-compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An if-and-only-if characterization of SNEC through weak-star-to-norm convergence of scaled Fréchet subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, and let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and lower semicontinuous around \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\). Then \(\varphi\) is SNEC at \(\bar x\) if and only if, for every choice of sequences
\[
x_k\overset{\varphi}{\to}\bar x,\qquad \lambda_k\downarrow0,\qquad x_k^*\in\lambda_k\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k),
\]
one has
\[
x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lVert x_k^*\rVert\to0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function lower semicontinuous near a domain point in an Asplund space is sequentially normally epi-compact there if and only if every weak-star-null sequence of scaled Fréchet subgradients, formed along function-value convergence with positive scales decreasing to zero, converges to zero in norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi\text{ is SNEC at }\bar x\iff\left[\forall\,x_k\overset{\varphi}{\to}\bar x,\ \lambda_k\downarrow0,\ x_k^*\in\lambda_k\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k),\quad x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}0\Rightarrow\lVert x_k^*\rVert\to0\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Horizontal normals to graphs of continuous functions in Asplund spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential realization of horizontal Fréchet normals and identification of the coderivative at zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, and let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be finite and continuous around \(\bar x\in X\). Then:

(i) If
\[
(x^*,0)\in\widehat N\big((\bar x,\varphi(\bar x));\operatorname{gph}\varphi\big),
\]
then there exist sequences \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(\lambda_k\downarrow0\), and \(x_k^*\to x^*\) such that
\[
x_k^*\in\widehat\partial(\lambda_k\varphi)(x_k)\cup\widehat\partial(-\lambda_k\varphi)(x_k)\qquad(k\in\mathbb N).
\]

(ii)
\[
D^*\varphi(\bar x)(0)=\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)\cup\partial^\infty(-\varphi)(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function finite and continuous near a point in an Asplund space, each horizontal Fréchet normal to its graph is a norm limit of Fréchet subgradients of vanishing positive or negative scalings of the function. The coderivative at zero is the union of the singular subdifferentials of the function and its negative.
assumptions_latex: \varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is finite and continuous around }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[(x^*,0)\in\widehat N((\bar x,\varphi(\bar x));\operatorname{gph}\varphi)\Rightarrow\exists\,x_k\to\bar x,\ \lambda_k\downarrow0,\ x_k^*\to x^*:\ \forall k\in\mathbb N,\ x_k^*\in\widehat\partial(\lambda_k\varphi)(x_k)\cup\widehat\partial(-\lambda_k\varphi)(x_k)\right]\land\left[D^*\varphi(\bar x)(0)=\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)\cup\partial^\infty(-\varphi)(\bar x)\right]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean-value theorem for Lipschitz functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz specialization of the nonsmooth mean-value inclusion in the standing Asplund-space setting, with a limiting/basic-subgradient refinement under lower regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an Asplund space and let \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be Lipschitz continuous on an open set containing \([a,b]\). Then there exists \(c\in(a,b)\) such that \[\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)\in\langle\partial^0\varphi(c),b-a\rangle.\] If \(\varphi\) is also lower regular throughout \((a,b)\), then there exists \(c\in(a,b)\) such that \[\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)\in\langle\partial\varphi(c),b-a\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the standing Asplund-space setting, a Lipschitz function satisfies a mean-value inclusion with a symmetric basic subgradient. Lower regularity along the open segment yields the corresponding inclusion with the basic limiting subdifferential; the two conclusions need not use the same interior point.

\varphi\text{ is Lipschitz continuous on an open set containing }[a,b]
\varphi\text{ is lower regular on }(a,b)\text{ for the second conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists c_1\in(a,b):\ \varphi(b)-\varphi(a)\in\langle\partial^0\varphi(c_1),b-a\rangle;\quad \text{under lower regularity, }\exists c_2\in(a,b):\ \varphi(b)-\varphi(a)\in\langle\partial\varphi(c_2),b-a\rangle

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Subdifferential Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Mordukhovich subdifferential on an Asplund Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an Asplund Banach space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). The limiting subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is \[\partial f(\bar x):=\left\{x^*\in X^*: \begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }x_k\to\bar x,\ f(x_k)\to f(\bar x),\\ x_k^*\in\widehat\partial f(x_k),\ x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}x^*\end{array}\right\}.\] It retains nonconvex first-order information while supporting sequential calculus under appropriate qualification conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential consists of weak-star limits of Fréchet subgradients taken at nearby points whose function values converge to the reference value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x^*\in\partial f(\bar x)\iff \exists(x_k,x_k^*)\text{ satisfying the displayed sequential approximation}.\]

children.title: Fuzzy Asplund Calculus

knowledge_statements.title: Fuzzy Asplund Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asplund-space fuzzy sum rule for Fréchet subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be Asplund, let \(f_1:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), and let \(f_2:X\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\). For every \(x^*\in\widehat\partial(f_1+f_2)(\bar x)\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(x_i\in\bar x+\varepsilon B_X\) and \(x_i^*\in\widehat\partial f_i(x_i)\), for \(i=1,2\), such that \(|f_i(x_i)-f_i(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\) and \[\left\|x^*-x_1^*-x_2^*\right\|<\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Fréchet subgradient of a sum is approximated by Fréchet subgradients of the summands at nearby points with nearby function values.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1\) is lower semicontinuous and finite at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x^*\approx x_1^*+x_2^*\quad\text{for nearby Fréchet subgradients }x_i^*.\]

children.title: Sequential Approximation Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Approximation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer-limit representation connecting Fréchet and limiting subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a lower semicontinuous function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) on an Asplund Banach space and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the limiting subdifferential admits the sequential outer-limit representation \[\partial f(\bar x)=\mathop{\operatorname{Limsup}}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\ f(x)\to f(\bar x)}}^{w^*}\widehat\partial f(x).\] Thus \(x^*\in\partial f(\bar x)\) precisely when nearby Fréchet subgradients converge weak-star to \(x^*\) along a sequence maintaining convergence of function values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential is the weak-star sequential outer limit of nearby Fréchet subdifferentials along points with convergent function values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial f(\bar x)=\mathop{\operatorname{Limsup}}_{x\to_f\bar x}^{w^*}\widehat\partial f(x).\]

notation.meaning: x tends to the reference point while f(x) tends to its reference value

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Asplund Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural boundary for universal Fréchet fuzzy calculus in Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Banach space \(X\), the Asplund property is equivalent to validity of the Fréchet fuzzy sum rule for all lower semicontinuous \(f_1:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and locally Lipschitz \(f_2:X\to\mathbb R\) at common finite points. Consequently, if \(X\) is not Asplund, there exist such \(f_1,f_2\), a point \(\bar x\), a subgradient \(x^*\in\widehat\partial(f_1+f_2)(\bar x)\), and a positive tolerance for which no nearby Fréchet subgradients of the summands satisfy the fuzzy decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outside Asplund spaces, the Fréchet fuzzy sum rule cannot hold uniformly for all lower-semicontinuous and locally Lipschitz summands.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{Universal Fréchet fuzzy sum calculus fails on }X.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Amenable Composite Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local amenability of an extended-real composite under the basic qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is amenable at \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) if, on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\), \(f=g\circ F\), where \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and the basic qualification \[N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x))\cap\ker F'(\bar x)^*=\{0\}\] holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An amenable function is locally a smooth mapping followed by a proper closed convex function, with no nonzero abnormal normal annihilated by the derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x))\cap\ker F'(\bar x)^*=\{0\}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Subamenable Composite Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite subamenability expressed through metric subregularity of the domain constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is subamenable at \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) if locally \(f=g\circ F\), where \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable and \(g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and the set-valued mapping \(M(x):=F(x)-\operatorname{dom}g\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\). Equivalently, locally there is \(\kappa>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}g))\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),\operatorname{dom}g).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subamenability replaces the amenable abnormal-normal condition by a local error bound for the smooth preimage of the convex domain.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable and \(g\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}g))\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(F(x),\operatorname{dom}g)\quad\text{locally}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Qualification Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order chain rule for an amenable smooth-convex composite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), let \(g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and set \(f=g\circ F\). If \(F(\bar x)\in\operatorname{dom}g\) and \[N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x))\cap\ker F'(\bar x)^*=\{0\},\] then the limiting and horizon subdifferential chain rules are exact: \[\partial f(\bar x)=F'(\bar x)^*\partial g(F(\bar x)),\qquad \partial^\infty f(\bar x)=F'(\bar x)^*N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The amenability qualification excludes abnormal multipliers and makes both limiting and horizon subdifferential chain rules exact.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex and finite at \(F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial(g\circ F)(\bar x)=F'(\bar x)^*\partial g(F(\bar x)),\quad \partial^\infty(g\circ F)(\bar x)=F'(\bar x)^*N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(\bar x)).\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar composite showing failure of the exact chain rule when qualification is absent.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Subdifferential Calculus and Related Topics p. 296

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be \(F(x)=x^2\), let \(g=\delta_{\{0\}}\), and set \(f=g\circ F=\delta_{\{0\}}\). At \(\bar x=0\), \(F'(0)=0\) and \(\partial g(0)=\mathbb R\), so \(F'(0)^*\partial g(0)=\{0\}\). However, \(\partial f(0)=N_{\{0\}}(0)=\mathbb R\). The qualification fails maximally because \[N_{\operatorname{dom}g}(F(0))\cap\ker F'(0)^*=\mathbb R.\] Hence, without qualification, the derivative-pullback expression can be a strict subset of the composite subdifferential, so the exact chain-rule formula and the usual qualified upper inclusion can fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared inner map and singleton indicator violate qualification: the derivative pullback is zero, but the composite subdifferential is the whole line.

children.title: Transversality Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Geometric separation conditions for interacting sets or mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^n\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in A\cap B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N_A(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_B(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.\]

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to A at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone transversality condition for intersection calculus.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Calculus of Generalized Normals p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in A\cap B\). The limiting-normal transversality qualification at \(\bar x\) is \[N_A(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_B(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.\] Equivalently, there are no nonzero opposing limiting normals \(a^*\in N_A(\bar x)\) and \(b^*\in N_B(\bar x)\) satisfying \(a^*+b^*=0\). If this qualification holds, then in finite dimensions the normal-cone intersection estimate is \[N_{A\cap B}(\bar x)\subseteq N_A(\bar x)+N_B(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two locally closed sets are transversal when they have no nonzero opposing limiting normals; in finite dimensions this condition yields the limiting normal-cone intersection estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Transversality Qualifications

children.title: Horizon Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Conditions excluding adverse horizon-direction interactions.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon Qualifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Horizon-subgradient qualification excluding singular cancellation in sum calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,f_2:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near a common finite point \(\bar x\). The horizon qualification for their sum is \[\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.\] It excludes nonzero singular subgradients that cancel across the summands. Under the usual local closedness assumptions, it yields the limiting sum-rule estimate \[\partial(f_1+f_2)(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f_1(\bar x)+\partial f_2(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizon qualification requires that no nonzero singular subgradients of two summands cancel, thereby supporting the limiting subdifferential sum rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.\]

children.title: Metric Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Regularity conditions expressed through metric behavior of constraints or mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(M:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,0)\), where \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,0)\) precisely when the displayed local error bound holds; equivalently, \(D^*M(\bar x,0)(0)=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Mordukhovich coderivative of the set-valued mapping
distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coderivative criterion for a metric-regularity qualification.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Calculus Rules for Normals and Coderivatives p. 261
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The metric qualification at \((\bar x,0)\) requires constants \(\kappa>0\) and neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(0\) such that
\[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(x,M^{-1}(y)\bigr)\leq \kappa\,\operatorname{dist}\bigl(y,M(x)\bigr)\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in U\times V.\]
For a mapping with locally closed graph between finite-dimensional spaces, this metric regularity condition is equivalent to the coderivative abnormality test
\[D^*M(\bar x,0)(0)=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint mapping is metrically regular when nearby solution distances obey a uniform residual error bound; in finite dimensions this is equivalent to excluding nonzero zero-direction coderivative elements.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Qualifications

children.title: Abnormal Multiplier Exclusion
children.top_down_role: Common geometric consequence linking the qualification families.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
\(D\subset\mathbb R^m\) is locally closed near \(F(\bar x)\), and \(F(\bar x)\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda\in N_D(F(\bar x))\) and \(\nabla F(\bar x)^\top\lambda=0\) imply \(\lambda=0\).

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the constraint set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: No-nonzero-abnormal-multiplier condition for a smooth geometric constraint.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Calculus Rules for Normals and Coderivatives p. 261
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the feasible system \(F(x)\in D\), abnormal multipliers are excluded at \(\bar x\) when
\[\bigl[\lambda\in N_D(F(\bar x)),\ \nabla F(\bar x)^\top\lambda=0\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\lambda=0.\]
Equivalently, the only normal to \(D\) at \(F(\bar x)\) annihilated by the adjoint derivative of \(F\) is the zero vector. This condition removes nontrivial multiplier systems whose objective multiplier is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No nonzero normal multiplier to the geometric constraint may be annihilated by the adjoint derivative of the constraint mapping.
knowledge_statements.title: Abnormal Multiplier Exclusion

children.title: Exact Sum Rules
children.top_down_role: Equality-level aggregation rules under sufficient regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) and \(g\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\). If
\[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\cap\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)\neq\varnothing,\]
then at every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\),
\[\partial(f+g)(\bar x)=\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x).\]
Thus every subgradient of the sum admits an exact decomposition into subgradients of the summands at the same base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the relative-interior qualification, the convex subdifferential of a sum equals the Minkowski sum of the two subdifferentials at the same point.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Sum Rules

children.title: Limiting Sum Rules
children.top_down_role: Sequential aggregation rules for limiting subdifferential objects.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), finite at \(\bar x\), and not both identically infinite locally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion under horizon qualification.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) and \(g\) be extended-real-valued functions on \(\mathbb R^n\), lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite there. If the horizon qualification
\[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}\]
holds, then the limiting subdifferential satisfies
\[\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x).\]
In particular, the qualification is automatic when one summand is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting subdifferential of a sum is contained in the sum of limiting subdifferentials when the summands have no opposing nonzero horizon subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Sum Rules

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting-Subdifferential Sum Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-function limiting-subdifferential calculus under a local Lipschitz/lower-semicontinuity hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f,g:\mathbf E\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). If one of \(f\) and \(g\) is locally Lipschitz near \(z\in\mathbf E\) and the other is lower semicontinuous near \(z\), then
\[
\partial_a(f+g)(z)\subseteq\partial_af(z)+\partial_ag(z).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one of two extended-real-valued functions is locally Lipschitz near the base point and the other is lower semicontinuous there, every limiting subgradient of their sum belongs to the sum of their limiting subdifferentials at that point.
assumptions_latex: \bigl(f\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }z\land g\text{ is lower semicontinuous near }z\bigr)\lor\bigl(g\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }z\land f\text{ is lower semicontinuous near }z\bigr)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_a(f+g)(z)\subseteq\partial_af(z)+\partial_ag(z).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting and horizon subdifferential sum rules with Lipschitz summands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sums of extended-real-valued functions when one summand is lower semicontinuous and all remaining summands are locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\ge 2\), let \(\varphi_1:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be lower semicontinuous around \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi_1\), and let \(\varphi_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\) for \(i=2,\ldots,s\). Then \[\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^s\varphi_i\right)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^s\partial\varphi_i(\bar x),\qquad \partial^\infty\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^s\varphi_i\right)(\bar x)=\partial^\infty\varphi_1(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one summand is lower semicontinuous near a point in its domain and every other summand is locally Lipschitz there, the limiting subdifferential of the finite sum is contained in the sum of the limiting subdifferentials, while the horizon subdifferential of the sum equals that of the possibly non-Lipschitz first summand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^s\varphi_i\right)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^s\partial\varphi_i(\bar x),\qquad \partial^\infty\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^s\varphi_i\right)(\bar x)=\partial^\infty\varphi_1(\bar x)

children.title: Fuzzy Sum Rules
children.top_down_role: Nearby-point aggregation rules in Asplund spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund Banach space, \(f_1:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), and \(f_2:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), suitable nearby \(x_1,x_2\) satisfy \(x^*\in\widehat\partial f_1(x_1)+\widehat\partial f_2(x_2)+\varepsilon B_{X^*}\).

notation.meaning: closed unit ball of the dual space

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(x_1,x_2\in X\) with
\[\|x_i-\bar x\|<\varepsilon,\qquad |f_i(x_i)-f_i(\bar x)|<\varepsilon\quad(i=1,2),\]
such that
\[x^*\in\widehat\partial f_1(x_1)+\widehat\partial f_2(x_2)+\varepsilon B_{X^*}.\]
Thus a Fréchet subgradient of the sum can be approximated by a sum of Fréchet subgradients evaluated at possibly different nearby points, with an arbitrarily small dual error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fréchet subgradient of a sum can be approximated by subgradients of the summands at nearby points, up to an arbitrarily small dual error.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(\bar z=(0,0)\), the sets satisfy \(C\cap D=\{\bar z\}\), while
\[N_C(\bar z)=\{(0,t):t\leq0\},\qquad N_D(\bar z)=\{(0,t):t\geq0\}.\]
Hence the opposing-normal qualification fails. Since \(f+g=\delta_{C\cap D}\),
\[\partial(f+g)(\bar z)=N_{\{\bar z\}}(\bar z)=\mathbb R^2,\]
but
\[\partial f(\bar z)+\partial g(\bar z)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R.\]
Thus removing the qualification can destroy even the limiting sum-rule inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangentially opposed epigraph and hypograph constraints violate the horizon qualification; their indicator sum has horizontal subgradients absent from the sum of the individual normal cones.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-subdifferential product inclusion for finite locally Lipschitz factors.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) and \(g\) are finite and locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then their product is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), and its limiting subdifferential obeys
\[\partial(fg)(\bar x)\subseteq f(\bar x)\,\partial g(\bar x)+g(\bar x)\,\partial f(\bar x).\]
The right-hand side uses the function values at the common base point and Minkowski addition of the scaled subdifferential sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For locally Lipschitz factors, every limiting subgradient of their product belongs to the value-weighted sum of the two limiting subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Rules

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed limiting-subdifferential product inclusion is false for arbitrary signed factor values. For example, f=-|x| and constant g=-1 at zero make the left side the interval [-1,1] while the stated right side contains only {-1,1}. A sign-aware rule or a Clarke-subdifferential formulation is required.

children.title: Quotient Rules
children.top_down_role: Generalized differentiation for ratios under denominator regularity.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) are locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f/g)(\bar x)\subseteq g(\bar x)^{-1}\partial f(\bar x)-f(\bar x)g(\bar x)^{-2}\partial g(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-subdifferential quotient inclusion away from zero denominators.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(g(\bar x)\neq0\), the denominator remains nonzero on some neighborhood of \(\bar x\), and \(f/g\) is locally Lipschitz there. Its limiting subdifferential satisfies
\[\partial\!\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)(\bar x)\subseteq \frac{1}{g(\bar x)}\partial f(\bar x)-\frac{f(\bar x)}{g(\bar x)^2}\partial g(\bar x).\]
The inclusion follows from reciprocal scalar composition together with the product calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Away from a zero denominator, quotient subgradients lie in the usual value-weighted combination of numerator and denominator limiting subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Rules

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Nonvanishing of the denominator alone does not justify the displayed formula for the limiting subdifferential because its coefficients may be negative. Taking f=-|x| and constant g=-1 at zero yields the same failure: the left side is [-1,1], whereas the proposed right side is {-1,1}.

children.title: Scalar Rescaling Rules
children.top_down_role: Behavior of generalized derivatives under scalar transformations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\alpha f)(\bar x)=\alpha\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(\partial^\infty(\alpha f)(\bar x)=\alpha\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive homogeneity of limiting and horizon subdifferentials.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every positive scalar \(\alpha\), scalar rescaling commutes exactly with the limiting and horizon subdifferentials:
\[\partial(\alpha f)(\bar x)=\alpha\,\partial f(\bar x),\qquad \partial^\infty(\alpha f)(\bar x)=\alpha\,\partial^\infty f(\bar x).\]
For \(\alpha=0\), the finite constant function has limiting subdifferential \(\{0\}\). Negative scaling is not covered because a lower subdifferential generally transforms into a corresponding upper-subdifferential object.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scalar multiplication scales limiting and horizon subdifferentials exactly; negative scaling generally requires an upper-subdifferential construction.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Rescaling Rules

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Degenerate Denominator Regimes
children.top_down_role: Obstructions arising near vanishing or irregular denominators.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quotient \(f/g\) is undefined at \(\bar x\), unbounded near \(\bar x\), and admits no local finite-valued quotient subdifferential rule there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of quotient calculus when the denominator vanishes at the base point.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Although \(f\) and \(g\) are smooth and satisfy \(f(0)=g(0)=0\), their quotient on its natural domain is
\[q(x)=\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac{1}{x}\quad\text{for }x\neq0.\]
The function \(q\) is undefined at \(0\), is unbounded on every punctured neighborhood of \(0\), and has no finite locally Lipschitz extension there. Consequently, the nonvanishing-denominator hypothesis in the quotient rule cannot simply be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the denominator vanishes, even smooth numerator and denominator functions can produce an undefined, locally unbounded quotient, so the ordinary quotient subdifferential rule fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Denominator Regimes

children.title: Stochastic Integral Interchange Calculus
children.top_down_role: Subdifferential interchange for parameterized integrals and expectations.

children.title: Integral Interchange
children.top_down_role: Subdifferential passage through parameterized integration.

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a complete finite measure space, and \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is a normal integrand with \(f(\omega,\cdot)\) convex for almost every \(\omega\).
For some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(|f(\omega,x)-f(\omega,y)|\leq L(\omega)\|x-y\|\) for \(x,y\in U\), where \(L\in L^1(\mu)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial F(\bar x)=\left\{\int_\Omega v\,d\mu:v\text{ is measurable and }v(\omega)\in\partial f(\omega,\bar x)\text{ a.e.}\right\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex finite-dimensional subdifferential interchange under an integrable local Lipschitz bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(F(x)=\int_\Omega f(\omega,x)\,d\mu(\omega)\). Under the normal-integrand, convexity, and integrable local Lipschitz hypotheses, \(F\) is finite and locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), and
\[\partial F(\bar x)=\left\{\int_\Omega v(\omega)\,d\mu(\omega):v\text{ is measurable and }v(\omega)\in\partial f(\omega,\bar x)\text{ for almost every }\omega\right\}.\]
The integral on the right is the set of integrals of all integrable measurable subgradient selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex normal integrand with an integrable local Lipschitz bound, subdifferentiation commutes with integration through integrable measurable selections of pointwise subgradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Interchange

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports the interchange equality, and the assumptions do not require integrability of f(·,x0) at any point. An integrable Lipschitz modulus controls differences but does not by itself make the integral functional finite. The measurable-selection conditions also require authoritative validation.

children.title: Expectation Interchange
children.top_down_role: Generalized differentiation of expected-value functionals.

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb P)\) is a complete probability space, and \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is a normal integrand with \(f(\omega,\cdot)\) convex almost surely.
Near \(\bar x\), the sample functions have an almost-sure Lipschitz modulus \(L\) with \(\mathbb E[L]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\mathbb E[f(\cdot,\bar x)]=\mathbb E_A[\partial f(\cdot,\bar x)]\), where the right side is the Aumann expectation.

notation.meaning: Aumann expectation of a random set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-space specialization of convex integral subdifferentiation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Phi(x)=\mathbb E[f(\cdot,x)]\). Under the stated convex normal-integrand and integrable Lipschitz assumptions,
\[\partial\Phi(\bar x)=\mathbb E_A[\partial f(\cdot,\bar x)] := \left\{\mathbb E[v]:v\text{ is measurable, integrable, and }v(\omega)\in\partial f(\omega,\bar x)\text{ almost surely}\right\}.\]
Thus every expected-objective subgradient is the expectation of an integrable measurable selection of sample subgradients, and every such selection expectation is an expected-objective subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex random integrands with integrably bounded local slopes, the subdifferential of the expectation equals the Aumann expectation of the sample subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Interchange

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expectation-interchange equality has no cited source, and integrability of the random baseline f(·,x̄) is not assumed. Integrability of the Lipschitz modulus alone does not ensure that the expected-value objective is finite or that the stated Aumann expectation formula applies.

children.title: Measurable Selection Requirements
children.top_down_role: Measurability structure supporting integrated generalized derivatives.

assumptions_latex: The probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is complete, and \(f:\mathbb R^n\times\Omega\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a jointly measurable normal integrand.
At the reference point \(x\), the multifunction \(S(\omega)=\partial f(x,\omega)\) has nonempty closed values almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Aumann integral \(\int_\Omega S\,d\mathbb P\) is well defined and nonempty.

notation.meaning: Limiting or otherwise contextually fixed subdifferential of the sample integrand.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional measurability and integrable-selection conditions for stochastic subdifferential integration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The measurable-selection requirement at \(x\) is that \(S(\omega)=\partial f(x,\omega)\) be graph measurable, meaning \(\operatorname{gph}S\in\mathcal F\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)\), and admit an integrable selection. Thus there must exist an \(\mathcal F\)-measurable map \(s:\Omega\to\mathbb R^n\) such that \(s(\omega)\in S(\omega)\) almost surely and \(\mathbb E\lVert s\rVert<\infty\). A commonly checkable stronger requirement is an integrable bound \(\sup_{v\in S(\omega)}\lVert v\rVert\le m(\omega)\) almost surely for some \(m\in L^1(\Omega)\). Under these conditions, the Aumann integral is the nonempty set \(\{\mathbb E s:s\text{ is an integrable selection of }S\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subdifferential integration requires a graph-measurable random closed set with at least one integrable measurable selection; an integrable bound on all selected subgradients is a standard sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Selection Requirements

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The measurable-selection and integrable-boundedness claims are plausible, but no inspectable source fixes the subdifferential notion or supports the asserted measurability and nonemptiness conditions. The listed assumptions also omit the integrable-selection condition needed by the conclusion.

children.title: Interchange Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failures associated with measurability, integrability, or domination gaps.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(x=0\), \(\partial_C\mathbb E[f(\cdot,\omega)](0)\ne\mathbb E[\partial_C f(0,\omega)]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure when sample derivatives lack an integrable local domination bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(\omega>0\), the function \(f(\cdot,\omega)\) is smooth and satisfies \(\partial_C f(0,\omega)=\{0\}\). Hence \(\mathbb E[\partial_C f(0,\omega)]=\{0\}\). Direct integration gives \(F(0)=0\) and, for \(x\ne0\), \(F(x)=|x|\arctan(1/|x|)\). Consequently \(\partial_C F(0)=[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\), so subdifferentiation and expectation do not interchange. The obstruction is the absence of an integrable local Lipschitz modulus: sample derivatives become concentrated near \(\omega=0\), and no integrable random variable uniformly bounds them on any neighborhood of \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without integrable local domination, every sample derivative may vanish at the reference point while the expected objective develops a nonzero cusp, invalidating subdifferential interchange.
knowledge_statements.title: Interchange Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample and its calculations are mathematically plausible and fit the failure-boundary container, but this nontrivial example has no source record or standard-field rationale.

children.title: Paired Differential Representation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Algebraic calculus for paired differential representations.

children.title: Quasidifferential Calculus
children.top_down_role: Algebraic operations for quasidifferential representations.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is directionally differentiable at \(x\).
The sets \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty, convex, and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordered pair \([A,B]\) represents the quasidifferential of \(f\) at \(x\).

notation.meaning: Directional derivative of the function at the reference point.
Support function of a compact convex set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demyanov-style finite-dimensional quasidifferential representation and elementary pair arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is quasidifferentiable at \(x\) with quasidifferential \([A,B]\) when, for every \(h\in\mathbb R^n\), \[f'(x;h)=\max_{a\in A}\langle a,h\rangle+\min_{b\in B}\langle b,h\rangle.\] If \(f_i\) have pairs \([A_i,B_i]\) at \(x\), then \(f_1+f_2\) has pair \([A_1+A_2,B_1+B_2]\). For a scalar \(\lambda\ge0\), the pair for \(\lambda f\) is \([\lambda A,\lambda B]\); for \(\lambda<0\), it is \([\lambda B,\lambda A]\). These pairs are representations and need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasidifferential represents every directional derivative as a support function plus a lower support function; sums and scalar multiples are computed by Minkowski pair arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasidifferential Calculus

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional quasidifferential representation and pair arithmetic fit the container, but no source supports the selected max-plus-min convention or the calculus formulas.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Difference-of-Sublinear Closure under Order-Bounded Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator decomposition underlying composition of quasidifferentiable mappings in Banach K-spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $Y,Z$ be Banach $K$-spaces. Suppose $S,T\in\mathcal P(X,Y)$ and $P,Q\in\mathcal P(Y,Z)$, with $P$ and $Q$ order bounded. Then $R=(P-Q)\circ(S-T)$ can be expressed as the difference of two sublinear operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a difference of two order-bounded sublinear operators with a difference of two sublinear operators produces an operator that can again be represented as a difference of two sublinear operators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R=(P-Q)\circ(S-T)\text{ is expressible as a difference of two sublinear operators}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasidifferentiability of Banach K-Space Compositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule for quasidifferentiable mappings when the outer quasidifferential has bounded regular-operator representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a Banach space, let $Y,Z$ be Banach $K$-spaces, and let $\Omega_1\subset X$ and $\Omega_2\subset Y$ be open. Suppose $H:\Omega_1\to\Omega_2$ is quasidifferentiable at $x\in\Omega_1$, and $G:\Omega_2\to Z$ is Hadamard differentiable and quasidifferentiable at $y=H(x)$. If $G$ has a quasidifferential $\mathcal DG(y)=[\partial G(y),\bar\partial G(y)]$ such that both representing sets consist of regular operators and are bounded in the space of regular operators, then $F=G\circ H$ is quasidifferentiable at $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasidifferentiable inner mapping composed with an outer mapping that is both Hadamard differentiable and quasidifferentiable remains quasidifferentiable when the two sets representing an outer quasidifferential are bounded sets of regular operators.
assumptions_latex: G:\Omega_2\to Z\text{ is Hadamard differentiable and quasidifferentiable at }y
\mathcal DG(y)=[\partial G(y),\bar\partial G(y)]\text{ with both sets consisting of regular operators and bounded in their space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=G\circ H\text{ is quasidifferentiable at }x.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasidifferentiable Mappings into Banach K-Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-valued quasidifferentiability, its support-set representation, and elementary closure properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X$ be a Banach space, $\Omega\subset X$ be open, $Y$ be a Banach $K$-space, and $x\in\Omega$. A mapping $H:\Omega\to Y$ is quasidifferentiable at $x$ if it is directionally differentiable there and $H'_x$ is the sum of a continuous sublinear operator and a continuous superlinear operator. Its quasidifferential $\mathcal DH(x)$ is the corresponding equivalence class $[U,V]$ of support-set pairs satisfying $H'_x(g)=\max_{A\in U}A(g)+\min_{B\in V}B(g)$ for every $g\in X$. If $H_1$ and $H_2$ are quasidifferentiable at $x$, then $H_1+H_2$ is quasidifferentiable at $x$ and $\mathcal D(H_1+H_2)(x)=\mathcal DH_1(x)+\mathcal DH_2(x)$. If $H$ and a function $f$ are quasidifferentiable at $x$, then $fH$ is quasidifferentiable at $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping into a Banach K-space is quasidifferentiable when its directional derivative decomposes into continuous sublinear and superlinear parts. Its quasidifferential is the equivalence class of support-set pairs representing that derivative. Quasidifferentiability is preserved by addition and by multiplication of a quasidifferentiable mapping by a quasidifferentiable function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\text{ is quasidifferentiable at }x\iff H\text{ is directionally differentiable at }x\text{ and }H'_x(g)=\max_{A\in U}A(g)+\min_{B\in V}B(g)\ \forall g\in X\text{ for a quasidifferential class }[U,V];\quad \mathcal D(H_1+H_2)(x)=\mathcal DH_1(x)+\mathcal DH_2(x),\quad fH\text{ is quasidifferentiable at }x.

children.title: Codifferential Calculus
children.top_down_role: Algebraic operations for codifferential representations.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is defined near \(x\).
The sets \(\underline d f(x),\overline d f(x)\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\) are nonempty, convex, and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normalized pair \([\underline d f(x),\overline d f(x)]\) is a codifferential of \(f\) at \(x\).

notation.meaning: Lower codifferential set under the max-plus-min convention.
Upper codifferential set under the max-plus-min convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional normalized codifferential under the max-plus-min convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \([\underline d f(x),\overline d f(x)]\) is a codifferential at \(x\) when \(\max_{(a,v)\in\underline d f(x)}a=0\), \(\min_{(b,w)\in\overline d f(x)}b=0\), and, as \(h\to0\), \[f(x+h)-f(x)=\max_{(a,v)\in\underline d f(x)}\bigl(a+\langle v,h\rangle\bigr)+\min_{(b,w)\in\overline d f(x)}\bigl(b+\langle w,h\rangle\bigr)+o(\lVert h\rVert).\] For codifferentiable \(f_1,f_2\), a codifferential of \(f_1+f_2\) is obtained by taking the Minkowski sums of the respective lower sets and of the respective upper sets, followed by normalization if necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A codifferential is a normalized pair of compact convex affine models whose maximum-plus-minimum expansion approximates the function increment to first order.
knowledge_statements.title: Codifferential Calculus

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits codifferential calculus, but the normalization and max-plus-min convention require a direct, inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal rule for codifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure and codifferential formula for a reciprocal at a nonzero function value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If $f_1$ is codifferentiable at $x\in X$ and $f_1(x)\ne0$, then $f=1/f_1$ is codifferentiable at $x$ and
\[
Df(x)=-\frac{1}{f_1(x)^2}Df_1(x).
\]
If $f_1$ is continuously codifferentiable at $x$, then $1/f_1$ is continuously codifferentiable there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point where a codifferentiable function is nonzero, its reciprocal is codifferentiable and has codifferential minus the original codifferential divided by the squared function value. The continuous variant is preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{1}{f_1}\text{ is codifferentiable at }x,\qquad D\!\left(\frac{1}{f_1}\right)(x)=-\frac{1}{f_1(x)^2}Df_1(x),\text{ with the corresponding continuous-codifferentiability conclusion under the stronger hypothesis.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product rule for codifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure and Leibniz formula for the product of two codifferentiable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If $f_1$ and $f_2$ are codifferentiable at $x\in X$, then $f=f_1f_2$ is codifferentiable at $x$ and
\[
Df(x)=f_1(x)Df_2(x)+f_2(x)Df_1(x).
\]
If both functions are continuously codifferentiable at $x$, then their product is continuously codifferentiable there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The product of two functions codifferentiable at x is codifferentiable there, with the usual Leibniz-type codifferential formula. The continuous variant is preserved as well.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_1f_2\text{ is codifferentiable at }x,\qquad D(f_1f_2)(x)=f_1(x)Df_2(x)+f_2(x)Df_1(x),\text{ with the corresponding continuous-codifferentiability conclusion under the stronger hypothesis.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-combination rule for codifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure and codifferential formula for finite real linear combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $c_i\in\mathbb{R}$. If $f_1,\ldots,f_N$ are codifferentiable at $x\in X$, then $f=\sum_{i=1}^N c_i f_i$ is codifferentiable at $x$ and
\[
Df(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N c_iDf_i(x).
\]
If the $f_i$ are continuously codifferentiable at $x$, then $f$ is continuously codifferentiable there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite real linear combinations preserve codifferentiability, and the resulting codifferential is the corresponding linear combination. The continuous variant is preserved as well.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=\sum_{i=1}^N c_if_i\text{ is codifferentiable at }x,\qquad Df(x)=\sum_{i=1}^N c_iDf_i(x),\text{ with the corresponding continuous-codifferentiability conclusion under that stronger hypothesis.}
