knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite maximum and minimum rules for codifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure and component formulas for finite pointwise maxima and minima of codifferentiable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and suppose each $\varphi_i$ is codifferentiable at $x$. Define
\[
f_1(y)=\max_{i\in I}\varphi_i(y),\qquad f_2(y)=\min_{i\in I}\varphi_i(y).
\]
Then $f_1$ and $f_2$ are codifferentiable at $x$. Writing $D\varphi_i(x)=[\underline d\varphi_i(x),\bar d\varphi_i(x)]$, one may take
\[
\underline d f_1(x)=\operatorname{co}\!\left\{\underline d\varphi_k(x)-\sum_{i\in I\setminus\{k\}}\bar d\varphi_i(x)+\{[\varphi_k(x)-f_1(x),0_n]\}:k\in I\right\},
\]
\[
\bar d f_1(x)=\sum_{i\in I}\bar d\varphi_i(x),\qquad \underline d f_2(x)=\sum_{i\in I}\underline d\varphi_i(x),
\]
\[
\bar d f_2(x)=\operatorname{co}\!\left\{\bar d\varphi_k(x)-\sum_{i\in I\setminus\{k\}}\underline d\varphi_i(x)+\{[\varphi_k(x)-f_2(x),0_n]\}:k\in I\right\}.
\]
If all $\varphi_i$ are continuously codifferentiable at $x$, then so are $f_1$ and $f_2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite pointwise maxima and minima preserve codifferentiability. Their lower and upper codifferential components are given by the displayed convex-hull and Minkowski-sum formulas, and the continuous variant is preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_1=\max_{i\in I}\varphi_i\text{ and }f_2=\min_{i\in I}\varphi_i\text{ are codifferentiable at }x\text{ with the displayed component formulas; under continuous codifferentiability of all }\varphi_i,\text{ both are continuously codifferentiable.}

children.title: Difference-of-Convex Calculus
children.top_down_role: Calculus organized through convex-difference decompositions.

assumptions_latex: The functions \(g,h:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) are proper convex and finite near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The directional derivative of \(f\) is represented by \([\partial g(x),-\partial h(x)]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local finite-dimensional calculus for explicit difference-of-convex decompositions.

source_refs.locator: 4.4.4 Difference-of-convex functions p. 224

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), convex directional differentiation yields \[f'(x;d)=\max_{u\in\partial g(x)}\langle u,d\rangle-\max_{v\in\partial h(x)}\langle v,d\rangle.\] Hence \([\partial g(x),-\partial h(x)]\) is a quasidifferential pair for \(f\). If \(f_i=g_i-h_i\) are difference-of-convex functions, then \(f_1+f_2=(g_1+g_2)-(h_1+h_2)\), and for \(\lambda<0\), \(\lambda f=(-\lambda)h-(-\lambda)g\). The decomposition is not intrinsic: adding the same convex function to both components leaves \(f\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a difference of finite convex functions, the directional derivative is the difference of their support functions, and DC decompositions obey explicit sum and scalar arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.title: Difference-of-Convex Calculus

children.title: Paired-Representation Translations
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences among paired generalized differential representations.

assumptions_latex: The function \(f\) is codifferentiable at \(x\) under the max-plus-min convention.
The active zero-level faces of both codifferential sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active slope faces form a quasidifferential pair for \(f\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translations among normalized codifferentials, quasidifferentials, and explicit DC directional representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Taking directional limits in the codifferential expansion gives \[f'(x;h)=\max_{v\in A}\langle v,h\rangle+\min_{w\in B}\langle w,h\rangle,\] where \(A=\{v:(0,v)\in\underline d f(x)\}\) and \(B=\{w:(0,w)\in\overline d f(x)\}\). Thus \([A,B]\) is a quasidifferential. Conversely, a quasidifferential pair \([A,B]\) defines the first-order codifferential pair \([\{0\}\times A,\{0\}\times B]\). For an explicit DC decomposition \(f=g-h\) with convex components finite near \(x\), the corresponding quasidifferential is \([\partial g(x),-\partial h(x)]\). All three representations are generally nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-level slope faces translate a codifferential into a quasidifferential; a quasidifferential embeds back as zero-offset affine sets, while a DC decomposition supplies a canonical pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Paired-Representation Translations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivative Chain Rule for a Strictly Differentiable Inner Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal and mixed coderivative pullback inclusions, with equality and regularity inheritance under the corresponding regularity hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:X\to Y\) be strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\), let \(\bar y=g(\bar x)\), and let \(\bar z\in(F\circ g)(\bar x)\). Suppose that \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is closed around \((\bar y,\bar z)\), that \(F\) is PSNC there, and that \[D_M^*F(\bar y,\bar z)(0)\cap\ker\nabla g(\bar x)^*=\{0\}.\] The latter two conditions hold automatically if \(F\) is Lipschitz-like around \((\bar y,\bar z)\). Then, for every \(z^*\in Z^*\) and \(D^*\in\{D_N^*,D_M^*\}\), \[D^*(F\circ g)(\bar x,\bar z)(z^*)\subset\nabla g(\bar x)^*D^*F(\bar y,\bar z)(z^*).\] If \(F\) is \(N\)-regular, respectively \(M\)-regular, at \((\bar y,\bar z)\), then equality holds for the corresponding coderivative and \(F\circ g\) has the corresponding regularity at \((\bar x,\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly differentiable inner mapping, the normal or mixed coderivative of the composition is contained in the adjoint-derivative pullback of the corresponding coderivative of the outer multifunction. Corresponding regularity makes the rule exact and passes to the composition.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Regularity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke regularity as the interface between directional derivatives and subdifferential support functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\) precisely when \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^\circ(\bar x;h)\quad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R^n.\] At a Clarke-regular point, its ordinary directional derivative therefore satisfies \[f'(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial_C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\quad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R^n.\] Without Clarke regularity, the inequality \(f'(\bar x;h)\le f^\circ(\bar x;h)\) may be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clarke regularity means that ordinary and Clarke directional derivatives coincide in every direction. At a regular point, the ordinary directional derivative is the support function of the Clarke subdifferential; without regularity, the Clarke derivative may be larger.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
The ordinary one-sided directional derivative \(f'(\bar x;h)\) exists for every \(h\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clarke regularity is equivalent to \(f'(\bar x;h)=f^\circ(\bar x;h)\) for every \(h\).

knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Rule Regularity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete strict Clarke-chain-rule inclusion caused by failure of outer regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2\) be given by \(f(y_1,y_2)=|y_1|-|y_2|\) and \(F(t)=(t,t)\). Both maps are locally Lipschitz and \(F\) is smooth, but \(f\) is not Clarke regular at \((0,0)\). Since \((f\circ F)(t)=0\), one has \(\partial_C(f\circ F)(0)=\{0\}\). In contrast, \(\partial_C f(0,0)=[-1,1]^2\), and therefore \(F'(0)^T\partial_C f(0,0)=[-2,2]\). Thus the standard Clarke chain-rule inclusion is strict; smoothness of the inner map alone does not ensure equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth inner map does not guarantee exact Clarke chain calculus: a nonregular outer function can make the chain-rule inclusion strict.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_C(f\circ F)(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq F'(0)^T\partial_Cf(0,0)=[-2,2]\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-normal inclusion for a smooth inverse image under a basic normal qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) be locally closed near \(F(\bar x)\), and set \(S=F^{-1}(C)\). Suppose the inverse-image qualification \(N_C(F(\bar x))\cap\ker F'(\bar x)^T=\{0\}\) holds. knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Image Qualification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate derivative example where both tangent linearization and normal pullback fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(F(x)=x^2\), let \(C=\{0\}\), and take \(\bar x=0\). Then \(S=F^{-1}(C)=\{0\}\), so \(T_S(0)=\{0\}\) and \(N_S(0)=\mathbb{R}\). However, \(F'(0)=0\), whence the linearized tangent set is \(\{d:F'(0)d\in T_C(0)\}=\mathbb{R}\), while the adjoint normal pullback is \(F'(0)^TN_C(0)=\{0\}\). The normal qualification fails because \(N_C(0)\cap\ker F'(0)^T=\mathbb{R}\). Thus neither exact tangent nor normal inverse-image calculus survives this degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Chain Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-coderivative chain inclusion with intermediate-point and abnormal-multiplier qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(G:\mathbb{R}^m\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^p\), define \(H=G\circ F\), and fix \((\bar x,\bar z)\in\operatorname{gph}H\). Define the intermediate-point mapping by \(S(x,z)=F(x)\cap G^{-1}(z)\). Assume \(S\) is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar z)\), that \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is locally closed near every \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with \(\bar y\in S(\bar x,\bar z)\), and that \(\operatorname{gph}G\) is locally closed near every corresponding \((\bar y,\bar z)\). Suppose, for every \(\bar y\in S(\bar x,\bar z)\), that \[y^*\in D^*G(\bar y,\bar z)(0),\quad 0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y^*=0.\] Then, for every \(z^*\in\mathbb{R}^p\), \[D^*H(\bar x,\bar z)(z^*)\subset\bigcup_{\bar y\in S(\bar x,\bar z)}D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\bigl(D^*G(\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite-dimensional set-valued mappings, inner semicompactness of the intermediate-point mapping and exclusion of abnormal intermediate multipliers yield a limiting-coderivative chain-rule inclusion over all feasible intermediate points.
assumptions_latex: \(S(x,z)=F(x)\cap G^{-1}(z)\) is inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar z)\)
The graphs of \(F\) and \(G\) are locally closed near all relevant reference pairs
For every \(\bar y\in S(\bar x,\bar z)\), \(y^*\in D^*G(\bar y,\bar z)(0)\) and \(0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\) imply \(y^*=0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(z^*\in\mathbb{R}^p\), \(D^*(G\circ F)(\bar x,\bar z)(z^*)\subset\bigcup_{\bar y\in S(\bar x,\bar z)}D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(D^*G(\bar y,\bar z)(z^*))\).

notation.meaning: set of intermediate points y satisfying y in F(x) and z in G(y)

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Maximum Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivative and Clarke subdifferential of a finite maximum of smooth functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,r\), be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), and define \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le r}f_i(x)\). With active set \(I(\bar x)=\{i:f_i(\bar x)=f(\bar x)\}\), the function \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\), with \[f'(\bar x;d)=\max_{i\in I(\bar x)}\langle\nabla f_i(\bar x),d\rangle.\] Moreover, \(f\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\), and \[\partial_Cf(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite smooth maximum differentiates by maximizing active directional slopes, while its Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of active gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\) for every \(i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(\bar x;d)=\max_{i\in I(\bar x)}\langle\nabla f_i(\bar x),d\rangle\) and \(\partial_Cf(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}\)

notation.meaning: indices attaining the maximum at the reference point

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Minimum Calculus

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,r\), be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), and define \(f(x)=\min_{1\le i\le r}f_i(x)\). Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz near \( ar x\), and suppose that near \( ar x\), every value \(f(x)\) equals one of finitely many continuously differentiable selections \(f_1(x),\ldots,f_r(x)\). Let \(I_e( ar x)\) contain indices \(i\) for which points \(x_k	o ar x\) exist where \(f\) is differentiable, \(f(x_k)=f_i(x_k)\), and \(
abla f(x_k)	o

abla f_i( ar x):i\in I_e( ar x)\},\qquad \partial_Cf( ar x)=\operatorname{co}\partial_Bf( ar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand subdifferential contains gradients of essentially active smooth pieces, and convexifying it gives the Clarke subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Selection Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivative and subdifferential representation for the largest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb{S}^n\), let \(E\) be the eigenspace associated with \(\lambda_{\max}(X)\), and let the columns of \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}\) form an orthonormal basis of \(E\). For every symmetric direction \(H\), \[\lambda_{\max}'(X;H)=\lambda_{\max}(U^THU).\] The largest-eigenvalue function is convex and its convex and Clarke subdifferentials coincide, with \[\partial\lambda_{\max}(X)=\{UZU^T:Z\in\mathbb{S}_+^r,\ \operatorname{tr}Z=1\}.\] In particular, a simple leading eigenvalue with unit eigenvector \(u\) has the unique gradient \(uu^T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The leading eigenvalue differentiates through its top eigenspace; its subgradients are trace-one positive semidefinite matrices supported on that eigenspace.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) has orthonormal columns spanning the top eigenspace of \(X\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\max}'(X;H)=\lambda_{\max}(U^THU)\) and \(\partial\lambda_{\max}(X)=\{UZU^T:Z\succeq0,\operatorname{tr}Z=1\}\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectral formulas are standard and fit the representation container, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied for the eigenspace directional-derivative and subdifferential formulas.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Danskin's theorem for compactly indexed convex maxima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional-derivative and convex-subdifferential formulas for a compactly indexed pointwise maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let I\subset\mathbb{R}^n be compact and let \varphi:\mathbb{R}^d\times I\to\mathbb{R} be continuous, with \varphi(\cdot,i) convex for every i\in I. Define f(x):=\max_{i\in I}\varphi(x,i) and I_{\max}(x):=\arg\max_{i\in I}\varphi(x,i). Then f'(x;y)=\max_{i\in I_{\max}(x)}\varphi'(x,i;y). If additionally every \varphi(\cdot,i) is differentiable and i\mapsto\nabla_x\varphi(x,i) is continuous on I for every x, then \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\{\nabla_x\varphi(x,i):i\in I_{\max}(x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional bounds for a nonsmooth supremum value function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth Danskin inequalities comparing the value function's Clarke and upper directional slopes with derivatives of active branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be closed, with \(Y\) bounded, and suppose (L1)--(L3) hold. For the value function \(v(x)=\max_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\), its maximizer set \(M(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\), and any \(\bar x\in X\), \(v\) is locally Lipschitz at \(\bar x\). Moreover, for every \(d x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\sup_{y\in M(\bar x)}L(\cdot,\cdot)^\circ((\bar x,y);(d x,0))\ge v^\circ(\bar x;d x)\ge\limsup_{\tau\downarrow0}\frac{v(\bar x+\tau d x)-v(\bar x)}{\tau}\ge\sup_{y\in M(\bar x)}L(\cdot,y)'(\bar x;d x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standing upper-semicontinuity, uniform local-Lipschitz, and directional-differentiability assumptions, the maximum value function is locally Lipschitz. Its Clarke derivative and upper one-sided slope are bounded above by active joint Clarke derivatives and below by active ordinary directional derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathcal O_x\) and \(Y\subset\mathcal O_y\) are closed, and \(Y\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is locally Lipschitz at \(\bar x\), and the displayed chain of inequalities holds for every \(d x\in\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional upper-stability criterion for the Danskin property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for the directional-envelope identity based on upper stability of values and directional derivatives along rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be compact and \(\bar x\in X\). Assume that for every \((d x,\bar y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal O_y\), \[\limsup_{y\to\bar y,\,\tau\downarrow0}L(\bar x+\tau d x,y)\le L(\bar x,\bar y).\] Assume also that, for every \((d x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal O_y\) and all sufficiently small \(t>0\), \[L(\cdot,y)'(\bar x+t d x;d x)=\lim_{\tau\downarrow0}\frac{L(\bar x+(t+\tau)d x,y)-L(\bar x+t d x,y)}{\tau}\] exists and is bounded in \(t\). Finally, assume that for every \((d x,\bar y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal O_y\), \[\limsup_{y\to\bar y,\,\tau\downarrow0}L(\cdot,y)'(\bar x+\tau d x;d x)\le L(\cdot,\bar y)'(\bar x;d x).\] Then \(v\) has the Danskin property at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact parameter set, the Danskin property follows when branch values are upper stable along every ray, the branch derivatives along each ray exist and remain bounded for small positive displacements, and those derivatives are upper stable as the parameter and displacement approach their reference values.

For every \((d x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal O_y\), the stated ray derivative exists for all sufficiently small \(t>0\) and is bounded in \(t\).
The stated upper-limit inequality for the ray directional derivatives holds for every \((d x,\bar y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathcal O_y\).

assumptions_latex: \(f_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is open.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f_i:U\to\mathbb{R}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be continuously differentiable. Define \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\) and \(I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}\). Then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at every \(\bar x\in U\), with
\[
f'(\bar x;d)=\max_{i\in I(\bar x)}\langle\nabla f_i(\bar x),d\rangle
\quad(d\in\mathbb{R}^n).
\]
Moreover, its Clarke subdifferential is
\[
\partial_C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}\{\nabla f_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite smooth maximum has directional derivative equal to the largest active directional derivative, and its Clarke subdifferential is the convex hull of active gradients.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Index Envelopes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(Y\) be compact, and let \(\phi:U\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous. Suppose \(x\mapsto\phi(x,y)\) is continuously differentiable and \((x,y)\mapsto\nabla_x\phi(x,y)\) is continuous. Define \(v(x)=\max_{y\in Y}\phi(x,y)\) and \(S(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in Y}\phi(x,y)\). Then \(S(\bar x)\) is nonempty and compact, and for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
v'(\bar x;d)=\max_{y\in S(\bar x)}\langle\nabla_x\phi(\bar x,y),d\rangle.
\]
Consequently, \(v\) is directionally differentiable at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact index set, the directional derivative of a smooth supremal value is the largest parameter derivative among current maximizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Index Envelopes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(Y\) be compact, and suppose \(\phi:U\times Y\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous, differentiable in \(x\), and has jointly continuous \(\nabla_x\phi\). Define \(v(x)=\min_{y\in Y}\phi(x,y)\) and \(S(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}\phi(x,y)\). The set \(S(\bar x)\) may contain several points, but for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
v'(\bar x;d)=\min_{y\in S(\bar x)}\langle\nabla_x\phi(\bar x,y),d\rangle.
\]
Thus no arbitrary selection from \(S(\bar x)\) may replace the optimization over active solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With multiple minimizers, the value derivative is the smallest parameter directional derivative across all active solutions, not the derivative at an arbitrary selection.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique-Solution Envelopes

assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous near \((\bar x,y)\) for active \(y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(v(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}\phi(x,y)\), let \(S(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_y\phi(x,y)\). Assume \(\phi\) is proper and lower semicontinuous near every \((\bar x,y)\) with \(y\in S(\bar x)\), the mapping \(S\) is inner semicompact at \(\bar x\), and
\[
(x^*,0)\in\partial^\infty\phi(\bar x,y)\ \Longrightarrow\ x^*=0
\]
for every \(y\in S(\bar x)\). Then the limiting subdifferential satisfies
\[
\partial v(\bar x)\subset\bigcup_{y\in S(\bar x)}\{x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n:(x^*,0)\in\partial\phi(\bar x,y)\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness and singular qualification, every limiting subgradient of an infimal value lifts to a joint subgradient with zero solution-coordinate component.
knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Subdifferential Calculus

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v(x)=\inf_y\phi(x,y)\) and \(S(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_y\phi(x,y)\). Suppose \(S\) is inner semicompact at \(\bar x\), and every first-order minimizing path in direction \(d\) admits a limit \(\bar y\in S(\bar x)\) and velocity \(w\in DS(\bar x\mid\bar y)(d)\). If \(\phi\) is Hadamard directionally differentiable and such tangent solution paths attain the first-order infimum, then
\[
v'(\bar x;d)=\inf_{\bar y\in S(\bar x)}\ \inf_{w\in DS(\bar x\mid\bar y)(d)}
\phi'((\bar x,\bar y);(d,w)).
\]
Thus solution-map stability is an explicit input to value-function calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Value derivatives are obtained from integrand derivatives along tangent directions of optimizing solution paths; compactness and stability of the solution map control validity.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Mapping Interface

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outside \(C\), \(d_C\) is differentiable with gradient \((x-P_Cx)/d_C(x)\); on \(C\), \(\partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap\mathbb{B}\).

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Distance Function p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and define \(d_C(x)=\inf_{z\in C}\|x-z\|\). The function \(d_C\) is convex and \(1\)-Lipschitz. If \(x\notin C\), its projection \(P_Cx\) is unique and
\[
\nabla d_C(x)=\frac{x-P_Cx}{\|x-P_Cx\|}.
\]
If \(x\in C\), then
\[
\partial d_C(x)=N_C(x)\cap\mathbb{B},
\qquad
d_C'(x;h)=\operatorname{dist}(h,T_C(x)).
\]
Here \(N_C(x)\), \(T_C(x)\), and \(\mathbb{B}\) denote the convex normal cone, tangent cone, and closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a closed convex set is one-Lipschitz; its gradient outside the set points from the projection, while its boundary subgradients are bounded normals.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Function Calculus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivative of the Euclidean projector onto a convex polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty closed convex polyhedron. For \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), set \(p=P_C(x)\) and define the critical cone
\[
K=T_C(p)\cap(x-p)^\perp.
\]
Then the Euclidean projection mapping \(P_C\) is globally Lipschitz and Hadamard directionally differentiable at \(x\). For every \(h\in\mathbb{R}^n\), its directional derivative is the projection onto the critical cone:
\[
P_C'(x;h)=P_K(h).
\]
Equivalently, \(P_C'(x;h)\) is the unique minimizer of \(\min_{w\in K}\|h-w\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex polyhedron, the directional derivative of the nearest-point projector is the projection of the perturbation onto the associated critical cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Mapping Calculus

children.title: Moreau-Envelope Calculus
children.top_down_role: Differential structure of Moreau regularizations.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_\lambda f\) is continuously differentiable and \(\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical convex Moreau envelope on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: G. Moreau Envelopes p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). Define
\[
e_\lambda f(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2\right\},
\qquad
p_\lambda(x)=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x).
\]
The minimizer \(p_\lambda(x)\) is unique for every \(x\), the envelope \(e_\lambda f\) is finite and continuously differentiable, and
\[
\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\frac{x-p_\lambda(x)}{\lambda}.
\]
Moreover, \(\nabla e_\lambda f\) is \(1/\lambda\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex Moreau envelope is smooth; its gradient is the scaled residual between a point and its proximal point.
knowledge_statements.title: Moreau-Envelope Calculus

children.title: Proximal-Mapping Calculus
children.top_down_role: Generalized differential behavior of proximal mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}=(I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}\) and the proximal mapping is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent and firm-nonexpansiveness calculus for convex proximal mappings.

source_refs.locator: G. Moreau Envelopes p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the point \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) is characterized by
\[
0\in\partial f(p)+\lambda^{-1}(p-x).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}=(I+\lambda\partial f)^{-1}.
\]
For all \(x,z\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the mapping is firmly nonexpansive:
\[
\|\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(z)\|^2
\leq
\langle\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(z),x-z\rangle.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex proximal map is the resolvent of the subdifferential and is firmly nonexpansive, hence single-valued and nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.title: Proximal-Mapping Calculus

children.title: Regularization Transfer
children.top_down_role: Transfer of variational properties between an original function and its proximal regularization.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}e_\lambda f=\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{x:\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=0\}\), with equal minimum values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of minimizers and stationarity through convex Moreau regularization.

source_refs.locator: G. Moreau Envelopes p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, let \(\lambda>0\), and assume \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\neq\varnothing\). Then
\[
\inf_x e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_x f(x)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname*{argmin}_x e_\lambda f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_x f(x).
\]
Using \(\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=\lambda^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x))\), one also has
\[
\nabla e_\lambda f(x)=0
\Longleftrightarrow
x=
\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)
\Longleftrightarrow
0\in\partial f(x)
\Longleftrightarrow
x\in\operatorname*{argmin}f.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex Moreau regularization preserves the minimum value and minimizers, while converting the original optimality condition into ordinary gradient stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularization Transfer

children.title: Single-Valuedness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local regimes supporting stable single-valued proximal behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proximal subproblem is strongly convex and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) is single-valued for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global uniqueness threshold for proximal points of a weakly convex function.

source_refs.locator: G. Moreau Envelopes p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and \(\rho\)-weakly convex, meaning that \(y\mapsto f(y)+(\rho/2)\|y\|^2\) is convex. If \(0<\lambda<1/\rho\), with \(1/0=+\infty\), then for each \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) the function
\[
y\mapsto f(y)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\|y-x\|^2
\]
is \((1/\lambda-\rho)\)-strongly convex. Hence it has at most one minimizer; whenever the minimum is attained, \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)\) is single-valued. In finite dimensions, proper lower semicontinuity and weak convexity ensure attainment for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly convex function has a unique proximal point whenever the proximal parameter is smaller than the reciprocal weak-convexity modulus.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Valuedness Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) are nonempty closed convex sets with nonempty intersection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\bigcap_i C_i\), \(N_{\cap_i C_i}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex normal-cone rule under relative-interior qualification.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Calculus of Generalized Normals p. 18
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets and assume
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\neq\varnothing.
\]
Then, for every \(x\in C:=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\), the convex normal cone to the intersection satisfies the exact sum rule
\[
N_C(x)=N_{C_1}(x)+\cdots+N_{C_m}(x).
\]
Equivalently, every \(x^*\in N_C(x)\) admits a decomposition \(x^*=x_1^*+\cdots+x_m^*\) with \(x_i^*\in N_{C_i}(x)\) for each \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a common relative-interior point condition, the normal cone to a finite convex intersection is exactly the sum of the individual normal cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Normal Calculus

children.title: Cartesian-Product Normal Calculus
children.top_down_role: Normal-cone behavior for product sets.

assumptions_latex: \(C_i\subset X_i\) is locally closed at \(\bar x_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
Each \(X_i\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{C_1\times\cdots\times C_m}(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_m)=N_{C_1}(\bar x_1)\times\cdots\times N_{C_m}(\bar x_m)\).

notation.meaning: Mordukhovich limiting normal cone to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian products and limiting normals in Euclidean spaces.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_i\subset X_i\) be locally closed at \(\bar x_i\in C_i\), where \(X_i\) is finite-dimensional for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Under the canonical identification \((X_1\times\cdots\times X_m)^*=X_1^*\times\cdots\times X_m^*\), the limiting normal cone factors exactly as
\[
N_{C_1\times\cdots\times C_m}(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_m)
=
N_{C_1}(\bar x_1)\times\cdots\times N_{C_m}(\bar x_m).
\]
The analogous equality holds for regular normal cones. Thus no transversality qualification is needed for a Cartesian product itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting normal cone to a finite Cartesian product is exactly the Cartesian product of the component normal cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian-Product Normal Calculus

children.title: Intersection Transversality
children.top_down_role: Geometric qualifications supporting sharp intersection formulas.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in A\cap B\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to the indicated set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic limiting-normal transversality condition for two-set intersections.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For locally closed sets \(A,B\subset X\) and \(\bar x\in A\cap B\), the limiting-normal transversality condition at \(\bar x\) is
\[
N_A(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_B(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(a^*\in N_A(\bar x)\), \(b^*\in N_B(\bar x)\), and \(a^*+b^*=0\), then \(a^*=b^*=0\). Under this condition, the standard limiting-normal intersection rule gives
\[
N_{A\cap B}(\bar x)\subset N_A(\bar x)+N_B(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transversality excludes nonzero opposing normals from the two sets and qualifies the limiting-normal intersection inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Transversality

children.title: Normal-Calculus Exactness Failure
children.top_down_role: Degenerate set interactions that weaken normal formulas.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_A(\bar x)+N_B(\bar x)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R\subsetneq\mathbb R^2=N_{A\cap B}(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete tangential intersection where the normal sum is not exact.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(A=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t\ge s^2\}\), \(B=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t\le -s^2\}\), and \(\bar x=(0,0)\). Then \(A\cap B=\{\bar x\}\), while
\[
N_A(\bar x)=\{(0,-\lambda):\lambda\ge0\},\qquad
N_B(\bar x)=\{(0,\lambda):\lambda\ge0\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
N_A(\bar x)+N_B(\bar x)=\{0\}\times\mathbb R
\subsetneq
\mathbb R^2=N_{A\cap B}(\bar x).
\]
Thus the normal-sum expression need not equal the intersection normal when transversality fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two oppositely tangent parabolic regions intersect only at the origin, whose full normal space strictly exceeds the sum of branch normals.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Calculus Exactness Failure

children.title: Finite-Union Normal Calculus
children.top_down_role: Branch-sensitive normals for finite unions.

assumptions_latex: \(C=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\), where each \(C_i\subset\mathbb R^n\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=\bigcap_{i\in I(\bar x)}\widehat N_{C_i}(\bar x)\) and \(N_C(\bar x)\subset\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}N_{C_i}(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Active branch indices at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular and limiting normals to a finite union of locally closed branches.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.3 Calculus of Generalized Normals p. 18
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i\subset\mathbb R^n\), and define \(I(\bar x)=\{i:\bar x\in C_i\}\). The regular normal cone obeys the exact active-branch formula
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=\bigcap_{i\in I(\bar x)}\widehat N_{C_i}(\bar x).
\]
For limiting normals, finite branch selection yields the generally nonexact estimate
\[
N_C(\bar x)\subset\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}N_{C_i}(\bar x).
\]
Hence every limiting normal is inherited from at least one active branch, whereas simultaneous activity restricts regular normals through intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular normals to a finite union intersect across active branches, while each limiting normal comes from at least one active branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Union Normal Calculus

children.title: Sum Coderivative Calculus
children.top_down_role: Coderivative behavior for sums of set-valued mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(F_i:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have locally closed graphs near \((\bar x,\bar y_i)\), with \(\bar y=\bar y_1+\bar y_2\).
The decomposition map for \(\bar y\) is locally inner semicompact.
The abnormal coderivative qualification holds at every relevant decomposition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*(F_1+F_2)(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{y_1+y_2=\bar y}\bigl(D^*F_1(\bar x,y_1)(y^*)+D^*F_2(\bar x,y_2)(y^*)\bigr)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-coderivative upper estimate for pointwise sums in Asplund spaces.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.2 Sequential Normal Compactness for Sums and Related Operations with Maps p. 349
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y\) be Asplund spaces and \(S(x)=F_1(x)+F_2(x)\). Suppose the graphs are locally closed, the decomposition mapping \((x,y)\mapsto\{(y_1,y_2):y_i\in F_i(x),\ y_1+y_2=y\}\) is inner semicompact near \((\bar x,\bar y)\), and the standard abnormal coderivative qualification holds. Then, for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
D^*S(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\subset
\bigcup_{\substack{\bar y_1+\bar y_2=\bar y\\ \bar y_i\in F_i(\bar x)}}
\left[D^*F_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(y^*)+D^*F_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(y^*)\right].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness and abnormal-normal qualifications, the coderivative of a multifunction sum is bounded by sums of coderivatives over feasible decompositions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sum Coderivative Calculus

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivative sum rule with a Lipschitz-like summand
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal and mixed coderivative sum rule in which Lipschitz-like behavior supplies the required qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}(F_1+F_2)\) and \((\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\in S(\bar x,\bar y)\). Suppose \(\operatorname{gph}F_i\) is locally closed around \((\bar x,\bar y_i)\) for \(i=1,2\), \(S\) is inner semicontinuous at \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar y_1,\bar y_2)\), and either \(F_1\) is Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar y_1)\) or \(F_2\) is Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar y_2)\). Then, for every \(y^*\in Y^*\) and \(D^*\in\{D_N^*,D_M^*\}\),
\[
D^*(F_1+F_2)(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset D^*F_1(\bar x,\bar y_1)(y^*)+D^*F_2(\bar x,\bar y_2)(y^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an inner-semicontinuously varying chosen decomposition, locally closed component graphs, and a Lipschitz-like summand, the componentwise sum estimate holds for both normal and mixed coderivatives.

children.title: Composition Coderivative Calculus
children.top_down_role: Coderivative behavior for compositions of set-valued mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) have locally closed graphs near the relevant points.
The intermediate-point map is locally inner semicompact at \((\bar x,\bar z)\).
The abnormal chain-rule qualification holds for every relevant \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*(G\circ F)(\bar x,\bar z)(z^*)\subset\bigcup_{\bar y}D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\bigl(D^*G(\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)\bigr)\).

notation.meaning: Set of intermediate points joining the reference pair

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting-coderivative chain rule for multifunction composition in Asplund spaces.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.3 Sequential Normal Compactness for Compositions of Maps p. 354
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Y,Z\) be Asplund spaces, \(H=G\circ F\), and
\[
M(\bar x,\bar z)=F(\bar x)\cap G^{-1}(\bar z).
\]
Assume local closedness, inner semicompactness of the intermediate-point mapping, and the abnormal chain-rule qualification at every \(\bar y\in M(\bar x,\bar z)\). Then, for every \(z^*\in Z^*\),
\[
D^*H(\bar x,\bar z)(z^*)
\subset
\bigcup_{\bar y\in M(\bar x,\bar z)}
D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\bigl(D^*G(\bar y,\bar z)(z^*)\bigr),
\]
where the outer coderivative is applied to every element of the inner coderivative set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A qualified composition coderivative lies in the union of successive coderivative images over all feasible intermediate points.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition Coderivative Calculus

children.title: Coderivative Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Normal-compactness and transversality conditions supporting coderivative calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), \(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\), and \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\) is graph-feasible.
The limiting coderivatives are taken at the displayed graph points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^*\in D^*G(\bar y,\bar z)(0)\) and \(0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\) imply \(y^*=0\).

notation.meaning: Zero functional in the appropriate dual space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: No-abnormal-multiplier qualification for the multifunction chain rule.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.3 Sequential Normal Compactness for Compositions of Maps p. 354
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible triple \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar z)\) with \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\) and \(\bar z\in G(\bar y)\), the basic coderivative chain-rule qualification is
\[
\left.
\begin{array}{c}
y^*\in D^*G(\bar y,\bar z)(0),\\
0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\end{array}
\right\}
\Longrightarrow y^*=0.
\]
It excludes a nonzero intermediate dual vector that is simultaneously abnormal for the outer graph and annihilated by the inner coderivative. For multiple feasible intermediate points, the condition is imposed at each such point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The chain-rule qualification rules out any nonzero intermediate multiplier that is outer-abnormal and simultaneously annihilated by the inner coderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Coderivative Qualifications

knowledge_statements.title: Inclusion-versus-Equality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrast between qualified multifunction inclusions and smooth exact identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Qualified limiting-coderivative sum and composition rules for general set-valued mappings are upper inclusions. In contrast, let \(X,Y,Z\) be Banach spaces, let \(f_1,f_2:X\to Y\), \(f:X\to Y\), and \(g:Y\to Z\) be single-valued mappings that are continuously Fréchet differentiable on neighborhoods of the relevant points, and let \(\bar x\in X\). Then, for every \(y^*\in Y^*\) and \(z^*\in Z^*\), the corresponding coderivative rules are exact:
\[
D^*(f_1+f_2)\bigl(\bar x,f_1(\bar x)+f_2(\bar x)\bigr)(y^*)
= Df_1(\bar x)^*y^*+Df_2(\bar x)^*y^*,
\]
\[
D^*(g\circ f)\bigl(\bar x,g(f(\bar x))\bigr)(z^*)
= Df(\bar x)^*Dg(f(\bar x))^*z^*.
\]
Thus qualifications that ensure an upper inclusion for multifunctions do not alone imply equality; smooth single-valued structure yields the displayed exact identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualified multifunction calculus generally supplies upper inclusions, whereas continuously differentiable single-valued mappings satisfy exact adjoint sum and chain identities.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y,Z\) are Banach spaces and \(\bar x\in X\).
\(f_1,f_2:X\to Y\), \(f:X\to Y\), and \(g:Y\to Z\) are continuously Fréchet differentiable on neighborhoods of the relevant points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(y^*\in Y^*\) and \(z^*\in Z^*\), the smooth single-valued coderivative sum and composition rules are the exact adjoint identities displayed in the statement, while the corresponding general qualified multifunction rules are upper inclusions.

notation.meaning: Adjoint of the Fréchet derivative of a smooth mapping
Limiting coderivative of a mapping at a graph point

children.title: Sequential Normal Compactness Calculus
children.top_down_role: Compactness mechanisms preserving Banach-space calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space and \(C_1,C_2\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in C_1\cap C_2\).
At least one set is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{C_1\cap C_2}(\bar x)\subset N_{C_1}(\bar x)+N_{C_2}(\bar x)\), with weak-star abnormal escape excluded by SNC.

notation.meaning: Weak-star convergence in the dual space

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(C\subset X\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in C\) when every sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\), satisfying \(x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0\) also satisfies \(\lVert x_k^*\rVert\to0\). If \(C_1,C_2\) are locally closed, at least one is SNC at \(\bar x\), and
\[
N_{C_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{C_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\},
\]
then the Banach-space limiting-normal intersection calculus is preserved:
\[
N_{C_1\cap C_2}(\bar x)\subset N_{C_1}(\bar x)+N_{C_2}(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SNC converts weak-star vanishing normals into norm-vanishing ones, preventing compactness loss in qualified Banach-space intersection calculus.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Normal Compactness Calculus

children.title: Qualification Failure
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of regularity conditions required by first-order calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(C_1,C_2\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in C_1\cap C_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Qualification fails exactly when \(N_{C_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{C_2}(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Limiting normal cone to the indicated set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for the two-set limiting-normal qualification.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The basic two-set normal qualification fails at \(\bar x\in C_1\cap C_2\) precisely when
\[
N_{C_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{C_2}(\bar x)\bigr)\ne\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, there exist \(x_1^*\in N_{C_1}(\bar x)\) and \(x_2^*\in N_{C_2}(\bar x)\), not both zero, such that
\[
x_1^*+x_2^*=0.
\]
At this boundary the standard limiting-normal intersection inclusion is no longer guaranteed by the qualification theorem; failure of the condition does not by itself assert that the inclusion fails for every particular pair of sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualification fails when the sets admit nonzero limiting normals that cancel; then the standard intersection rule is no longer guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failure

children.title: Transversality Failure
children.top_down_role: Degenerate geometric alignment among component sets or mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(A,B\subset\mathbb R^n\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in A\cap B\).
There exists \(v\ne0\) with \(v\in N_A(\bar x)\) and \(-v\in N_B(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limiting-normal transversality condition fails at \(\bar x\), so stability and normal-intersection conclusions requiring it cannot be invoked.

notation.meaning: A nonzero common opposing normal direction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric loss of transversality through a shared opposing normal.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Transversality of \(A\) and \(B\) fails at \(\bar x\) when there exists a nonzero covector \(v\) such that
\[
v\in N_A(\bar x),\qquad -v\in N_B(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
N_A(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_B(\bar x)\bigr)\ne\{0\}.
\]
The direction \(v\) is normal to both sets with opposite orientations and therefore records first-order tangency or opposing constraint activity. Any normal-intersection or stability result whose hypothesis is the zero-intersection condition lies beyond its guaranteed regime at this point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transversality fails when the sets share a nonzero normal direction with opposite orientations, indicating first-order tangency or opposing activity.
knowledge_statements.title: Transversality Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An abnormal normal interaction at \(\bar x\in C_1\cap C_2\) is certified by covectors \(x_1^*,x_2^*\) satisfying
\[
x_1^*\in N_{C_1}(\bar x),\qquad
x_2^*\in N_{C_2}(\bar x),\qquad
x_1^*+x_2^*=0,
\]
with \((x_1^*,x_2^*)\ne(0,0)\). Membership in the two normal cones and the displayed linear cancellation are directly checkable. Such a pair is exactly a nontrivial homogeneous multiplier and certifies failure of the zero-opposing-normal qualification used in limiting-normal intersection calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonzero-compatible normal covectors that sum to zero form a direct certificate of abnormal interaction and qualification failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Abnormal Normal Interactions

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{C\cap D}(0,0)\supsetneq N_C(0,0)+N_D(0,0)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y):y\geq x^2\}\) and \(D=\{(x,y):y\leq0\}\). Then \(C\cap D=\{(0,0)\}\), so \(N_{C\cap D}(0,0)=\mathbb{R}^2\). In contrast, \(N_C(0,0)=\{(0,\beta):\beta\leq0\}\) and \(N_D(0,0)=\{(0,\beta):\beta\geq0\}\), whence \(N_C(0,0)+N_D(0,0)=\{0\}\times\mathbb{R}\). Thus the standard normal-cone inclusion is strict; the missing horizontal normals demonstrate loss of exactness under tangential contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two tangential closed sets can have an intersection normal cone strictly larger than the sum of their individual normal cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonzero horizon multipliers obstruct the basic finite-dimensional limiting-subdifferential chain-rule qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A horizon obstruction to the composition \(f\circ F\) at \( ar x\) is a vector \(y^*
eq0\) satisfying \(y^*\in\partial^\infty f(F( ar x))\) and \(
abla F( ar x)^*y^*=0\). Equivalently, an obstruction exists precisely when \(\partial^\infty f(F( ar x))\cap\ker
abla F( ar x)^*
eq\{0\}\). Such a multiplier is annihilated by the derivative pullback and therefore violates the usual horizon qualification for the limiting-subdifferential chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero horizon subgradient annihilated by the inner derivative is an obstruction to the usual composition qualification.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous near \(F(\bar x)\), with \(f(F(\bar x))<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(F(\bar x))\cap\ker \nabla F(\bar x)^*\neq\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A singular-subdifferential obstruction for the sum \(f+g\) at \(\bar x\) is a vector \(v\neq0\) such that \(v\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) and \(-v\in\partial^\infty g(\bar x)\). Thus an obstruction exists exactly when \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)]\neq\{0\}\). Its absence is the qualification normally imposed to derive the limiting inclusion \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subset\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposing nonzero singular subgradients obstruct the standard qualification used in limiting-subdifferential sum calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous with \(f(\bar x)\) finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\neq\{0\}\) is possible when local Lipschitz continuity is lost.

notation.meaning: Horizon subdifferential of f at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonzero horizon subgradients mark the failure of automatic qualifications supplied by local Lipschitz continuity.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}\). Without local Lipschitz continuity this conclusion can fail: for \(f(x)=\sqrt{|x|}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), one has \(\partial^\infty f(0)=\mathbb{R}\). Consequently, qualifications involving horizon subgradients no longer hold automatically, and sum or composition calculus may require separate noncancellation conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitz continuity forces a trivial horizon subdifferential; its loss permits nonzero horizon directions that obstruct calculus.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(F(\bar x))\cap\ker\nabla F(\bar x)^*\neq\{0\}\) invalidates the standard qualification.

notation.meaning: Horizon subdifferential of the outer function.
Adjoint derivative of the inner mapping.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The standard horizon qualification for the limiting chain rule is \(\partial^\infty f(F( ar x))\cap\ker
abla F( ar x)^*=\{0\}\). Breakdown occurs when some \(y^*
eq0\) belongs to \(\partial^\infty f(F( ar x))\) while \(
abla F( ar x)^*y^*=0\). At this boundary the derivative cannot detect a nonzero singular direction of the outer function, so the usual limiting-subdifferential chain-rule conclusion is not guaranteed by this qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The horizon qualification breaks down when the inner derivative annihilates a nonzero horizon subgradient of the outer function.

children.title: Nonregular Composition Failure

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(h\circ F)(0)=[-1,1]\supsetneq F'(0)^*\partial h(F(0))=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Derivative of the inner scalar mapping.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample to exact pullback when the outer function has a singular cusp.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Subdifferential Calculus and Related Topics p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(t)=\sqrt{|t|}\) and \(F(x)=x^2\), the composition is \((h\circ F)(x)=|x|\), hence \(\partial(h\circ F)(0)=[-1,1]\). Although \(\partial h(0)=\mathbb{R}\), one has \(F'(0)=0\), and therefore \(F'(0)^*\partial h(0)=\{0\}\). Thus the formal pullback misses every nonzero subgradient of the composition; the failure is enabled by the outer singularity together with degeneracy of the inner derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular outer cusp composed with a degenerate smooth map makes the formal subgradient pullback strictly too small.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonregular Composition Failure

children.title: Active-Selection Failure
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of selection calculus under unstable active branches.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\neq\operatorname{co}\{-1,1\}=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-gradient convexification fails for the limiting subdifferential of a nonregular lower envelope.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Subdifferential Calculus p. 77
source_refs.source_title: Introduction to Nonsmooth Optimization: Theory, Practice and Software

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}\), where \(f_1(x)=x\) and \(f_2(x)=-x\). Both branches are active at \(0\), with gradients \(1\) and \(-1\). Nevertheless, the limiting subdifferential is \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\), whereas convexifying the active gradients gives \(\operatorname{co}\{1,-1\}=[-1,1]\). Hence an active-selection formula modeled on the regular finite-maximum rule overestimates the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonregular lower envelope, convexifying all active branch gradients can strictly overestimate the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Selection Failure

children.top_down_role: Irregular generalized derivatives near changing active branches.

notation.meaning: One-sided directional derivative at zero in direction d.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|=\min\{x,-x\}\), the selected smooth branch changes when a path crosses \(0\). The directional derivative exists in every direction and equals \(f'(0;d)=-|d|\), but it is not a linear function of \(d\). Moreover, \(\partial f(0)=\{-1,1\}\), while the Clarke subdifferential is \([-1,1]\). Thus branch switching creates nonregularity and separates limiting calculus from convexified active-branch calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Switching between two smooth branches can produce a nonlinear directional derivative and a nonconvex limiting subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact chain-rule equality can be lost when an outer singular direction is annihilated by the inner derivative. knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Compactness Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical loss of norm-sequential compactness underlying infinite-dimensional failures of finite-dimensional limiting arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(X=\ell^2\), the canonical vectors satisfy \(e_k\rightharpoonup0\), but \(\|e_j-e_k\|=\sqrt{2}\) whenever \(j\neq k\). Hence the bounded sequence \((e_k)\) has no norm-convergent subsequence. Therefore, a finite-dimensional variational argument that obtains a strongly convergent subsequence solely from boundedness cannot be transferred unchanged to this setting; an appropriate compactness hypothesis or a calculus formulated using suitable weaker topologies is needed for that step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In infinite dimensions, boundedness alone does not ensure a norm-convergent subsequence, so finite-dimensional compactness steps cannot be transferred unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\ell^2\) is equipped with its norm topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k\rightharpoonup0\) while \((e_k)\) has no norm-convergent subsequence.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f''(\bar x;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+td)-f(\bar x)-t f'(\bar x;d)}{\tfrac12t^2}\), when the limit exists.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The second directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) along \(d\), with half-quadratic normalization, is the extended-real limit \[f''(\bar x;d):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+td)-f(\bar x)-t f'(\bar x;d)}{\tfrac12t^2},\] provided this limit exists. It measures the second-order remainder along the fixed ray \(\bar x+td\). For a twice differentiable function, it reduces to \(f''(\bar x;d)=\langle d,\nabla^2f(\bar x)d\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second directional derivative is the normalized second-order remainder along a fixed one-sided ray.

assumptions_latex: \(\bar v\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a reference first-order covector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,w'\to w}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w')\).

notation.meaning: Second-order difference quotient relative to the covector v.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.5 Second-Order Subdifferential Calculus p. 335

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), define the second-order difference quotient \[\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+tw)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.\] The second subderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\bar v\) is the extended-real function \[d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w').\] The perturbation \(w'\to w\) makes this a lower, epigraphically stable second-order object rather than a fixed-ray limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second subderivative is the lower limit of normalized second-order difference quotients under simultaneous step and direction perturbations.

children.title: Second Epi-Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Second-order models organized through epigraphical limiting behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\), and \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)=\operatorname*{e\!\!-lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\), when this epi-limit exists.

notation.meaning: Second-order difference quotient based at the subgradient pair.
Epigraphical limit as the positive parameter decreases to zero.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional second epi-derivative relative to a fixed subgradient pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), form the extended-real function \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v):\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). If these functions epi-converge as \(t\downarrow0\), their epi-limit is the second epi-derivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\bar v\): \[d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v):=\operatorname*{e\!\!-lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v).\] The value at \(w\) may be infinite and records the second-order variational growth along perturbations whose directions converge to \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second epi-derivative is the epigraphical limit of subgradient-corrected second-order difference quotients, when that limit exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Second Epi-Derivatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf and is internally coherent, but no citation supports the normalization or the convention distinguishing a second epi-derivative from a second subderivative.

children.title: Epigraphical-Limit Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between second subderivative families and epigraphical convergence.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\), and \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The epi-liminf of \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) is \(d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\); epi-convergence holds exactly when the epi-limsup agrees with it.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of epi-limits in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the lower epigraphical limit satisfies \[(\operatorname*{e\!\!-liminf}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v))(w)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,w'\to w}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w')=d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w).\] Consequently, \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges if and only if its epigraphical upper limit equals this lower limit. In that case, \[d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)=d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second subderivative is the epi-liminf of the second-order quotients; it becomes the second epi-derivative when the matching epi-limsup agrees.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical-Limit Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed epi-liminf relation is plausible and fits the leaf, but the precise sequential convention and the asserted equality with the second subderivative require an inspectable source.

children.title: Twice Epi-Differentiable Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where stable second-order epigraphical models are available.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\), and \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) precisely when \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges to a proper extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper twice epi-differentiability relative to a specified subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) when there exists a proper lower semicontinuous function \(q:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) such that \[\operatorname*{e\!\!-lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)=q.\] Equivalently, for each \(w\), the epi-liminf and epi-limsup of the quotient family coincide at \(w\), with the resulting common function proper. Under this condition, \(q=d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)=d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice epi-differentiability means that the corrected second-order quotient family epi-converges to a proper lower semicontinuous function.
knowledge_statements.title: Twice Epi-Differentiable Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the terminal container, but conventions differ over whether properness of the epi-limit is part of twice epi-differentiability. A source is required to settle the stated version.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Prox-regularity and amenability of second subderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity of second subderivatives and graphical derivatives under prox-regularity, proper twice epi-differentiability, and full amenability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is prox-regular and properly twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\), then there exists \(\rho\ge 0\) such that \(\mathrm d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)+\rho\lvert\cdot\rvert^2\) is convex and \(D(\partial f)(\bar x\mid\bar v)+\rho I\) is maximal monotone. Consequently, \(\mathrm d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) is prox-regular everywhere. In particular, these properties hold whenever \(f\) is fully amenable at \(\bar x\), and then \(\mathrm d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) is fully amenable everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a prox-regular, properly twice epi-differentiable function, a quadratic shift makes the second subderivative convex and the shifted graphical derivative of the subgradient mapping maximal monotone. The second subderivative is therefore prox-regular everywhere; under full amenability it is fully amenable everywhere.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is prox-regular at }\bar x\text{ for }\bar v
f\text{ is properly twice epi-differentiable at }\bar x\text{ for }\bar v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\rho\ge0:\ \mathrm d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)+\rho\lvert\cdot\rvert^2\text{ is convex and }D(\partial f)(\bar x\mid\bar v)+\rho I\text{ is maximal monotone};\quad \mathrm d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\text{ is prox-regular everywhere},\quad f\text{ fully amenable at }\bar x\Rightarrow \mathrm d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\text{ is fully amenable everywhere}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The outer second-order tangent set to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) is \[T_C^2(\bar x,w):=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }t_k\downarrow0\text{ and }z_k\to z\text{ such that}\\ \bar x+t_kw+\tfrac12t_k^2z_k\in C\text{ for every }k\end{array}\right\}.\] Equivalently, it is the Painlevé-Kuratowski outer limit \(\operatorname*{Limsup}_{t\downarrow0}2(C-\bar x-tw)/t^2\). It may be empty even when \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-order tangent set contains accelerations realized by feasible sequences whose first-order velocity is fixed.

children.title: Parabolic Tangent Sets
children.top_down_role: Feasible geometry captured through parabolic perturbations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^{2,\mathrm{in}}(\bar x,w)=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{t\downarrow0}2(C-\bar x-tw)/t^2\subset T_C^2(\bar x,w)\).

notation.meaning: Inner or adjacent parabolic tangent set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the inner-limit sense to distinguish this node from the outer second-order tangent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inner parabolic tangent set to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\) is \[T_C^{2,\mathrm{in}}(\bar x,w):=\left\{z:\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(\bar x+tw+\tfrac12t^2z,C)}{\tfrac12t^2}=0\right\}.\] Equivalently, \(T_C^{2,\mathrm{in}}(\bar x,w)=\operatorname*{Liminf}_{t\downarrow0}2(C-\bar x-tw)/t^2\). Hence \(T_C^{2,\mathrm{in}}(\bar x,w)\subset T_C^2(\bar x,w)\). Equality expresses parabolic derivability of \(C\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner parabolic tangent set consists of accelerations feasible to second order for every sufficiently small step, up to vanishing error.
knowledge_statements.title: Parabolic Tangent Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inner-limit construction is mathematically plausible, but “parabolic tangent set” is also used for the outer second-order tangent set. A source is needed to establish that this immutable leaf is intended to contain the inner/adjacent version and its derivability criterion.

children.title: Direction-Conditioned Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Dependence of curved feasible approximations on a selected tangent direction.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A second-order correction exists along \(w\) exactly when \(T_C^2(\bar x,w)\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential feasibility with fixed first-order direction and bounded second-order correction.

source_refs.locator: F. Tangent-Normal Relations p. 217

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The direction \(w\) is second-order feasible for \(C\) at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(t_k\downarrow0\) and a convergent sequence \(z_k\to z\) satisfying \[\bar x+t_kw+\tfrac12t_k^2z_k\in C\quad\text{for every }k.\] This condition is equivalent to \(T_C^2(\bar x,w)\neq\varnothing\). It implies \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\), whereas first-order tangency alone need not supply a bounded acceleration correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is second-order feasible when some bounded convergent acceleration correction makes a sequence of curved trial points feasible.

children.title: Curvature Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Variation of second-order feasible geometry across directions and base points.

assumptions_latex: \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), \(g(\bar x)=0\), and \(Dg(\bar x)\) is surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^2(\bar x,w)=\{z:Dg(\bar x)z+D^2g(\bar x)[w,w]=0\}\).

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the regular equality set \(C=\{x:g(x)=0\}\), Taylor expansion of the constraint along the parabolic path gives the exact representation \[T_C^2(\bar x,w)=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:Dg(\bar x)z+D^2g(\bar x)[w,w]=0\right\}.\] Thus changing \(w\) changes the admissible acceleration set through the quadratic term \(D^2g(\bar x)[w,w]\). Surjectivity of \(Dg(\bar x)\) ensures that the displayed linear equation in \(z\) is solvable for every tangent direction \(w\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a regular smooth equality set, admissible accelerations solve a linearized constraint forced by the constraint's directional curvature.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order normal object associated with \(C\) is the coderivative of its normal-cone mapping. children.title: Curvature Objects
children.top_down_role: Variational representations of local set curvature.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, \(\bar x\in C\), \(\bar v\in N_C(\bar x)\), and \(w\in K_C(\bar x,\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_C(\bar x,\bar v;w):=-\sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x,w)}(\bar v)\), with extended-real conventions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-function curvature convention associated with a second-order tangent set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a critical direction \(w\), define the directional curvature functional of the primal-dual pair \((\bar x,\bar v)\) by \[\kappa_C(\bar x,\bar v;w):=-\sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x,w)}(\bar v)=-\sup_{z\in T_C^2(\bar x,w)}\langle\bar v,z\rangle.\] The value is extended real; in particular, the support function is \(-\infty\) when the second-order tangent set is empty. The minus sign matches the second-subderivative convention for the indicator function of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional curvature is encoded by the negative support of the second-order tangent set evaluated at the selected normal.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Objects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The negative-support curvature functional is coherent, including the empty-set convention, but neither its sign nor its identification as the intended curvature object is supported by a citation.

children.title: Primal-Dual Curvature Relations
children.top_down_role: Correspondences between second-order tangent geometry and dual normal behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, \((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}N_C\), and \(w\in K_C(\bar x,\bar v)\).
\(C\) is parabolically derivable along \(w\) and parabolically regular at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) in that direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=-\sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x,w)}(\bar v)=\kappa_C(\bar x,\bar v;w)\).

notation.meaning: Second subderivative relative to the normal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator-function primal-dual identity under directional parabolic regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated parabolic derivability and regularity assumptions, the primal second-order model of the indicator function and the dual support model of the tangent curvature agree: \[d^2\delta_C(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=-\sigma_{T_C^2(\bar x,w)}(\bar v)=\kappa_C(\bar x,\bar v;w).\] Thus the second-order cost of maintaining feasibility in the critical direction \(w\) is represented by pairing the normal \(\bar v\) with feasible accelerations and taking the negative support value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under parabolic regularity, the indicator's second subderivative equals the negative support of feasible accelerations at the selected normal.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Curvature Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal-dual identity fits the leaf, but “parabolically regular” is not defined and no source confirms that the stated directional hypotheses are sufficient for the equality.

children.title: Degenerate Curvature Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where second-order normal or curvature descriptions lose stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Curvature Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete collapse of coderivative curvature for the absolute-value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be defined by \(f(x)=|x|\), and define its limiting second-order subdifferential by \(\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v)(u):=D^*(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(u)\). At \((\bar x,\bar v)=(0,0)\),
\[
\partial^2f(0,0)(u)=
\begin{cases}
\mathbb R,&u=0,\\
\varnothing,&u\ne0.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus this convex function has an unbounded curvature value in the zero direction and an empty curvature value in every nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the absolute-value function at the interior subgradient zero, the limiting second-order subdifferential is the whole real line in direction zero and is empty in every nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^2f(0,0)(0)=\mathbb R\) and \(\partial^2f(0,0)(u)=\varnothing\) for every \(u\ne0\).

notation.meaning: limiting coderivative of a set-valued mapping

children.title: Limiting Second-Order Subdifferentials
children.top_down_role: Coderivative-based second-order generalized differentiation.

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Second-Order Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mordukhovich coderivative definition for an extended-real-valued function on an Asplund space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), and let \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\). The limiting second-order subdifferential of \(f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) is the set-valued mapping \(\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v):X^{**}\rightrightarrows X^*\) defined, for \(u\,\in X^{**}\), by
\[
\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v)(u):=D^*(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(u)
=\{z\in X^*:(z,-u)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}\partial f}(\bar x,\bar v)\}.
\]
Here \(N\) is the limiting normal cone in the dual pairing for \(X\times X^*\), and \(D^*\) is the corresponding limiting coderivative. Directions in \(X\) may be used through the canonical embedding \(X\hookrightarrow X^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting second-order subdifferential is the limiting coderivative of the limiting-subgradient mapping at a selected graph point; in a general Banach space its direction variable belongs to the bidual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^2f(\bar x,\bar v)(u)=\{z\in X^*:(z,-u)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}\partial f}(\bar x,\bar v)\}\) for \(u\in X^{**}\).

children.title: Combined Second-Order Subdifferentials

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Second-Order Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular graph-normal variant applied to the limiting subgradient mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be an Asplund space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and take \((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\). The combined second-order subdifferential is
\[
\breve\partial^{\,2}f(\bar x,\bar v)(u):=\widehat D^*(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(u)
=\{z\in X^*:(z,-u)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}\partial f}(\bar x,\bar v)\},
\]
for \(u\in X\), where \(\widehat N\) denotes the Fréchet normal cone. It is therefore the pointwise regular-normal counterpart of the limiting second-order subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The combined second-order subdifferential uses the Fréchet normal to the subgradient graph instead of its limiting normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\breve\partial^{\,2}f(\bar x,\bar v)=\widehat D^*(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)\).

children.title: Mixed Second-Order Subdifferentials
