However, the cited generalized-normal section does not directly support the full partial-smoothness pullback theorem, and the exact chain rule and prox-regularity hypotheses require authoritative confirmation.

children.title: Qualification Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Compatibility failures that obstruct sum or composition transfer.

knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for transversality in sum and smooth-preimage partial-smoothness calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1,M_2\subset E\) be active \(C^2\) manifolds through \(\bar x\), and let \(F:E\to Y\) be \(C^1\) with \(F(\bar x)\in M\subset Y\). Sum calculus is qualified when \(N_{M_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{M_2}(\bar x)]=\{0\}\). Composition through the preimage \(F^{-1}(M)\) is qualified when \(N_M(F(\bar x))\cap\ker DF(\bar x)^*=\{0\}\). The qualification boundary consists of data for which the corresponding intersection contains a nonzero normal; there the expected active intersection or preimage may fail to be a smooth manifold of the predicted dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualification fails when active manifolds have opposing nonzero normals or a nonzero outer normal is annihilated by the composition derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{M_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{M_2}(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}\) or \(N_M(F(\bar x))\cap\ker DF(\bar x)^*\ne\{0\}\) marks the relevant qualification boundary.

notation.meaning: normal space to the smooth manifold M at z
adjoint of the derivative of F at the reference point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the qualification-boundary leaf, and the displayed normal-intersection tests are plausible finite-dimensional transversality conditions. No citation supports their use as the exact sum and preimage qualifications for partial-smoothness calculus, and the ambient assumptions on E and Y are unstated.

children.title: Spectral Partial Smoothness
children.top_down_role: Active eigenspace and rank structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Partial Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral lifting for real symmetric matrices with eigenvalue multiplicities retained by the active manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be permutation-invariant and partly smooth at \(\lambda(\bar X)\) relative to a permutation-compatible \(C^2\) manifold \(m\). Define \(H(X)=h(\lambda(X))\) on the real symmetric matrices. If the multiplicity pattern of \(\bar X\) is compatible with \(m\), then \(H\) is partly smooth at \(\bar X\) relative to the spectral lift \(\mathcal M=\{U\operatorname{Diag}(z)U^\top:z\in m,\ U\text{ orthogonal}\}\) locally restricted to that multiplicity pattern. Its tangent and normal geometry are invariant under orthogonal conjugation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial smoothness of a symmetric eigenvalue function lifts to a matrix manifold encoding the active eigenvalue multiplicities and eigenspaces.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is permutation-invariant and partly smooth at \(\lambda(\bar X)\) relative to \(m\).
The local eigenvalue multiplicity pattern is compatible with \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=h\circ\lambda\) is partly smooth at \(\bar X\) relative to the local spectral lift \(\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: eigenvalue vector of a real symmetric matrix, in fixed order
spectral active manifold lifted from the eigenvalue manifold

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits a spectral lifting claim, but the meanings of permutation compatibility and multiplicity compatibility are not precise enough to verify that the displayed lift is locally a C2 manifold or that partial smoothness transfers. An authoritative spectral partial-smoothness theorem with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Primal–Dual Partial Smoothness
children.top_down_role: Coupled active structures in saddle and primal-dual systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Partial Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product active geometry for a standard convex–concave saddle system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Ax,y\rangle-g^*(y)\), where \(f\) and \(g^*\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions. If \(f\) is partly smooth at \(\bar x\) relative to \(M_x\) and \(g^*\) is partly smooth at \(\bar y\) relative to \(M_y\), then the nonsmooth primal–dual geometry is carried by \(M_x\times M_y\). The saddle subdifferential mapping satisfies \(\partial_xL(x,y)=\partial f(x)+A^*y\) and \(-\partial_yL(x,y)=\partial g^*(y)-Ax\); the bilinear coupling shifts the subgradients without changing their parallel spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partly smooth primal and dual terms induce a product active manifold; linear coupling translates their subgradients but preserves active tangent geometry.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g^*\) are proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions.
\(f\) and \(g^*\) are partly smooth relative to \(M_x\) and \(M_y\) at the reference pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled active structure is \(M_x\times M_y\), with the displayed translated primal and dual subdifferentials.

notation.meaning: adjoint of the linear coupling operator A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is reasonable for this topic, and the two subdifferential identities are standard. However, the spaces and domain of A are not introduced, and no source establishes the stronger assertion that the coupled active geometry is precisely the product manifold under the stated hypotheses.

children.title: Identification Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Degeneracies preventing finite or stable active-structure identification.

children.title: Active-Structure Branching Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Competing manifolds or strata near the reference point.

children.title: Nonunique Active Structures
children.top_down_role: Competing active manifolds or strata compatible with the same reference geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Active Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local failure of uniqueness for candidate identifying manifolds or strata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak A(\bar x,\bar v)\) denote the collection of admissible active \(C^2\) manifold germs associated with \((\bar x,\bar v)\), where \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\). The active structure is nonunique when there exist \(M_1,M_2\in\mathfrak A(\bar x,\bar v)\) such that every neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) satisfies \(M_1\cap U\ne M_2\cap U\). In this regime, convergence of iterates and subgradients to \((\bar x,\bar v)\) alone cannot specify which manifold germ must be identified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An active structure is nonunique when two genuinely different local manifold germs satisfy the admissibility requirements at the same point-subgradient pair.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathfrak A(\bar x,\bar v)\) is the prescribed family of admissible active manifold germs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathfrak A(\bar x,\bar v)/{\sim}_{\mathrm{germ}}|>1\) prevents unique active-manifold identification from local limit data alone.

notation.meaning: family of admissible active manifold germs
equality of manifolds on some neighborhood of the reference point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary role matches the leaf. The mathematical force of the statement depends entirely on the unspecified admissibility requirements defining the family of manifold germs, so the nonuniqueness and identification consequence cannot be verified without a cited framework.

children.title: Branching Active Structures
children.top_down_role: Local active pieces that split into multiple incident geometric branches.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Active Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A maximum of smooth pieces exhibits distinct active branches meeting at a switching stratum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x_1,x_2)=\max\{x_1,x_2\}\), the regions \(B_1=\{x:x_1>x_2\}\) and \(B_2=\{x:x_2>x_1\}\) are smooth branches on which \(f\) equals different affine functions, while \(S=\{x:x_1=x_2\}\) is their switching stratum. Sequences approaching any \(\bar x\in S\) from \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) have active index sets \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\), respectively, whereas the limiting active index set is \(\{1,2\}\). Thus no single branch represents all nearby approaches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of two coordinates has two smooth branches meeting on a tie line, and different approach directions select different active indices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Approaches to \(S\) from \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) select incompatible singleton active sets.

notation.meaning: open region on which the ith affine piece is uniquely active
switching stratum where both pieces are active

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role fits the branching leaf, and the active-index calculations for the maximum of two coordinates are directly correct. A specific source or explicit standard-field rationale is still required to support its interpretation as an active-structure identification failure example.

children.title: Branch-Selection Instability
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of the selected active branch to perturbations or approach directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Selection Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily small perturbations reverse the selected smooth branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f_\varepsilon(x_1,x_2)=\max\{x_1+\varepsilon,x_2-\varepsilon\}\). At \(x=(0,0)\), the first affine branch is uniquely active for \(\varepsilon>0\), the second is uniquely active for \(\varepsilon<0\), and both are active for \(\varepsilon=0\). Hence perturbations with arbitrarily small norm and opposite signs select different active branches, although \(f_\varepsilon\) converges uniformly to \(f_0\) on \(\mathbb R^2\). Branch selection is therefore discontinuous at the unperturbed tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrarily small signed perturbation of a two-piece maximum switches the uniquely active branch at the same reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active-branch selector at \(x=0\) is discontinuous as \(\varepsilon\to0\).

notation.meaning: scalar perturbation controlling which affine branch dominates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample role fits the leaf. The branch selections and global uniform convergence follow from the displayed formula, but the record supplies neither a citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale for the claimed branch-selection instability boundary.

children.title: Degenerate Normal Geometry
children.top_down_role: Insufficient transverse separation for stable identification.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Normal Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of transverse separation between competing active manifolds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_1,M_2\subset E\) be candidate active \(C^2\) manifolds through \(\bar x\). Their normal geometry is degenerate at \(\bar x\) when \(N_{M_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{M_2}(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}\). Equivalently, there is a nonzero vector normal to \(M_1\) whose negative is normal to \(M_2\). This abnormal normal prevents transverse intersection; consequently, the intersection may have an unstable dimension and small perturbations need not preserve the local active geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal geometry is degenerate when competing active manifolds possess opposing nonzero normals, so their intersection is not transverse.
assumptions_latex: \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are embedded \(C^2\) manifolds through \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{M_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{M_2}(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}\) characterizes failure of transversality.

notation.meaning: normal space to M at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits degenerate normal geometry, and the normal-space intersection is the standard failure of transversality for two smooth manifolds. The claims about unstable dimension and perturbation behavior require a specific manifold-transversality or variational-analysis source.

children.title: Identification Robustness Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Repeated switching or loss of finite identification under persistent perturbations.

children.title: Vanishing Identification Margins
children.top_down_role: Loss of geometric separation needed for stable active-structure detection.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Identification Margins
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collapse of strict-complementarity distance along an identifying sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and let \((x_k,v_k)\to(\bar x,\bar v)\) with \(v_k\in\partial f(x_k)\). Define the identification margin by \(\delta_k=\operatorname{dist}(v_k,\operatorname{rbd}\partial f(x_k))\), measured within \(\operatorname{aff}\partial f(x_k)\). Identification margins vanish when \(\delta_k\to0\). Then the subgradients approach the relative boundary of their admissible faces, so no uniform positive perturbation radius can keep all sufficiently large \(v_k\) in the corresponding relative interiors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identification margins vanish when subgradients approach the relative boundaries of their subdifferential faces, eliminating any uniform strict-complementarity buffer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta_k\to0\) implies that no uniform radius protects the relative-interior membership of all large-index subgradients.

notation.meaning: relative boundary of a convex set C
distance from the kth subgradient to the relative boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary role fits the leaf. The distance construction is plausible, but its interpretation as an identification margin across subdifferentials with potentially varying affine hulls, and the resulting uniform-perturbation conclusion, require a cited identification theorem or robustness framework.

children.title: Active-Set Chattering
children.top_down_role: Repeated switching among competing active pieces near a reference point.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Chattering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite switching among active labels near a limiting point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A(x)\) be a finite-valued active-set mapping and let \(x_k\to\bar x\). The sequence chatters when \(A(x_{k+1})\ne A(x_k)\) for infinitely many indices \(k\). Equivalently, the active-set sequence is not eventually constant. When two or more values of \(A\) occur infinitely often, no finite iteration identifies a single active set, even though the primal iterates converge to the same limiting point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active-set chattering is infinite switching of active labels along a convergent sequence, preventing finite identification.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) maps nearby points into a finite family of active sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Infinitely many changes in \(A(x_k)\) preclude eventual active-set identification.

notation.meaning: active index set assigned to x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary role fits this terminal container, and infinite changes are equivalent to failure of eventual constancy for the displayed sequence. The record nevertheless has no citation or explicit standard-field rationale establishing this as the intended active-set chattering notion.

children.title: Persistent Identification Inexactness
children.top_down_role: Residual perturbations that prevent finite stabilization of active geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Identification Inexactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence without eventual membership in the target active manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be the target active manifold through \(\bar x\), and let \(x_k\to\bar x\). Identification is persistently inexact when, for every \(K\), there exists \(k\ge K\) such that \(x_k\notin M\). Thus the iterates may approach \(M\), with \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,M)\to0\), while never attaining permanent manifold membership. If approximate subgradient errors remain comparable to or larger than the available identification margin, this behavior is not excluded by convergence alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identification remains inexact when convergent iterates fail to lie on the target manifold eventually, even if their distance to it vanishes.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is an embedded active manifold containing \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall K\,\exists k\ge K:\ x_k\notin M\) is failure of finite exact identification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary role fits the leaf, and the quantified condition correctly negates eventual membership in M. The additional assertion connecting persistent inexactness to subgradient errors and identification margins is not formalized or supported by a source.

children.title: Robustness Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Perturbation regimes separating stable identification from persistent failure.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustness Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior margin as a sharp local perturbation threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex set, let \(v\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and define \(\delta=\operatorname{dist}(v,\operatorname{rbd}C)>0\), with distance computed in \(\operatorname{aff}C\). For every perturbation \(e\in\operatorname{par}C\) satisfying \(\|e\|<\delta\), one has \(v+e\in\operatorname{ri}C\). Hence \(\delta\) is a certified robustness radius for preserving the relative-interior condition used in active-structure identification; no larger universal radius follows from this distance alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a convex set’s relative boundary gives a perturbation threshold that preserves relative-interior membership and its identification condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e\in\operatorname{par}C\) and \(\|e\|<\delta\) imply \(v+e\in\operatorname{ri}C\).

notation.meaning: linear space parallel to the affine hull of C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relative-interior ball statement is plausible convex geometry, but a certificate or condition may fit this threshold leaf more exactly than property. A source is required both for the relative-boundary radius statement and for the asserted sharpness that no larger universal radius follows from the distance alone.

children.title: KL Property Family
children.top_down_role: Pointwise, setwise, uniform, and metric desingularization variants.

children.title: Pointwise KL Geometry
children.top_down_role: Local desingularization near an individual critical point.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise KL Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property localized at one finite-valued reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) has the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property at \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), a number \(\eta>0\), and a concave function \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb R_+\), continuous at \(0\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\), \(\varphi\in C^1(0,\eta)\), and \(\varphi'>0\), such that \(\varphi'(f(x)-f(\bar x))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge1\) whenever \(x\in U\) and \(f(\bar x)<f(x)<f(\bar x)+\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise KL property bounds the reciprocal subgradient slope by a local concave desingularizing derivative near one reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed desingularized slope inequality holds locally above the value \(f(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: limiting subdifferential of f at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role exactly fits the pointwise KL leaf, and the formula resembles the standard limiting-subdifferential KL property. The record does not specify that E is an appropriate finite-dimensional Euclidean space and provides no authoritative definition with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz Property and Exponent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the local KL property through the limiting-subdifferential residual, including the power-type exponent convention and semialgebraic sufficient regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper lower semicontinuous function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ satisfies the KL property at $\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}(\partial f)$ if there exist $\alpha,\delta>0$ and a continuous concave function $\phi:[0,\alpha)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ such that $\phi(0)=0$, $\phi\in C^1(0,\alpha)$, $\phi'(s)>0$ for all $s\in(0,\alpha)$, and, for every $x\in\mathbb B(\bar x;\delta)$ satisfying $f(\bar x)<f(x)<f(\bar x)+\alpha$, $$\phi'(f(x)-f(\bar x))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq1.$$ If $\phi(s)=\gamma s^{1-\beta}$ for some $\gamma>0$ and $\beta\in[0,1)$, then $f$ has KL exponent $\beta$ at $\bar x$. Every proper closed semialgebraic function satisfies the KL property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower semicontinuous function has the pointwise KL property when a concave desingularizing function makes the local subdifferential residual satisfy the stated lower bound. A power desingularizer defines the KL exponent. Proper closed semialgebraic functions satisfy the KL property.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and lower semicontinuous}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathbb B(\bar x;\delta)\text{ with }f(\bar x)<f(x)<f(\bar x)+\alpha,\quad\phi'(f(x)-f(\bar x))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\geq1

source_evidence.locator: Theory of Error Bounds / 8.4.2. The Kurdyka-Łojaziewicz theory / Definition 8.4.2-extra-1

children.title: Setwise-Uniform KL Geometry
children.top_down_role: Uniform desingularization along compact critical sets.

children.title: Setwise KL Geometry
children.top_down_role: Desingularization behavior organized along critical sets rather than isolated points.

knowledge_statements.title: Setwise KL Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise KL property along a level set, without uniform constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(\Omega\subset\operatorname{dom}\partial f\) satisfy \(f\equiv\bar f\) on \(\Omega\). The function \(f\) has setwise KL geometry on \(\Omega\) if, for every \(\bar x\in\Omega\), there exist a neighborhood \(U_{\bar x}\), a number \(\eta_{\bar x}>0\), and a concave function \(\varphi_{\bar x}:[0,\eta_{\bar x})\to\mathbb{R}_+\), continuous at \(0\), with \(\varphi_{\bar x}(0)=0\) and \(\varphi_{\bar x}'(s)>0\), such that \[\varphi_{\bar x}'(f(x)-\bar f)\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge 1\] whenever \(x\in U_{\bar x}\) and \(0<f(x)-\bar f<\eta_{\bar x}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point of the constant-level set admits its own neighborhood, desingularizing function, and KL inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) satisfies a point-dependent KL inequality at every \(\bar x\in\Omega\).

notation.meaning: common value of f on the set

children.title: Uniform KL Geometry
children.top_down_role: Common desingularization control across neighborhoods of a critical set.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform KL Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single KL inequality valid near an entire constant-level set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and suppose \(f\equiv\bar f\) on \(\Omega\subset\operatorname{dom}\partial f\). Uniform KL geometry on \(\Omega\) means that there exist \(\varepsilon>0\), \(\eta>0\), and one concave function \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb{R}_+\), continuous at \(0\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\) and \(\varphi'(s)>0\), such that \[\varphi'(f(x)-\bar f)\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge1\] for every \(x\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\Omega)<\varepsilon\) and \(0<f(x)-\bar f<\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One neighborhood radius, value window, and desingularizing function work simultaneously around the whole level set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) obeys one common KL inequality throughout a tube around \(\Omega\).

children.title: Variant Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regularity settings where slope and metric formulations agree.

knowledge_statements.title: Variant Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coincidence of metric and subdifferential KL formulations under regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. At every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), the descending metric slope satisfies \[|\nabla f|(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x)).\] Consequently, at any \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), the metric KL inequality and the convex-subdifferential slope KL inequality are equivalent with the same neighborhood, value window, and desingularizing function. The same equality, with \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\), holds locally for continuously differentiable functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex functions, and locally for smooth functions, metric slope and subdifferential slope coincide, so their KL formulations are identical.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a Hilbert space; or \(f\) is continuously differentiable in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\nabla f|(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\), hence the corresponding KL variants are equivalent.
review_flags: Exact source locators for both the convex and smooth slope identities are required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex and continuously differentiable slope identities are plausible standard results, but the record combines two regimes without any locator supporting either identity or the resulting KL equivalence. Exact sources are required before the theorem can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Variant Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where competing KL formulations cease to be interchangeable.

knowledge_statements.title: Variant Separation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of regularity separates metric, limiting, and Clarke slope quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equality between metric and generalized-gradient slopes need not survive outside convex or subdifferentially regular regimes. For \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\), the descending metric slope at the origin is \[|\nabla f|(0)=1,\] whereas the Clarke subdifferential is \(\partial^{\mathrm C}f(0)=[-1,1]\), so \[\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial^{\mathrm C}f(0))=0.\] Thus replacing the metric slope by the Clarke subdifferential distance can change a positive descent measure into zero; equivalence of the associated KL inequalities requires additional regularity and cannot be asserted for arbitrary locally Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the nonsmooth local maximum −|x|, metric slope is one but Clarke slope is zero, demonstrating failure of unrestricted variant equivalence.
assumptions_latex: The generalized-gradient variant uses the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\nabla f|(0)=1\ne0=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial^{\mathrm C}f(0))\).
review_flags: The computation is elementary, but an authoritative locator for the comparison framework is absent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed counterexample computation is mathematically consistent and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no authoritative locator is supplied for the metric-slope and Clarke-slope comparison framework.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that, near \(\bar x\), a differentiable function \(f\) satisfies the classical gradient inequality \[|f(x)-f(\bar x)|^{\theta}\le C\|\nabla f(x)\|\] for constants \(C>0\) and \(\theta\in[1/2,1)\). Define \(\varphi(s)=C(1-\theta)^{-1}s^{1-\theta}\) for \(s\ge0\). Since \(\varphi'(s)=Cs^{-\theta}\) for \(s>0\), the gradient inequality on \(f(x)>f(\bar x)\) is represented as \[\varphi'(f(x)-f(\bar x))\|\nabla f(x)\|\ge1.\] Thus the classical exponent \(\theta\) corresponds to the KL desingularizing exponent \(1-\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical gradient inequality is represented in KL form by a power desingularizer proportional to s raised to one minus the gradient exponent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subanalytic Zero-Set Łojasiewicz Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform power comparison for continuous subanalytic functions on a compact subanalytic set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subset\mathbb R^n\) be compact and subanalytic, and let \(\phi,\psi:S\to\mathbb R\) be continuous subanalytic functions. If \(\phi^{-1}(0)\subseteq\psi^{-1}(0)\), then there exist \(\rho>0\) and \(N^*\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) such that \(\rho|\psi(x)|^{N^*}\le |\phi(x)|\) for every \(x\in S\). If also \(\psi^{-1}(0)\subseteq\phi^{-1}(0)\), then there exist \(\rho_1,\rho_2>0\) and \(N_1,N_2\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) such that \(\rho_1|\psi(x)|^{N_1}\le |\phi(x)|\le \rho_2|\psi(x)|^{1/N_2}\) for every \(x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inclusion of zero sets for two continuous subanalytic functions on a compact subanalytic domain gives a uniform one-sided power inequality. Equality of their zero sets gives a two-sided power comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Definable KL Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth KL theorem for functions definable in a fixed o-minimal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable in an o-minimal expansion of the real field. At every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), a number \(\eta>0\), and a continuous concave definable function \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb{R}_+\), with \(\varphi(0)=0\), \(\varphi\in C^1(0,\eta)\), and \(\varphi'>0\), such that
\[
\varphi'\!\left(f(x)-f(\bar x)\right)\operatorname{dist}\!\left(0,\partial f(x)\right)\ge 1
\]
whenever \(x\in U\) and \(f(\bar x)<f(x)<f(\bar x)+\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper lower-semicontinuous definable function satisfies a local nonsmooth Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz inequality at each point where its limiting subdifferential is defined.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is definable in a fixed o-minimal expansion of the real field.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has the KL property at \(\bar x\) with a definable concave desingularizing function.

children.title: Tame-Regime Inclusions

knowledge_statements.title: Tame-Regime Inclusions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusions are interpreted for real-valued functions through definability of their graphs or epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(n\ge 1\). Every semialgebraic subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is globally subanalytic and hence definable in \(\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{an}}\); every \(\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{an}}\)-definable set is definable in an o-minimal expansion of the real field. Consequently, for proper lower-semicontinuous functions whose epigraphs belong to these classes,
\[
\mathcal F_{\mathrm{sa}}
\subseteq
\mathcal F_{\mathrm{gsa}}
=
\mathcal F_{\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{an}}}
\subseteq
\mathcal F_{\mathrm{def}}.
\]
Local subanalytic functions enter the same local KL regime after restricting their graphs to relatively compact neighborhoods. Thus each preceding tame class inherits the definable KL property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semialgebraic and globally subanalytic functions form nested subclasses of o-minimally definable functions; local subanalytic functions join the hierarchy after bounded localization.
assumptions_latex: Function classes are identified through definability of epigraphs.
Subanalytic objects not globally subanalytic are considered locally on relatively compact neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{sa}}\subseteq\mathcal F_{\mathrm{gsa}}=\mathcal F_{\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{an}}}\subseteq\mathcal F_{\mathrm{def}}\), and proper lower-semicontinuous members are KL functions.

notation.meaning: functions definable in an o-minimal structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the inclusion container, but the identifications involving globally subanalytic and R_an-definable functions, the epigraph convention, bounded localization of subanalytic functions, and the resulting KL claim require a precise tame-geometry source. None is cited.

children.title: Finite Aggregation Closure

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Aggregation Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure under finite nonnegative sums and pointwise maxima in one o-minimal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be proper lower-semicontinuous functions definable in one o-minimal structure. For coefficients \(a_i\ge 0\), assume \(F=\sum_{i=1}^m a_i f_i\) is proper. Then \(F\) is definable and lower semicontinuous. The pointwise maximum \(G(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\) is likewise definable and lower semicontinuous whenever it is proper. Hence both \(F\) and \(G\) satisfy the KL property at every point of their limiting-subdifferential domains. This closure asserts existence of a desingularizer, not preservation of a specified KL exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite nonnegative sums and finite maxima of proper lower-semicontinuous definable functions remain definable KL functions, subject to properness.
assumptions_latex: \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable in one o-minimal structure.
\(a_i\ge0\), and the resulting aggregate is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i a_i f_i\) and \(\max_i f_i\) are lower-semicontinuous definable KL functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definable composition closure with continuity ensuring lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuous and definable, and let \(h:\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable in the same o-minimal structure. If \(F=h\circ g\) is proper, then \(F\) is lower semicontinuous and definable. Consequently, at every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial F\), the function \(F\) admits a local concave desingularizing function and satisfies the KL inequality. No numerical exponent is inherited solely from definability; exponent transfer requires additional metric regularity or nondegeneracy of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper composition of a lower-semicontinuous definable outer function with a continuous definable mapping remains a definable KL function.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable in the same structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\circ g\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous definable KL function.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closure property fits the container and its continuity hypothesis is sufficient for lower semicontinuity of the composition, but no inspectable source supports the definable composition closure and ensuing nonsmooth KL conclusion.

children.title: Separable Closure

knowledge_statements.title: Separable Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Cartesian sums, including the induced power-type exponent bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous functions, and define \(F(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_i f_i(x_i)\). If every \(f_i\) is definable in one o-minimal structure and \(F\) is proper, then \(F\) is definable and KL. Moreover, suppose near \(\bar x_i\) that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f_i(x_i))\ge c_i\lvert f_i(x_i)-f_i(\bar x_i)\rvert^{\theta_i},
\quad 0\le\theta_i<1,
\]
and that each local gap is nonnegative. Then \(F\) has the power-type KL exponent \(\theta=\max_i\theta_i\) at \(\bar x=(\bar x_i)_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite separable sums preserve definability and the KL property; under compatible nonnegative local gaps, the largest component exponent is valid for the sum.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable in the same structure.
Each component has a power-type KL inequality at \(\bar x_i\).
Component value gaps are locally nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is KL, and \(\max_i\theta_i\) is a valid local KL exponent under the stated power inequalities.

notation.meaning: Cartesian-separable sum of the component functions
valid KL exponent for the i-th component

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits Separable Closure, but the numerical max-exponent conclusion is substantially stronger than mere definable closure. It needs an exact theorem or derivation source covering the Cartesian-product subdifferential, norm comparison, sufficiently small component gaps, and the stated nonnegative-gap qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definable partial minimization under local uniform inf-compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable, and set \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}F(x,y)\). Fix \(\bar x\) with \(p(\bar x)\) finite. Suppose there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\alpha>p(\bar x)\) such that
\[
\{(x,y):x\in U,\ F(x,y)\le\alpha\}
\]
is compact. Then, after possibly shrinking \(U\), the infimum is attained, and \(p\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable on \(U\). Therefore \(p\) satisfies the KL property at every point of \(U\cap\operatorname{dom}\partial p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A definable marginal remains locally definable and KL when a compact common sublevel set guarantees attainment and lower semicontinuity.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and definable.
A common local sublevel set above \(p(\bar x)\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Locally around \(\bar x\), \(p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, definable, and KL.

notation.meaning: neighborhood on which uniform inf-compactness holds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits Marginal Transfer, but the stated compact common sublevel condition does not transparently guarantee attainment for every x in a shrunken neighborhood unless nearby marginal values are also controlled below alpha. An exact source is required to determine the sufficient uniform inf-compactness and value-function hypotheses.

children.title: Desingularization Function-Exponent Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Quantitative classifications of local critical geometry.

children.title: General Desingularizing Functions
children.top_down_role: Nonparametric desingularization profiles.

knowledge_statements.title: General Desingularizing Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonparametric desingularizers for the local nonsmooth KL inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\). A general desingularizing function for \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is a function \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb{R}_+\), for some \(\eta>0\), such that \(\varphi(0)=0\), \(\varphi\) is continuous on \([0,\eta)\), concave and \(C^1\) on \((0,\eta)\), and \(\varphi'(s)>0\). It desingularizes \(f\) on a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) when
\[
\varphi'(f(x)-f(\bar x))\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge1
\]
for every \(x\in U\) satisfying \(0<f(x)-f(\bar x)<\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A desingularizing function is an increasing concave profile whose derivative rescales the subgradient slope so that it is uniformly bounded below near a reference level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi\) is a desingularizer precisely when it has the stated regularity and satisfies the displayed KL inequality locally.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the General Desingularizing Functions topic, uses consistent notation, and contains no apparent unsafe TeX, but it has no cited definition, section, or page locator.

children.title: Power-Type KL Exponents
children.top_down_role: Exponent-based desingularization classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Power-Type KL Exponents
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power desingularizers under the convention \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f)\gtrsim(f-f_*)^\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\). A number \(\theta\in[0,1)\) is a power-type KL exponent of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(c>0\), \(\eta>0\), and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge c\bigl(f(x)-f(\bar x)\bigr)^\theta
\]
whenever \(x\in U\) and \(0<f(x)-f(\bar x)<\eta\). Equivalently, the KL inequality holds with \(\varphi(s)=\bigl(c(1-\theta)\bigr)^{-1}s^{1-\theta}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KL exponent is a power controlling how quickly the subgradient slope may vanish relative to the objective-value gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The power slope inequality is equivalent to a desingularizer proportional to \(s^{1-\theta}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Power-Type KL Exponents and consistently uses the slope convention with theta in [0,1). The normalization of the equivalent desingularizer is correct under that convention, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: KL Exponent Calculus
children.top_down_role: Propagation, comparison, and best-exponent questions.

children.title: Exponent Calculus
children.top_down_role: Behavior of KL exponents under structured operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponent Calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power transformation rule for a nonnegative objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f\) has a local minimum at \(\bar x\), write \(r(x)=f(x)-f(\bar x)\ge0\), and assume
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge c\,r(x)^\theta
\]
locally on \(0<r(x)<\eta\), where \(\theta\in[0,1)\). For \(q\ge1\), define \(g(x)=r(x)^q\). At points where the limiting-subdifferential chain rule gives \(\partial g(x)=q r(x)^{q-1}\partial f(x)\), one has
\[
\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial g(x))\ge cq\,g(x)^{\,1-(1-\theta)/q}.
\]
Thus \(1-(1-\theta)/q\) is a valid exponent for \(g\). Positive affine rescaling of the value gap leaves \(\theta\) unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Raising a nonnegative objective gap to power q transforms exponent theta into one minus (one minus theta) divided by q.
assumptions_latex: \(f-f(\bar x)\) is locally nonnegative and has exponent \(\theta\).
The stated limiting-subdifferential chain rule holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=(f-f(\bar x))^q\) has valid exponent \(1-(1-\theta)/q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits Exponent Calculus, but the power rule is conditional on an exact limiting-subdifferential chain rule whose applicable hypotheses are not stated beyond assuming the equality. A precise source is needed for the intended calculus regime and exponent formula.

children.title: Exponent Transfer
children.top_down_role: Passage of exponent information across related functions, formulations, or reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponent Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariant transfer through a locally nonsingular smooth change of variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have KL exponent \(\theta\in[0,1)\) at \(\bar y\). Let \(T:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a \(C^1\) diffeomorphism between neighborhoods of \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y=T(\bar x)\), with \(DT\) and \(DT^{-1}\) locally bounded, and set \(g=f\circ T\). If the limiting chain rule
\[
\partial g(x)=DT(x)^{\mathsf T}\partial f(T(x))
\]
holds locally, then the least singular value of \(DT(x)\) is uniformly positive near \(\bar x\). Consequently the KL slope inequality for \(f\) transfers to \(g\) with the same exponent \(\theta\), though generally with a different constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally well-conditioned smooth change of variables preserves a KL exponent when the limiting-subdifferential chain rule is exact.
assumptions_latex: The exact limiting-subdifferential chain rule holds locally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T\) has KL exponent \(\theta\) at \(\bar x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits Exponent Transfer and appropriately conditions invariance on a nonsingular smooth map and an exact limiting-subdifferential chain rule. No source establishes those hypotheses and the same-exponent conclusion in the claimed nonsmooth setting.

children.title: Exponent Sharpness
children.top_down_role: Best attainable exponent behavior and comparison with conservative estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponent Sharpness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness means minimality under the slope-exponent convention used here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\), define the admissible exponent set
\[
E(f,\bar x)=\left\{\theta\in[0,1):\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge c\bigl(f(x)-f(\bar x)\bigr)^\theta\ \text{locally for some }c>0\right\},
\]
where the inequality is imposed only when the value gap is positive and sufficiently small. The sharp KL exponent is
\[
\theta_*(f,\bar x)=\inf E(f,\bar x).
\]
An exponent is attained and sharp when \(\theta_*\in E(f,\bar x)\). If the gap is restricted below \(1\), every \(\theta'\ge\theta\) is admissible whenever \(\theta\) is, so smaller exponents give stronger slope estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sharp KL exponent is the smallest admissible power, or the infimum when no smallest exponent is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_*(f,\bar x)=\inf E(f,\bar x)\), with sharp attainment precisely when this infimum belongs to \(E(f,\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: set of locally admissible KL exponents

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition has the correct role for Exponent Sharpness and correctly distinguishes the infimum from attained sharpness. However, the admissibility condition compresses the neighborhood and value-radius quantifiers into the word 'locally', and no source fixes this terminology or convention.

children.title: Exponent Degradation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structures or operations that weaken quantitative desingularization.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponent Degradation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular inner mappings can worsen exponents even though definability and the KL property survive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(t)=t^2\), which has sharp KL exponent \(1/2\) at \(0\). For an integer \(k\ge2\), take the definable smooth but singular mapping \(T_k(x)=x^k\). The composite is \(g_k(x)=f(T_k(x))=x^{2k}\), and
\[
|g_k'(x)|=2k|x|^{2k-1}=2k\,g_k(x)^{1-1/(2k)}.
\]
Hence \(g_k\) has sharp exponent \(1-1/(2k)>1/2\). As \(k\to\infty\), these exponents approach \(1\). Thus definability alone preserves existence of a KL inequality but not its exponent; nonsingularity or an equivalent slope-comparison condition is essential for exponent invariance under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a quadratic with increasingly singular monomials worsens its sharp exponent toward one, showing that definability alone cannot preserve numerical exponents.
assumptions_latex: The KL exponent convention is \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f)\gtrsim(f-f_*)^\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The singular composition \(x\mapsto x^{2k}\) has sharp exponent \(1-1/(2k)\), strictly worse than the quadratic exponent \(1/2\).

notation.meaning: order of degeneracy of the inner mapping

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is exactly appropriate, and the monomial family is internally consistent with the shard's exponent convention. Nevertheless, the record supplies neither an external citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale, so it does not satisfy the evidence contract.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi'(f(x)-\bar f)\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge 1\) uniformly near \(K\).

children.title: Finite-Cover Uniformization

On each \(U_i\), the same level \(\bar f\) has a KL inequality with desingularizer \(\varphi_i\) and value radius \(\eta_i>0\).

children.title: Stratified Uniformization
children.top_down_role: Uniform KL organization assembled across a finite stratification.

assumptions_latex: A neighborhood of \(K\) has a finite stratification \(\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_m\}\).
For every active stratum \(S_i\), a desingularizer \(\varphi_i\) gives the KL inequality at the common level \(\bar f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finitely many stratum-wise inequalities admit one common desingularizer near \(K\).

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformization across finitely many strata carrying compatible KL data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the stratum-wise inequalities hold on neighborhoods \(V_i\) of \(K\cap S_i\), with value radii \(\eta_i>0\). After discarding inactive strata, set \(\eta=
\min_i\eta_i\) and \(\Phi=

Then every \(x\in\bigcup_i(V_i\cap S_i)\) satisfying \(0<f(x)-\bar f<\eta\) obeys \[\Phi'(f(x)-\bar f)\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\ge1.\] Consequently, finitely many compatible stratum-wise KL estimates yield one estimate, although the active local formula may change when \(x\) crosses strata.

children.title: Cover–Stratum Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between neighborhood covers and stratified critical geometry.

children.title: Uniformization Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of common control on noncompact or inconsistent critical sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point of \(K=\{p:p\ge2\}\) has a local KL desingularizer, but no common desingularizer works uniformly on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit increasing-flatness obstruction when compactness is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and \(f(p)=0\) with \(0\in\partial f(p)\) for every \(p\in K\). Each restriction \(f|_{I_p}\) has a local KL inequality. A common desingularizer would, for all \(p\ge2\) and sufficiently small \(s>0\), require \[\varphi'(s)\,p s^{1-1/p}\ge1.\] Taking the strongest requirement over \(p\) forces nonintegrable growth comparable to \(1/(s\log(1/s))\), contradicting finiteness of \(\varphi(s)\) at positive \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noncompact family of increasingly flat polynomial wells is locally KL at every minimum but has no uniform desingularizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniformization Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the uniformization-boundary leaf. The increasing-flatness construction is plausible, but the absence of a source is material because lower semicontinuity at component boundaries, the local limiting-subdifferential KL inequalities, and the claimed nonintegrable uniform obstruction all require independent verification.

The chain rule gives \((f\circ x)'(t)=-\|\dot x(t)\|^2\) almost everywhere.
The trajectory eventually lies in a uniform KL neighborhood at limiting value \(\bar f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(t_0\) after entry into the KL neighborhood and assume \(f(x(t))>\bar f\) for \(t\ge t_0\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient-descent and relative-error convergence framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_k=x^{k+1}-x^k\). Assume for every \(k\) that \[f(x^{k+1})+a\|d_k\|^2\le f(x^k),\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\le b\|d_k\|.\] Then the objective values converge to a common value on the compact cluster set. Uniformizing the KL inequality on that set yields \[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\|d_k\|<\infty.\] Consequently, \((x^k)\) converges to some \(x^\ast\); closedness of the limiting-subdifferential graph together with \(d_k\to0\) gives \(0\in\partial f(x^\ast)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded sequences with sufficient decrease, relative error, value continuity, and the KL property have finite length and converge critically.
knowledge_statements.title: Abstract Discrete Descent Sequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the abstract discrete-descent leaf, and the assumptions resemble a standard KL convergence framework. A specific source is required to verify that the stated subsequence value-continuity hypothesis, cluster-set KL assumption, relative-error indexing, and subdifferential closedness argument are jointly sufficient for finite length and critical convergence.

children.title: Residual-Controlled Inexact Sequence Family
children.top_down_role: Finite-length interfaces under controlled residual errors.

children.title: Relative-Error Sequences
children.top_down_role: Discrete descent sequences with residual control relative to available progress measures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative-error condition is \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\le b\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\) for one constant \(b>0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard relative-error hypothesis in abstract KL sequence analysis
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relative-error interface without additive perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Writing \(d_k=x^{k+1}-x^k\), the sequence satisfies the relative-error condition when there is a constant \(b>0\), independent of \(k\), such that for every \(k\) one can select \(w^{k+1}\in\partial f(x^{k+1})\) with \[\|w^{k+1}\|\le b\|d_k\|.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\le b\|d_k\|\). Thus vanishing successive displacements force the stationarity residual to vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative error means that each new stationarity residual is uniformly bounded by the size of the preceding step.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Error Sequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, and the selected-subgradient formulation is standard in finite dimensions when the limiting subdifferential is nonempty and the distance is attained. No source is given for this convention or for the asserted equivalence in the stated generality.

children.title: Inexact Descent Sequences
children.top_down_role: Discrete descent behavior under persistent or summable computational inaccuracies.

assumptions_latex: \((\varepsilon_k)\) and \((\delta_k)\) are nonnegative summable error sequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inexact descent permits additive summable errors in both sufficient decrease and residual control.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: common summably perturbed abstract descent model
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Summably perturbed sufficient-descent and relative-error sequence model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d_k=x^{k+1}-x^k\). The sequence is an inexact \((a,b,\varepsilon,
\delta)\)-descent sequence for \(f\) if, for every \(k\), \[f(x^{k+1})+a\|d_k\|^2\le f(x^k)+\varepsilon_k,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x^{k+1}))\le b\|d_k\|+
\delta_k,\] where \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_k<\infty\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_k<\infty\). The exact abstract descent model is recovered when \(\varepsilon_k=
\delta_k=0\) for all \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact descent sequence allows summable violations of descent and summable additive stationarity residuals.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Descent Sequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the inexact-descent leaf, and the formulas consistently describe additive summable descent and residual errors. The exact perturbation model is not canonical, and summability requirements used in KL convergence results vary, so an authoritative source is required before retaining this formulation.

children.title: Residual-Control Regimes
children.top_down_role: Error scales compatible with finite-length KL consequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Control Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard admissible regimes for additive residuals in KL-based inexact descent analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d_k=\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert\), \(q_{k+1}=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x_{k+1}))\), and suppose \(q_{k+1}\le b d_k+\varepsilon_{k+1}\). Common residual-control regimes are: step-relative control, \(\varepsilon_{k+1}\le \sigma d_k\); summable control, \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_{k+1}<\infty\); and vanishing tail control, \(E_k:=\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}\varepsilon_{j+1}<\infty\) with \(E_k\to0\). The first regime preserves a pure relative-error inequality with constant \(b+\sigma\); the latter two permit perturbed finite-length estimates when the descent and KL hypotheses absorb the error tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residuals may be controlled relative to step lengths or by a summable vanishing tail; these regimes support perturbed KL finite-length arguments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon_{k+1}\le\sigma d_k\), or \(\sum_k\varepsilon_{k+1}<\infty\), supplies an admissible residual-control regime for the corresponding perturbed KL analysis.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but summable residuals are not universally sufficient without a specifically sourced inexact-descent/KL framework and its error-absorption hypotheses.

children.title: Inexactness Failure Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Residual regimes where finite-length or convergence transfer can break down.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexactness Failure Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent additive errors can destroy convergence even for an analytic KL objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\), choose \(x_k=(-1)^k\), and fix \(a>0\). Then \(f(x_{k+1})=f(x_k)=1/2\), \(d_k=2\), and the inexact descent inequality \(f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k)-a d_k^2+\eta_{k+1}\) holds with \(\eta_{k+1}=4a\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x_{k+1}))=1\le b d_k+\varepsilon_{k+1}\) whenever \(b\ge1/2\) and \(\varepsilon_{k+1}\ge0\). Thus errors bounded away from zero can finance nonzero steps indefinitely: the sequence has two cluster points and neither finite length nor single-limit convergence follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant error budget can exactly offset descent, allowing an analytic-objective sequence to alternate forever between two noncritical points.
assumptions_latex: The descent model permits a nonnegative additive error \(\eta_{k+1}\).
No summability or vanishing condition is imposed on \(\eta_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_k d_k=\infty\) and \(x_k\) does not converge, despite satisfaction of the displayed inexact inequalities.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed counterexample is internally consistent and the content kind fits, but it has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: KL Convergence-Rate Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Qualitative convergence consequences and exponent-controlled rate regimes.

children.title: Cluster-Set Collapse Principle
children.top_down_role: Exclusion of nontrivial critical cluster sets by finite-length geometry.

children.title: Single-Limit Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence behavior in which a bounded trajectory approaches one critical point.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Limit Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite length yields convergence to one critical point in a complete ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be complete and let \((x_k)\subset X\) satisfy \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}d(x_{k+1},x_k)<\infty\). Then there exists \(x_\star\in X\) such that \(x_k\to x_\star\). If additionally \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(f\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, \(f(x_k)\to f(x_\star)\), and there are \(v_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) with \(v_k\to0\), then closedness of the limiting-subdifferential graph along function values gives \(0\in\partial f(x_\star)\). Hence the sequence has a single critical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-length sequence in a complete space converges; subdifferential closedness makes its limit critical when residuals vanish.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is complete and the sequence has finite length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\to x_\star\), and under the additional variational assumptions \(0\in\partial f(x_\star)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is standard and correctly distinguishes convergence from criticality, but no source supports the finite-length and limiting-subdifferential closedness claims.

children.title: Cluster-Set Collapse
children.top_down_role: Elimination of nontrivial connected or multi-point critical cluster sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Cluster-Set Collapse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite length collapses every nonempty cluster set to a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence \((x_k)\) in a metric space, define its cluster set by \(\omega(x_0)=\{\bar x:\text{ some subsequence }x_{k_j}\to\bar x\}\). If \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}d(x_{k+1},x_k)<\infty\), then for all \(m>n\), \(d(x_m,x_n)\le\sum_{k=n}^{m-1}d(x_{k+1},x_k)\), whose right-hand side tends to zero as \(n\to\infty\). Consequently, any two cluster points coincide. Thus \(\omega(x_0)\) is empty or a singleton; in a complete space it equals \(\{x_\star\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-length sequence cannot have two distinct cluster points; completeness guarantees that its cluster set contains exactly its limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\omega(x_0)\rvert\le1\), and in a complete space \(\omega(x_0)=\{x_\star\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but it lacks a citation and its statement includes proof-style derivation that should be removed before promotion.

children.title: Finite-Length Mechanism
children.top_down_role: Geometric role of bounded trajectory length in collapsing cluster behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Length Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A KL tail estimate converts objective desingularization into summability of steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_k=f(x_k)-f_\star\ge0\), let \(\varphi:[0,\eta)\to\mathbb R_+\) be increasing with \(\varphi(0)=0\), and suppose that from some index \(k_0\) onward the KL, descent, and relative-error inequalities yield \(\sum_{j=k}^{m}\lVert x_{j+1}-x_j\rVert\le C\varphi(r_k)+C\lVert x_k-x_{k-1}\rVert\) for every \(m\ge k\ge k_0\). Passing to the supremum over \(m\) gives a finite tail bound. Therefore \(\sum_{j=k_0}^{\infty}\lVert x_{j+1}-x_j\rVert<\infty\), and the remaining path length tends to zero as \(k\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The KL inequality, descent, and relative error produce a uniform tail bound, making all step lengths summable.
assumptions_latex: \(r_k\downarrow0\) and the displayed uniform tail estimate holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j=k_0}^{\infty}\lVert x_{j+1}-x_j\rVert<\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the container, but the decisive KL tail estimate is assumed without an authoritative source establishing the hypotheses under which it holds.

children.title: Strong KL Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Strong desingularization regimes and their qualitative rates.

children.title: Finite-Termination Regime
children.top_down_role: Desingularization settings associated with stabilization after finitely many iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Termination Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-type KL exponent zero forces finite termination under a standard gap recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_k=f(x_k)-f_\star\ge0\) be nonincreasing and suppose that for some \(\mu>0\) and all sufficiently large \(k\), \(r_k-r_{k+1}\ge\mu r_{k+1}^{2\theta}\). In the exponent-zero regime \(\theta=0\), every index with \(r_{k+1}>0\) satisfies \(r_k-r_{k+1}\ge\mu\). Since \(r_k\ge0\), at most \(\lceil r_{k_0}/\mu\rceil\) such positive-gap steps can occur after the recurrence begins. Hence \(r_K=0\) for some finite \(K\); if zero gap makes the descent scheme stationary, then \(x_k=x_K\) for all \(k\ge K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With KL exponent zero, each positive-gap step decreases the gap by a fixed amount, so only finitely many such steps are possible.
assumptions_latex: Zero objective gap is absorbing for iterate termination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\theta=0\), there is a finite \(K\) with \(r_K=0\), and under absorption \(x_k=x_K\) for all \(k\ge K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recurrence supports finite gap termination at exponent zero, but iterate termination additionally depends on a scheme-specific absorption property and no KL-rate source is cited.

children.title: Linear-Rate Regime
children.top_down_role: Desingularization settings associated with geometric local decay.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rate Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-type KL exponents up to one half yield geometric objective-gap decay under the stated recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\theta\le 1/2\), let \(0\le r_k\le R\) for all \(k\ge k_0\), and suppose \(r_k-r_{k+1}\ge\mu r_{k+1}^{2\theta}\) for all \(k\ge k_0\), where \(R>0\) and \(\mu>0\). Then \(r_{k+1}^{2\theta}\ge R^{2\theta-1}r_{k+1}\), so with \(\rho=(1+\mu R^{2\theta-1})^{-1}\in(0,1)\), one has \(r_k\le r_{k_0}\rho^{k-k_0}\). For \(0<\epsilon<r_{k_0}\), every \(k\) satisfying \(k-k_0\ge\left\lceil\log(r_{k_0}/\epsilon)/\log(1/\rho)\right\rceil\) therefore satisfies \(r_k\le\epsilon\); equivalently, that ceiling is an upper bound on the number of recurrence steps sufficient to attain the requested accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a KL exponent strictly above zero and at most one half, the objective gap contracts geometrically, so logarithmically many recurrence steps suffice to reach a prescribed positive accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With \(\rho=(1+\mu R^{2\theta-1})^{-1}\in(0,1)\), \(r_k\le r_{k_0}\rho^{k-k_0}\), and \(O(\!\log(1/\epsilon)\!)\) recurrence steps suffice for \(r_k\le\epsilon\).

children.title: Strong-Regime Transition
children.top_down_role: Boundary between finite termination and asymptotic linear behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Regime Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The power-KL recurrence changes character at exponents zero and one half.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the recurrence \(r_k-r_{k+1}\ge\mu r_{k+1}^{2\theta}\) for a nonnegative objective gap. At \(\theta=0\), the right-hand side is constant whenever the next gap is positive, yielding finite termination. For \(0<\theta\le1/2\), boundedness of \(r_k\) converts \(r_{k+1}^{2\theta}\) into a positive multiple of \(r_{k+1}\), yielding geometric decay. For \(1/2<\theta<1\), this conversion fails near zero and the natural bound becomes polynomial, \(r_k=O(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)})\). Thus \(\theta=1/2\) is the linear-to-sublinear transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponent zero gives termination, exponents through one half give linear decay, and larger exponents give polynomial decay.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rate regimes are finite for \(\theta=0\), geometric for \(0<\theta\le1/2\), and polynomial for \(1/2<\theta<1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property and its exponent thresholds fit the transition leaf, but the KL recurrence classification and polynomial rate have no supporting citation.

children.title: Sublinear-Rate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Weaker exponent regimes producing polynomial decay.

knowledge_statements.title: Sublinear-Rate Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-type KL exponents above one half produce polynomial objective decay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1/2<\theta<1\), and let the nonnegative, nonincreasing sequence \((r_k)\) satisfy \(r_k-r_{k+1}\ge\mu r_{k+1}^{2\theta}\) for all \(k\ge k_0\). Then there exists \(C>0\), depending on \(r_{k_0}\), \(\mu\), and \(\theta\), such that \(r_k\le C(k-k_0+1)^{-1/(2\theta-1)}\). Hence objective-gap accuracy \(r_k\le\epsilon\) is attained after \(O(\epsilon^{-(2\theta-1)})\) recurrence steps. The exponent deteriorates continuously as \(\theta\) approaches one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Above KL exponent one half, the objective gap decays polynomially, with complexity determined by the exponent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_k=O(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)})\), with objective-gap complexity \(O(\epsilon^{-(2\theta-1)})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the topic and the recurrence yields the stated polynomial order, but no authoritative KL-rate source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Observable Rate Conversion Interface
children.top_down_role: Conversion between convergence observables.

children.title: Iterate Rates
children.top_down_role: Convergence speed measured through distance between iterates and limiting points.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterate Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A KL tail bound converts objective-gap decay into distance-to-limit decay.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x_k\to x_\star\) and the KL finite-length estimate gives \(\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert\le C r_k^{1-\theta}\), where \(r_k=f(x_k)-f(x_\star)\). If \(0<\theta\le1/2\) and \(r_k\le C_0\rho^k\) for some \(\rho\in(0,1)\), then \(\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert=O(\rho^{(1-\theta)k})\). If \(1/2<\theta<1\) and \(r_k=O(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)})\), then \(\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert=O(k^{-(1-\theta)/(2\theta-1)})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The KL tail estimate turns geometric or polynomial objective decay into corresponding rates for distance from the limiting iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterate rate is geometric for \(0<\theta\le1/2\) and \(O(k^{-(1-\theta)/(2\theta-1)})\) for \(1/2<\theta<1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional rate conversion is algebraically consistent, but the asserted KL distance-tail estimate requires an authoritative source and precise framework.

children.title: Objective-Value Rates
children.top_down_role: Convergence speed measured through objective-value gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Value Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The canonical KL gap recurrence directly determines objective-value convergence rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_k=f(x_k)-f_\star\ge0\) and assume that eventually \(r_k-r_{k+1}\ge\mu r_{k+1}^{2\theta}\), with \(\mu>0\) and \(0\le\theta<1\). Then \(\theta=0\) gives \(r_k=0\) after finitely many steps; \(0<\theta\le1/2\) gives \(r_k\le C\rho^k\) for some \(C>0\) and \(\rho\in(0,1)\); and \(1/2<\theta<1\) gives \(r_k\le Ck^{-1/(2\theta-1)}\). These are rates for objective values, independent of any additional error bound converting gaps into iterate distances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The KL recurrence yields finite, geometric, or polynomial objective-gap decay according to the power exponent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective gaps terminate for \(\theta=0\), decay geometrically for \(0<\theta\le1/2\), and decay as \(O(k^{-1/(2\theta-1)})\) for \(1/2<\theta<1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind and three objective-gap regimes fit the leaf, but the canonical recurrence and rate classification are uncited.

children.title: Residual Rates
children.top_down_role: Convergence speed measured through slopes, subgradients, or algorithmic residuals.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Rates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative error and decrement bounds convert KL objective rates into stationarity-residual rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_k=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x_k))\), and suppose \(q_k\le B\sqrt{r_{k-1}-r_k}+\varepsilon_k\). If \(1/2<\theta<1\), \(r_{k-1}-r_k=O(k^{-2\theta/(2\theta-1)})\), and \(\varepsilon_k=O(k^{-\theta/(2\theta-1)})\), then \(q_k=O(k^{-\theta/(2\theta-1)})\). In a geometric regime, if \(r_{k-1}-r_k=O(\rho^k)\) and \(\varepsilon_k=O(\rho^{k/2})\) for \(\rho\in(0,1)\), then \(q_k=O(\rho^{k/2})\). Thus residual rates require both objective-decrement and inexactness control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity residuals inherit polynomial or geometric rates from objective decrements only when additive inexactness decays at least as quickly.
assumptions_latex: The additive residual \(\varepsilon_k\) has the stated rate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_k=O(k^{-\theta/(2\theta-1)})\) in the sublinear regime, or \(q_k=O(\rho^{k/2})\) under the stated geometric bounds.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated conclusions follow conditionally from the displayed decrement and error rates, but the residual inequality and its connection to the KL framework lack an authoritative source.

children.title: Observable Rate Conversion
children.top_down_role: Transfer of rate information among iterate, value, and residual observables.

assumptions_latex: The nonnegative sequences \(g_k\), \(d_k\), and \(r_k\) represent objective gap, distance to the limiting solution set, and residual, respectively.
For all sufficiently large \(k\), \(d_k\leq C_g g_k^{\alpha}\) and \(r_k\leq C_r g_k^{\beta}\), where \(C_g,C_r>0\) and \(\alpha,\beta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any established objective-gap estimate transfers by monotone substitution: \[g_k\leq \rho_k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad d_k\leq C_g\rho_k^{\alpha},\qquad r_k\leq C_r\rho_k^{\beta}.\] Thus \(g_k=O(k^{-q})\) gives \(d_k=O(k^{-\alpha q})\) and \(r_k=O(k^{-\beta q})\), while \(g_k=O(\tau^k)\), with \(0<\tau<1\), gives \(d_k=O(\tau^{\alpha k})\) and \(r_k=O(\tau^{\beta k})\). The conversion is valid only for observables controlled by the stated local comparison inequalities.

notation.meaning: Distance of the iterate to the limiting solution set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts an objective-gap rate into distance and residual rates through explicit local comparison inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(g_k,d_k,r_k\geq0\) and, eventually, \(d_k\leq C_g g_k^{\alpha}\) and \(r_k\leq C_r g_k^{\beta}\). For every nonnegative comparison sequence \(\rho_k\) satisfying \(g_k\leq\rho_k\), monotonicity of positive powers yields \[d_k\leq C_g\rho_k^{\alpha},\qquad r_k\leq C_r\rho_k^{\beta}.\] In particular, polynomial and geometric gap rates are converted by multiplying the corresponding exponent by \(\alpha\) or \(\beta\). No converse conversion follows unless reverse comparison inequalities are also available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power-type comparison inequalities convert objective-gap rates into iterate-distance and residual rates by multiplying polynomial or geometric exponents.
knowledge_statements.title: Observable Rate Conversion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conversion principle is mathematically correct under the stated power-comparison inequalities and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source or explicit standard-field rationale supports the nontrivial rate-conversion claim.
